parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed when 3.0 kg of charcoal (assume pure carbon) burns completely.
parts.answer: 11 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen used.
parts.answer: 8.0 kg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Burning charcoal in a closed room can produce a poisonous gas. Name the gas and state why it forms.
parts.answer: carbon monoxide; incomplete combustion / not enough oxygen
parts.working: B1 carbon monoxide; B1 limited oxygen supply

practice.stem: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂   [Ar: C, 12; O, 16; Fe, 56]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of iron, in tonnes, that can be made from 8.0 tonnes of iron(III) oxide.
parts.answer: 5.6 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon monoxide needed to react with 8.0 tonnes of iron(III) oxide.
parts.answer: 4.2 tonnes

practice.stem:
2.4 g of magnesium is added to a solution containing 0.15 mol of hydrochloric acid.
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂   [Ar: Mg, 24; Cl, 35.5]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of magnesium in 2.4 g.
parts.answer: 0.10 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show which reactant is in excess.
parts.answer: Magnesium is in excess: 0.10 mol Mg needs 0.20 mol HCl, but only 0.15 mol HCl is present.
parts.working: M1 compare 0.10 mol Mg needing 0.20 mol HCl (or 0.15 mol HCl needs 0.075 mol Mg); A1 Mg in excess

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of magnesium chloride formed.
parts.answer: 7.13 g (allow 7.1 g)

practice.stem:
A student makes blue copper(II) sulfate crystals by adding 4.00 g of copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid, then filtering and crystallising.
CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O   [Ar: H, 1; O, 16; S, 32; Cu, 64]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of copper(II) oxide used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sulfuric acid needed to react with all of the copper(II) oxide.
parts.working: 1 : 1 so 0.0500 mol H₂SO₄ (M1); Mr 98 so 4.90 g (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals, CuSO₄·5H₂O, that can be obtained.

practice.stem:
2.7 g of aluminium foil is heated in 7.1 g of dry chlorine gas.
2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃   [Ar: Al, 27; Cl, 35.5]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of aluminium and of chlorine at the start.
parts.answer: Al 0.100 mol; Cl₂ 0.100 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that chlorine is the limiting reactant.
parts.answer: 0.100 mol Al needs 0.150 mol Cl₂, but only 0.100 mol is present

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of aluminium chloride formed. [Mr: AlCl₃, 133.5]

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the mass of aluminium left unreacted.

practice.stem:
A camping stove used by trekkers in the northern areas runs on a small cylinder containing 1.16 kg of butane.
2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O   [Ar: H, 1; C, 12; O, 16]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of butane in 1.16 kg. [Mr: C₄H₁₀, 58]
parts.answer: 20 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide released, in kg, when the whole cylinder is burned completely.
parts.working: 2 : 8 ratio so 80 mol CO₂ (M1); 80 × 44 = 3520 g = 3.52 kg (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water formed, in kg.

practice.stem:
4.20 g of the carbonate of a Group II metal M is heated until there is no further change in mass. 2.00 g of the metal oxide remains.
MCO₃ → MO + CO₂   [Ar: C, 12; O, 16]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide given off and the number of moles of carbon dioxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the relative formula mass of MCO₃.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the relative atomic mass of M and identify M.
parts.answer: 24; magnesium

parts.label: d
parts.text: Check your answer by calculating the expected mass of the oxide MO.

practice.stem:
Blue copper(II) nitrate decomposes on heating to leave black copper(II) oxide.
2Cu(NO₃)₂ → 2CuO + 4NO₂ + O₂
3.76 g of copper(II) nitrate is heated until there is no further change. [Ar: N, 14; O, 16; Cu, 64]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of copper(II) nitrate heated. [Mr: Cu(NO₃)₂, 188]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of copper(II) oxide left in the tube.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the masses of nitrogen dioxide and of oxygen given off, and show that together they account for the loss in mass.

practice.stem: 1.20 g of a Group II metal X is burned in chlorine. 4.75 g of the chloride XCl₂ is formed. [Ar: Cl, 35.5]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chlorine that combined with the metal and the number of moles of chlorine atoms.
parts.answer: 3.55 g; 0.100 mol Cl atoms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the number of moles of X and its relative atomic mass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify X.
parts.answer: magnesium

practice.stem: In a sulfuric acid plant, sulfur is burned to sulfur dioxide, which is converted to sulfur trioxide and then to sulfuric acid. Overall one mole of sulfur gives one mole of sulfuric acid. [Ar: H, 1; O, 16; S, 32]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write one overall equation, starting from sulfur, oxygen and water, for making sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: 2S + 3O₂ + 2H₂O → 2H₂SO₄ (or S + 1½O₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₄)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of sulfuric acid, in tonnes, that can be made from 64 tonnes of sulfur. [Mr: H₂SO₄, 98]
parts.answer: 196 tonnes
parts.working: 64 t ÷ 32 = 2.0 × 10⁶ mol S → 2.0 × 10⁶ mol H₂SO₄ (M1); × 98 = 196 t (A1). Or by ratio 32 t → 98 t.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen, in tonnes, used in the process.
parts.answer: 96 tonnes
parts.working: 1.5 mol O₂ per mol S → 3.0 × 10⁶ mol (M1); × 32 = 96 t (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the formula of aluminium sulfate?
A AlSO₄
B Al₂SO₄
C Al₃(SO₄)₂
D Al₂(SO₄)₃
parts.answer: D Al₂(SO₄)₃
parts.working: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻: two Al³⁺ (+6) balance three SO₄²⁻ (−6), so Al₂(SO₄)₃. C swaps the numbers.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Balance the equation for the reduction of iron(III) oxide in a blast furnace:
…Fe₂O₃ + …CO → …Fe + …CO₂
parts.answer: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Balance the equation for the complete combustion of propane, a gas in LPG cylinders:
…C₃H₈ + …O₂ → …CO₂ + …H₂O
parts.answer: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the balanced equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
parts.working: B1 correct balanced formulae; B1 state symbols

practice.stem: Use the charges on the ions to write the formula of each compound.

parts.label: a
parts.text: lithium oxide
parts.answer: Li₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: magnesium nitride
parts.answer: Mg₃N₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: zinc carbonate
parts.answer: ZnCO₃

parts.label: d
parts.text: ammonium carbonate
parts.answer: (NH₄)₂CO₃
parts.working: two NH₄⁺ balance one CO₃²⁻; brackets needed

practice.stem: Write a balanced symbol equation for each reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium burns in chlorine to form sodium chloride.
parts.answer: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calcium reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide and hydrogen.
parts.answer: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂

practice.stem: Balance each equation by writing numbers in the spaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: …Al + …O₂ → …Al₂O₃
parts.answer: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: …Na + …H₂O → …NaOH + …H₂
parts.answer: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: …C₂H₆ + …O₂ → …CO₂ + …H₂O (complete combustion of ethane)
parts.answer: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the neutralisation of any acid by any alkali.
parts.answer: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aqueous silver nitrate is added to aqueous sodium chloride. Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction.
parts.answer: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Aqueous barium chloride is added to aqueous sodium sulfate. Write the ionic equation and name the spectator ions.
parts.answer: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s); spectator ions: Na⁺ and Cl⁻
parts.working: B1 equation; B1 both spectator ions

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula of ammonium phosphate, which contains NH₄⁺ and PO₄³⁻ ions.
parts.answer: (NH₄)₃PO₄

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the formula of iron(III) hydroxide.
parts.answer: Fe(OH)₃

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the formula of calcium nitrate.
parts.answer: Ca(NO₃)₂

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calcium carbonate reacts with dilute nitric acid. Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to aqueous iron(II) sulfate. A green precipitate forms. Which is the ionic equation for this reaction?
A Fe²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s)
B Fe²⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → FeOH(s)
C FeSO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s) + Na₂SO₄(aq)
D Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s)
parts.answer: A Fe²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s)
parts.working: Iron(II) ions need two hydroxide ions; Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻ are spectator ions. C is a full equation, not an ionic one; D is for iron(III), which gives a red-brown precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation, with state symbols, for the thermal decomposition of solid zinc carbonate.
parts.answer: ZnCO₃(s) → ZnO(s) + CO₂(g)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aqueous lead(II) nitrate is added to aqueous potassium iodide and a bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide forms. Write the ionic equation, with state symbols.
parts.answer: Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → PbI₂(s)
parts.working: B1 balanced ionic equation; B1 state symbols

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the spectator ions in the reaction in (b).
parts.answer: potassium ions (K⁺) and nitrate ions (NO₃⁻)

practice.stem: Write the formula of each compound.

parts.label: a
parts.text: chromium(III) sulfate
parts.answer: Cr₂(SO₄)₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: tin(IV) oxide
parts.answer: SnO₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: copper(I) oxide
parts.answer: Cu₂O

parts.label: d
parts.text: vanadium(V) oxide
parts.answer: V₂O₅

parts.label: e
parts.text: State what the Roman numeral in a name such as tin(IV) oxide tells you.
parts.answer: the oxidation number (charge) of the metal in the compound

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of atoms shown in one formula unit of ammonium phosphate, (NH₄)₃PO₄.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of atoms shown in one formula unit of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the ratio of aluminium ions to sulfate ions in aluminium sulfate and explain it using the charges.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Ammonia reacts with sulfuric acid to make the fertiliser ammonium sulfate. Write the balanced equation.
parts.answer: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zinc powder is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction.
parts.answer: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
parts.working: B1 correct species; B1 state symbols

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the spectator ion in (a).
parts.answer: sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Chlorine gas is bubbled into aqueous potassium bromide. Write the ionic equation.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of any carbonate ion with dilute acid.
parts.answer: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O

practice.stem: Scrap aluminium cans are dropped into blue aqueous copper(II) sulfate. A red-brown solid forms and the blue colour fades.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of aluminium with aqueous copper(II) ions.
parts.answer: 2Al(s) + 3Cu²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Cu(s)
parts.working: B1 species; B1 balanced (atoms and charge) with state symbols

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the total charge is the same on both sides of your equation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of magnesium with any dilute acid.
parts.answer: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of ammonium chloride with sodium hydroxide on warming.
parts.answer: NH₄Cl + NaOH → NaCl + NH₃ + H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: In some power stations, sulfur dioxide in waste gases is removed by reacting it with calcium oxide to form calcium sulfite, CaSO₃. Write the equation.
parts.answer: CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the type of oxide, why calcium oxide removes sulfur dioxide.
parts.answer: CaO is a basic oxide; SO₂ is an acidic oxide; they react (neutralise) to form a salt

practice.stem: 0.10 mol of an iron oxide, FeₓOᵧ, is completely reduced by carbon monoxide. 0.40 mol of CO is used, and 0.30 mol of iron and 0.40 mol of carbon dioxide are produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the mole data to deduce the simplest mole ratio of oxide : CO : Fe : CO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the number of iron atoms and oxygen atoms in one formula unit of the oxide, and write its formula.
parts.answer: 3 Fe and 4 O; Fe₃O₄
parts.working: 3 Fe on right so 3 Fe in oxide (M1); 4CO₂ has 8 O, 4CO supplies 4 O, so oxide supplies 4 O (M1); Fe₃O₄ (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the balanced equation.
parts.answer: Fe₃O₄ + 4CO → 3Fe + 4CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the volume of 0.25 mol of oxygen gas at room temperature and pressure? [molar volume = 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
A 0.25 dm³
B 6.0 dm³
C 24 dm³
D 96 dm³
parts.answer: B 6.0 dm³
parts.working: V = 0.25 × 24 = 6.0 dm³. D divides 24 by 0.25 instead of multiplying.

practice.stem: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂   [Ar: Mg, 24; one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of magnesium in 0.48 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³, formed at room temperature and pressure when 0.48 g of magnesium reacts with excess acid.
parts.answer: 480 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which sample of gas has the largest volume at room temperature and pressure? [Ar: H, 1; C, 12; N, 14; O, 16]
A 1.0 g of hydrogen, H₂
B 32 g of oxygen, O₂
C 14 g of nitrogen, N₂
D 4.4 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂
parts.answer: B 32 g of oxygen, O₂
parts.working: Moles: H₂ 0.50, O₂ 1.0, N₂ 0.50, CO₂ 0.10. Equal moles of gas occupy equal volumes, so 1.0 mol O₂ (24 dm³) is largest. A is a trap: hydrogen is the lightest gas, but 1.0 g is only 0.50 mol.

practice.stem: [One mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.)]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles in 4.8 dm³ of methane at r.t.p.
parts.answer: 0.20 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of 600 cm³ of carbon dioxide at r.t.p. [Mr: CO₂, 44]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume, in cm³, occupied by 0.16 g of oxygen, O₂, at r.t.p. [Ar: O, 16]
parts.answer: 120 cm³

practice.stem:
Some antacid powders contain magnesium carbonate, which reacts with excess stomach acid.
MgCO₃ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of magnesium carbonate in 1.68 g. [Mr: MgCO₃, 84]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide, in cm³ at r.t.p., produced when 1.68 g reacts with excess acid. [molar volume 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
parts.answer: 480 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this antacid can make a person burp.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide gas is produced in the stomach

practice.stem:
Zinc granules react with dilute sulfuric acid.
Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of zinc in 0.65 g. [Ar: Zn, 65]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³ at r.t.p., formed with excess acid. [molar volume 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
parts.answer: 240 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name a piece of apparatus that could be used to measure this volume of gas.
parts.answer: gas syringe (or upturned measuring cylinder / burette over water)

practice.stem:
50 cm³ of methane from a Sui gas supply is burned completely in 150 cm³ of oxygen. All volumes are measured at room temperature and pressure.
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen that reacts with 50 cm³ of methane.
parts.answer: 100 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed.
parts.answer: 50 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of gas left at the end, measured at room temperature and pressure, and state what it contains.
parts.answer: 100 cm³: 50 cm³ of carbon dioxide and 50 cm³ of unreacted oxygen (water is a liquid at r.t.p.)
parts.working: M1 excess O₂ = 150 − 100 = 50 cm³; A1 total 100 cm³ (CO₂ + O₂)

practice.stem:
Ammonia is made at fertiliser plants from nitrogen and hydrogen. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of nitrogen that reacts exactly with 30 dm³ of hydrogen.
parts.answer: 10 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of ammonia formed if the reaction were complete.
parts.answer: 20 dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: In practice only 15% of the hydrogen is converted. Calculate the volume of ammonia formed.
parts.answer: 3.0 dm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why equal volumes of gases can be used directly in place of moles.
parts.answer: equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules/moles

practice.stem:
A car airbag inflates when sodium azide decomposes very quickly.
2NaN₃ → 2Na + 3N₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of nitrogen in 72 dm³ at r.t.p. [molar volume 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
parts.answer: 3.0 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium azide needed to produce 72 dm³ of nitrogen. [Mr: NaN₃, 65]
parts.working: 2 mol NaN₃ → 3 mol N₂ so 2.0 mol NaN₃ (M1); 2.0 × 65 = 130 g (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium formed. [Ar: Na, 23]

practice.stem:
A student adds a short length of magnesium ribbon to excess dilute hydrochloric acid in a conical flask connected to a gas syringe. The syringe reading rises from 0 to 96 cm³. [molar volume 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of hydrogen collected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of magnesium that reacted. [Ar: Mg, 24]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 1.00 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid that reacted with this magnesium, in cm³.
parts.answer: 8.0 cm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: The student's syringe reading may be too low. Suggest one reason.
parts.answer: gas escaped before the bung was replaced / leaking connection / syringe plunger sticks

practice.stem:
A hair-bleach solution contains hydrogen peroxide. 50.0 cm³ of the solution is completely decomposed using a little manganese(IV) oxide. 180 cm³ of oxygen is collected at room temperature and pressure.
2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of oxygen produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the hydrogen peroxide solution in mol/dm³.
parts.answer: 0.30 mol/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration in g/dm³. [Mr: H₂O₂, 34]
parts.answer: 10.2 g/dm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the role of the manganese(IV) oxide.
parts.answer: catalyst

practice.stem:
20 cm³ of ethene is burned completely in 100 cm³ of oxygen. All volumes are measured at r.t.p.
C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen used and the volume of oxygen left over.
parts.answer: 60 cm³ used; 40 cm³ left

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed.
parts.answer: 40 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the total volume of gas remaining after cooling to r.t.p.
parts.answer: 80 cm³
parts.working: 40 cm³ O₂ + 40 cm³ CO₂; water is a liquid at r.t.p. so its volume is ignored

parts.label: d
parts.text: The remaining gas is shaken with aqueous sodium hydroxide. State the final volume and name the gas left.
parts.answer: 40 cm³ of oxygen
parts.working: NaOH absorbs the acidic CO₂ (M1); 40 cm³ oxygen (A1)

practice.stem: 10 cm³ of a gaseous hydrocarbon, CₓHᵧ, is burned completely in 60 cm³ of oxygen (an excess). After cooling to r.t.p. the volume of gas is 45 cm³. After passing through aqueous sodium hydroxide, 15 cm³ of oxygen remains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the volume of carbon dioxide formed and the volume of oxygen that reacted.
parts.answer: CO₂ 30 cm³; O₂ used 45 cm³
parts.working: CO₂ = 45 − 15 = 30 cm³ (B1); O₂ left 15 so used 60 − 15 = 45 cm³ (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce x, the number of carbon atoms in one molecule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce y and give the molecular formula of the hydrocarbon.
parts.answer: y = 6; C₃H₆

practice.stem:
0.60 g of a Group II metal, M, reacts completely with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. 360 cm³ of hydrogen is collected at r.t.p. [molar volume 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
M + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of hydrogen produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the relative atomic mass of M.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify M and predict how its reaction with water compares with that of magnesium.
parts.answer: calcium; reacts faster/more vigorously with cold water than magnesium
parts.working: B1 calcium; B1 more reactive (down Group II)

practice.stem:
0.12 g of magnesium is added to 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. [molar volume 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of magnesium and of hydrochloric acid at the start. [Ar: Mg, 24]
parts.answer: Mg 0.00500 mol; HCl 0.00500 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show which reactant is limiting.
parts.answer: hydrochloric acid
parts.working: 0.00500 mol Mg needs 0.0100 mol HCl, only 0.00500 mol present

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³ at r.t.p., produced.
parts.answer: 60 cm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: A student predicted 120 cm³. Explain the mistake.
parts.answer: the student assumed all the magnesium reacted (used Mg moles), but the acid runs out first

practice.stem: A sample of a hydrocarbon contains 2.4 g of carbon and 0.6 g of hydrogen. [Ar: H, 1; C, 12]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of the hydrocarbon.
parts.answer: CH₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: The relative molecular mass is 30. Deduce the molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₂H₆

practice.stem: A sample of an oxide of nitrogen contains 1.4 g of nitrogen and 3.2 g of oxygen. [Ar: N, 14; O, 16]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of the oxide.
parts.answer: NO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: The relative molecular mass of the oxide is 92. Deduce its molecular formula.
parts.answer: N₂O₄

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the empirical formula of a compound.
parts.answer: the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in the compound

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the empirical formula of: (i) glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆; (ii) ethene, C₂H₄; (iii) hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂.
parts.answer: (i) CH₂O (ii) CH₂ (iii) HO

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of a compound whose molecular and empirical formulae are the same.
parts.answer: e.g. H₂O, CO₂, CH₄

practice.stem:
A student heats magnesium ribbon in a crucible with a lid.
mass of empty crucible + lid = 24.18 g
mass of crucible + lid + magnesium = 24.54 g
mass of crucible + lid + magnesium oxide = 24.78 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen that combined with the magnesium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of magnesium oxide. [Ar: O, 16; Mg, 24]
parts.answer: MgO

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the lid of the crucible is lifted from time to time during heating.
parts.answer: to let air (oxygen) in while preventing loss of magnesium oxide smoke

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which change does NOT increase the rate of this reaction?
A raising the temperature of the acid
B using magnesium powder instead of ribbon
C using more concentrated acid
D using larger pieces of magnesium
parts.answer: D using larger pieces of magnesium
parts.working: Larger pieces have a smaller surface area, so collisions are less frequent and the rate falls. Powder (B) increases surface area and rate.

practice.stem: Zinc granules react with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect on the rate of reaction of using more concentrated hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: The rate increases (the reaction is faster).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain this effect in terms of particles.
parts.answer: There are more acid particles in the same volume, so collisions between particles are more frequent (more collisions per second).
parts.working: B1 more particles per unit volume; B1 higher collision frequency

practice.stem: A student follows the rate of reaction of marble chips with dilute hydrochloric acid by measuring the decrease in mass of the flask every 30 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the apparatus used to measure the mass of the flask and its contents.
parts.answer: (top-pan) balance

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a cotton-wool plug is put in the neck of the flask.
parts.answer: It lets gas escape but stops acid spray / liquid being lost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept the same if the experiment is repeated with smaller marble chips.
parts.answer: Any two of: mass of marble; volume of acid; concentration of acid; temperature.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe one other way of following the rate of this reaction.
parts.answer: Collect the CO₂ in a gas syringe and measure its volume at regular time intervals.

practice.stem: A student mixes different concentrations of sodium thiosulfate solution with the same volume of dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask standing on a paper marked with a cross. She measures how long it takes for the cross to disappear from view.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the independent variable and the dependent variable in this experiment.
parts.answer: independent: concentration of sodium thiosulfate; dependent: time for the cross to disappear

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the time taken is related to the rate of the reaction.
parts.answer: The shorter the time, the faster the rate (rate is proportional to 1/time).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way to make the experiment a fair test.
parts.answer: Keep the temperature / volume of acid / concentration of acid / total volume / the same cross the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Zinc reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. Why does the rate of reaction decrease as the reaction goes on?
A The activation energy increases.
B The concentration of the acid decreases.
C The temperature of the mixture increases.
D The zinc becomes a catalyst.
parts.answer: B The concentration of the acid decreases.
parts.working: As acid particles are used up their concentration falls, so collisions become less frequent. A rise in temperature would speed the reaction up, not slow it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction?
A It gives the particles more kinetic energy.
B It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy.
C It increases the concentration of the reactants.
D It makes the reaction more exothermic.
parts.answer: B It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy.
parts.working: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful. A describes the effect of heating, not of a catalyst.

practice.stem: Sodium thiosulfate solution reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the rate of this reaction. Use ideas about particles and collisions.
parts.answer: Rate increases. Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide more frequently; a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so there are more successful collisions per second.
parts.working: B1 rate increases; B1 particles have more kinetic energy / move faster; B1 more frequent collisions; B1 greater proportion of collisions with energy ≥ activation energy

practice.stem:
Marble chips (calcium carbonate) react with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The carbon dioxide is collected in a gas syringe.
Time / s: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100
Volume / cm³: 0, 46, 74, 90, 98, 100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of reaction between 0 s and 20 s, in cm³/s.
parts.answer: 2.3 cm³/s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate between 40 s and 60 s.
parts.answer: 0.8 cm³/s

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate decreases as the reaction proceeds.
parts.answer: The acid is used up so its concentration decreases; collisions become less frequent.
parts.working: B1 concentration of acid (reactant) decreases; B1 fewer collisions per second

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest the total volume of gas that would be collected if the experiment were left to finish.
parts.answer: about 100 cm³ (reaction almost complete)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why fine coal dust in the air of a coal mine in Balochistan can explode when a spark occurs, but a lump of coal burns slowly.
parts.answer: Dust has a much larger surface area (per unit mass); more coal particles are exposed to oxygen, so collisions are much more frequent; the reaction is so fast that heat and gas are released almost instantly (explosion).
parts.working: B1 larger surface area; B1 more frequent collisions with oxygen; B1 very fast reaction / rapid release of energy

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one other industry where fine powders could cause an explosion.
parts.answer: flour mills (or sugar / custard powder / sawmills)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could show that the manganese(IV) oxide is unchanged in mass at the end.
parts.answer: Weigh the manganese(IV) oxide before; after the reaction filter the mixture to collect the solid; wash and dry it, then weigh again; the mass is the same.
parts.working: B1 weigh before; B1 filter, wash and dry; B1 reweigh, same mass

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student repeats the experiment with the same mass of manganese(IV) oxide as a fine powder instead of granules. State and explain the effect on the rate.
parts.answer: The rate increases because the powder has a larger surface area, so more collisions happen at the catalyst surface per second.
parts.working: B1 faster; B1 larger surface area / more frequent collisions

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Excess calcium carbonate chips react with 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. The experiment is repeated at the same temperature with 100 cm³ of 0.50 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. How do the initial rate and the total volume of carbon dioxide compare with the first experiment?
A initial rate faster; total volume larger
B initial rate slower; total volume the same
C initial rate slower; total volume smaller
D initial rate the same; total volume larger
parts.answer: B initial rate slower; total volume the same
parts.working: Both acids contain 0.050 mol HCl, so the same volume of CO₂ forms; the second acid is less concentrated, so collisions are less frequent and the initial rate is slower. Option D wrongly assumes the larger volume of acid gives more gas.

practice.stem:
0.50 g of calcium carbonate lumps is added to 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid.
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂   [Mr: CaCO₃, 100; molar volume 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the acid is in excess and calculate the volume of carbon dioxide produced at r.t.p.
parts.answer: 120 cm³
parts.working: CaCO₃ = 0.50 ÷ 100 = 0.0050 mol, needs 0.010 mol HCl; HCl present = 0.050 mol, so in excess M1; CO₂ = 0.0050 mol M1; × 24 000 = 120 cm³ A1

parts.label: b
parts.text:
For each change, state how the initial rate and the final volume of gas compare with the original experiment.
(i) 0.50 g of powdered calcium carbonate is used.
(ii) 50 cm³ of 0.50 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid is used.
(iii) 1.00 g of calcium carbonate lumps is used.
parts.answer: (i) faster, same volume (120 cm³); (ii) slower, same volume (120 cm³, acid still in excess); (iii) faster or similar rate, double volume (240 cm³)
parts.working: B1 each; in (ii) 0.025 mol HCl still exceeds the 0.010 mol needed; in (iii) acid still in excess (0.020 needed), so 0.010 mol CO₂ = 240 cm³ (allow 'faster' as larger total surface area)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why increasing the pressure increases the rate of a reaction between two gases.
parts.answer: The same number of gas particles occupy a smaller volume (higher concentration), so collisions are more frequent.
parts.working: B1 particles closer together / more per unit volume; B1 more frequent collisions

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why food kept in a refrigerator goes bad more slowly than food left in a hot kitchen in Hyderabad in summer.
parts.answer: At low temperature the reacting particles (in the decay reactions) have less kinetic energy; fewer collisions per second have energy ≥ activation energy, so the rate of decay is lower.
parts.working: B1 less kinetic energy / move slower; B1 fewer successful collisions (fewer with energy ≥ Ea)

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says 'a catalyst increases the energy of the colliding particles'. Explain why this is wrong.
parts.answer: A catalyst does not change the particles' energy; it provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy, so more of the existing collisions are successful.
parts.working: B1 particle energy unchanged; B1 lower activation energy pathway

practice.stem:
0.12 g of magnesium ribbon reacts completely with excess dilute sulfuric acid in 40 s.
Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂   [Ar: Mg, 24; molar volume 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at r.t.p.
parts.answer: 120 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of reaction in cm³ of hydrogen per second.
parts.answer: 3.0 cm³/s

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate in moles of magnesium used per second.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the rate in the first 10 seconds is greater than the mean rate.
parts.answer: The acid concentration is highest at the start, so collisions are most frequent then.

practice.stem: A food-processing company in Multan studies how temperature affects the rate of a reaction that spoils cooking oil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A reaction takes 240 s at 20 °C. Assuming the rate doubles for every 10 °C rise, calculate the time taken at 50 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles and energy, why a rise in temperature increases the rate.
parts.answer: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide more often; a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or above the activation energy; so more successful collisions per second.
parts.working: B1 faster particles / more frequent collisions; B1 more particles with energy ≥ activation energy; B1 more successful collisions per unit time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rule 'rate doubles every 10 °C' does not mean the yield of product doubles.
parts.answer: Temperature changes how fast product forms, not how much; the amount depends on the quantity of limiting reactant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement is correct for a reversible reaction at equilibrium in a closed system?
A The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped.
B The concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
C The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.
D Only the forward reaction is taking place.
parts.answer: C The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.
parts.working: At dynamic equilibrium both reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant. B is a common error: concentrations are constant, not necessarily equal.

practice.stem: CoCl₂·6H₂O ⇌ CoCl₂ + 6H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the meaning of the symbol ⇌.
parts.answer: The reaction is reversible.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is seen when pink hydrated cobalt(II) chloride is heated, and what is seen when water is then added to the product.
parts.answer: It turns blue on heating; adding water turns it pink again.
parts.working: B1 pink → blue; B1 blue → pink

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by a closed system.
parts.answer: No substances can enter or leave (reactants and products cannot escape).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen when blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals are heated.
parts.answer: They turn white (and steam/water is given off).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is seen when water is added to the white solid, and state whether this change is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: It turns blue; exothermic (it gets hot).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Complete the equation: CuSO₄·5H₂O ⇌ ……… + ………
parts.answer: CuSO₄ + 5H₂O

parts.label: d
parts.text: State how this reaction is used as a chemical test.
parts.answer: White anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns blue when water is present (test for water).

practice.stem: A student heats some ammonium chloride in a boiling tube. The white solid disappears from the bottom of the tube and a white solid forms again near the cooler top.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the decomposition of ammonium chloride, using the reversible sign.
parts.answer: NH₄Cl ⇌ NH₃ + HCl

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why white solid forms again near the top of the tube.
parts.answer: The gases ammonia and hydrogen chloride cool near the top of the tube and react together to re-form ammonium chloride.
parts.working: B1 gases cool; B1 recombine (reverse reaction).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this is a reversible reaction but the mixture in the open tube does not reach equilibrium.
parts.answer: The tube is open, so gases escape; equilibrium needs a closed system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of a system in dynamic equilibrium.
parts.answer: The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal; the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant (in a closed system).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Inside a sealed bottle of fizzy drink: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq). When the bottle is opened, bubbles appear. Explain why.
parts.answer: Opening lowers the pressure of CO₂ gas above the liquid; equilibrium shifts left, so dissolved CO₂ comes out as gas.
parts.working: B1 pressure decreases; B1 equilibrium moves to the left/gas side.

practice.stem:
A sealed glass tube contains an equilibrium mixture of colourless dinitrogen tetroxide and brown nitrogen dioxide.
N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)   the forward reaction is endothermic

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sealed tube is placed in hot water. State and explain what happens to the colour of the gas.
parts.answer: It becomes darker brown; the forward reaction is endothermic, so increasing temperature moves the position of equilibrium to the right (more NO₂).
parts.working: B1 darker; B1 equilibrium shifts in endothermic direction / to the right

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the position of equilibrium of increasing the pressure.
parts.answer: Moves to the left; there are fewer moles of gas on the left (1) than on the right (2).
parts.working: B1 left; B1 fewer gas molecules on left

practice.stem: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the position of equilibrium.
parts.answer: No change; there are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side (2 and 2).
parts.working: B1 no effect; B1 equal moles of gas

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of adding a catalyst on the position of equilibrium and on the time taken to reach equilibrium.
parts.answer: Position unchanged; equilibrium is reached more quickly.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The forward reaction is exothermic. State the effect of lowering the temperature on the amount of hydrogen iodide at equilibrium.
parts.answer: It increases.
parts.working: B1 (equilibrium shifts to the exothermic direction)

practice.stem:
Ethanol is made industrially from ethene and steam at about 300 °C and 6000 kPa with a phosphoric acid catalyst.
C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the effect on the yield of ethanol of increasing the pressure. Explain.
parts.answer: Yield increases; there are fewer moles of gas on the right (1) than on the left (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The forward reaction is exothermic. State the effect on the yield of increasing the temperature.
parts.answer: Yield decreases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Unreacted ethene is separated and passed back through the reactor. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To increase the overall conversion / avoid waste of reactant and save cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g); the forward reaction is exothermic. Which change increases the equilibrium yield of SO₃?
A adding a catalyst
B decreasing the pressure
C increasing the pressure
D increasing the temperature
parts.answer: C increasing the pressure
parts.working: There are 3 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so higher pressure moves the equilibrium to the right. A catalyst only speeds up reaching equilibrium; a higher temperature favours the endothermic back reaction.

practice.stem:
Chromate ions and dichromate ions are in equilibrium in water:
2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
yellow                              orange

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dilute acid is added to the yellow solution. Predict the colour change and explain.
parts.answer: Yellow to orange; more H⁺ moves the equilibrium to the right, forming more Cr₂O₇²⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is then added. Predict the colour change and explain.
parts.answer: Orange to yellow; OH⁻ reacts with/removes H⁺, so equilibrium moves to the left.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this shows that the reaction is reversible.
parts.answer: The colour change can be made to go in both directions by changing conditions.

practice.stem:
Hydrogen for fertiliser factories is made from natural gas and steam:
CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g); the forward reaction is endothermic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the equilibrium yield of hydrogen.
parts.answer: Yield increases; the forward reaction is endothermic, so the equilibrium moves to the right to absorb heat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the equilibrium yield of hydrogen.
parts.answer: Yield decreases; there are more moles of gas on the right (4) than the left (2), so equilibrium moves to the left.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the process is carried out at a fairly low pressure even though high pressure would increase the rate.
parts.answer: Low pressure gives a higher yield (and is cheaper/safer).

practice.stem:
Methanol, used as a fuel, is made from carbon monoxide and hydrogen.
CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a high pressure is used.
parts.answer: There are fewer moles of gas on the right (1) than the left (3), so high pressure moves the equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield; it also increases the rate.
parts.working: B1 fewer gas moles on right / shifts right; B1 higher yield (allow faster rate)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The forward reaction is exothermic. Explain why a moderate temperature of about 250 °C is used rather than a much lower temperature.
parts.answer: A low temperature would give a higher yield because the equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction, but the rate would be too slow; 250 °C is a compromise giving an acceptable yield at a reasonable rate (a catalyst is also used).
parts.working: B1 lower T gives higher yield; B1 but rate too slow; B1 compromise between yield and rate

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of using a very high pressure.
parts.answer: Expensive equipment / energy costs / safety risk.

practice.stem:
A gaseous reaction X₂(g) + 3Y₂(g) ⇌ 2XY₃(g) is studied. The table shows the percentage of XY₃ at equilibrium.
At 200 atm: 300 °C 59%; 400 °C 34%; 500 °C 18%
At 400 °C: 100 atm 22%; 200 atm 34%; 300 atm 42%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Explain.
parts.answer: Exothermic: at constant pressure the yield decreases as the temperature increases, so equilibrium shifts left (the endothermic direction) on heating.
parts.working: B1 exothermic; B1 yield falls as temperature rises

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain the effect of pressure on the yield.
parts.answer: Yield increases with pressure because there are fewer moles of gas on the right (2) than on the left (4).
parts.working: B1 increases; B1 fewer gas moles on right

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the yield at 300 °C and 400 atm, choosing from: less than 40%, between 40% and 59%, more than 59%.
parts.answer: more than 59%
parts.working: B1 (yield at 300 °C is 59% at 200 atm and increases with pressure)

practice.stem: N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g); the forward reaction is endothermic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why nitrogen monoxide forms in car engines but hardly at all in the air at room temperature.
parts.answer: The forward reaction is endothermic, so high temperatures in the engine move equilibrium to the right (and speed up the reaction); at room temperature the equilibrium lies far to the left and the reaction is very slow.
parts.working: B1 endothermic favoured by high temperature; B1 rate/yield negligible at room temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect of increasing the pressure on the yield of nitrogen monoxide. Explain.
parts.answer: No effect; there are 2 moles of gas on each side.
parts.working: B1 no effect; B1 equal moles of gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Nitrogen monoxide is a pollutant. Name the device fitted to car exhausts that removes it.
parts.answer: Catalytic converter

practice.stem:
In a laboratory model of the Haber process, 1.00 mol of nitrogen and 3.00 mol of hydrogen are sealed in a vessel with a catalyst. At equilibrium 0.30 mol of ammonia is present.
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of nitrogen and of hydrogen left at equilibrium.
parts.answer: N₂ 0.85 mol; H₂ 2.55 mol
parts.working: M1 NH₃ 0.30 mol needs 0.15 mol N₂ and 0.45 mol H₂; A1 both values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of ammonia, by moles, in the equilibrium mixture. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mixture is described as dynamic even though the amounts no longer change.
parts.answer: Ammonia is still forming and decomposing, at equal rates.

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the oxidation number of sulfur in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
A −2
B +2
C +4
D +6
parts.working: x + 4(−2) = −2, so x = +6. C (+4) is sulfur in SO₂ or SO₃²⁻.

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define oxidation in terms of electrons.
parts.answer: Loss of electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define reduction in terms of oxygen.
parts.answer: Loss of oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Magnesium reacts with copper(II) sulfate solution: Mg + CuSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Cu. Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced. Explain using electrons.
parts.answer: Magnesium is oxidised because it loses electrons (Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻); copper(II) ions are reduced because they gain electrons (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu).
parts.working: B1 Mg oxidised; B1 Cu²⁺ reduced; B1 electron transfer explanation

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change is a reduction?
A Cl⁻ → Cl₂
B Cu²⁺ → Cu
C Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺
D Mg → Mg²⁺
parts.answer: B Cu²⁺ → Cu
parts.working: Cu²⁺ gains two electrons to become Cu, so it is reduced. The other three all lose electrons (oxidation); Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ is often mistaken because the charge 'changes' but the ion loses an electron.

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents
practice.stem: Zinc powder is added to blue aqueous copper(II) sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which substance is oxidised and explain in terms of electrons.
parts.answer: Zinc; it loses electrons (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe two observations.
parts.answer: Blue solution fades/becomes colourless; pink-brown solid (copper) forms on the zinc (and zinc dissolves / gets warm).

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents
practice.stem: Magnesium ribbon burns in air with a bright white flame: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the burning of magnesium is an oxidation, in terms of oxygen.
parts.answer: Magnesium gains oxygen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the change of magnesium atoms into magnesium ions.
parts.answer: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the change of oxygen molecules into oxide ions, and state whether this is oxidation or reduction.
parts.answer: O₂ + 4e⁻ → 2O²⁻; reduction

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Hot copper(II) oxide reacts with hydrogen: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Which substance is the reducing agent?
A CuO
B H₂
C Cu
D H₂O
parts.answer: B H₂
parts.working: Hydrogen removes oxygen from copper(II) oxide and is itself oxidised, so it is the reducing agent. CuO (A) is the oxidising agent.

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents
practice.stem:
Chlorine gas is bubbled into colourless aqueous potassium iodide.
Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour change seen.
parts.answer: colourless to brown (orange-brown)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation numbers of iodine before and after the reaction.
parts.answer: −1 in KI; 0 in I₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the oxidising agent. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Chlorine; it gains electrons / its oxidation number decreases from 0 to −1, so it oxidises iodide ions.

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the colour change when a reducing agent is added to acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII).
parts.answer: purple to colourless

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the colour change when an oxidising agent is added to aqueous potassium iodide.
parts.answer: colourless to brown

parts.label: c
parts.text: Iron(II) sulfate solution decolourises acidified potassium manganate(VII). State what happens to the iron(II) ions, giving the change in oxidation number.
parts.answer: They are oxidised to iron(III) ions; oxidation number changes from +2 to +3.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give the change in oxidation number of manganese when MnO₄⁻ forms Mn²⁺.

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which compound does nitrogen have an oxidation number of +4?
A HNO₃
B N₂O
C NH₃
D NO₂
parts.answer: D NO₂
parts.working: In NO₂: x + 2(−2) = 0, so x = +4. In HNO₃: +1 + x + 3(−2) = 0 gives +5, the usual distractor; N₂O gives +1 and NH₃ gives −3.

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents
practice.stem:
Orange bromine water is added to pale green aqueous iron(II) sulfate. The mixture turns yellow-brown.
Br₂ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2Br⁻ + 2Fe³⁺

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation numbers of iron before and after the reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the oxidising agent. Explain.
parts.answer: Bromine; it takes electrons from Fe²⁺ (bromine itself is reduced, 0 → −1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test to show that Fe³⁺ ions have formed, and the result.
parts.answer: Add aqueous sodium hydroxide; red-brown precipitate.

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents
practice.stem: In the blast furnace at a steel mill near Karachi, iron(III) oxide is reduced: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of carbon in CO and in CO₂.
parts.answer: +2 and +4

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the reducing agent. Explain using oxidation numbers.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide; carbon's oxidation number increases (+2 → +4) so CO is oxidised, and it reduces iron (+3 → 0).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the oxidation number of iron in Fe₂O₃.

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents
practice.stem:
Aqueous iron(III) chloride is added to aqueous potassium iodide.
2Fe³⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Fe²⁺(aq) + I₂(aq)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the two half-equations for this reaction.
parts.answer: Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺;  2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.
parts.answer: oxidising agent: Fe³⁺; reducing agent: I⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how many moles of electrons are transferred when 1 mole of iodine is formed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest an observation that shows the reaction has occurred.
parts.answer: The solution turns from yellow/orange to brown (iodine formed) — accept darker brown.

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents
practice.stem:
Railway lines in Pakistan are welded using the thermite reaction.
Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe   [Ar: O, 16; Al, 27; Fe, 56]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of iron in Fe₂O₃ and in Fe.
parts.answer: +3 and 0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the reducing agent and explain your answer in terms of oxidation number.
parts.answer: Aluminium; its oxidation number increases from 0 to +3 (it is oxidised).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of aluminium needed to react with 1.6 kg of iron(III) oxide, and the mass of iron formed.
parts.answer: 540 g aluminium; 1120 g iron

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents
practice.stem:
Hydrogen peroxide can behave in two ways.
Reaction 1: H₂O₂ is added to acidified aqueous potassium iodide; iodine forms and water is produced.
Reaction 2: H₂O₂ is added to acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII); bubbles of oxygen form and the purple colour disappears.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the oxidation number of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In reaction 1, state whether hydrogen peroxide acts as an oxidising agent or a reducing agent. Use oxidation numbers of oxygen to explain.
parts.answer: Oxidising agent; it oxidises I⁻ to I₂ and its oxygen is reduced from −1 to −2 (in water).

parts.label: c
parts.text: In reaction 2, state whether hydrogen peroxide acts as an oxidising agent or a reducing agent. Explain.
parts.answer: Reducing agent; it reduces purple manganate(VII) (decolourised) and its oxygen is oxidised from −1 to 0 (O₂).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the colour change in reaction 1.
parts.answer: Colourless to yellow-brown/brown.

practice.subtopic: Redox, oxidation number, oxidising & reducing agents
practice.stem:
A pharmacy tests an iron tablet. The tablet is dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and titrated with 0.0200 mol/dm³ potassium manganate(VII). 20.0 cm³ is needed.
MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the change in oxidation number of manganese and of iron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why 1 mole of MnO₄⁻ reacts with 5 moles of Fe²⁺.
parts.answer: Each Mn gains 5 electrons; each Fe²⁺ loses only 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iron, as Fe²⁺, in the tablet. [Ar: Fe, 56]

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which conditions are used in the Contact process to convert sulfur dioxide into sulfur trioxide?
A 200 °C, 200 kPa, nickel catalyst
B 300 °C, 6000 kPa, phosphoric acid catalyst
C 450 °C, 200 kPa, vanadium(V) oxide catalyst
D 450 °C, 20 000 kPa, iron catalyst
parts.answer: C 450 °C, 200 kPa, vanadium(V) oxide catalyst
parts.working: The Contact process uses about 450 °C, about 200 kPa (2 atm) and V₂O₅. Option D is the Haber process; option B is for making ethanol from ethene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two uses of sulfur dioxide.
parts.answer: Food preservative (kills bacteria); bleach in making wood pulp for paper.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process used to make sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: Contact process

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one large-scale use of sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: Making fertilisers (e.g. ammonium sulfate) / detergents / car batteries

practice.stem: Boiling points: nitrogen −196 °C; hydrogen −253 °C; ammonia −33 °C. In the Haber process only about 15 % of the gases are converted to ammonia in each pass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how ammonia is separated from the unreacted gases after the reactor.
parts.answer: The mixture is cooled; ammonia has a much higher boiling point (−33 °C) so it condenses to a liquid; nitrogen and hydrogen stay as gases.
parts.working: B1 cooling; B1 ammonia condenses because of its higher boiling point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is done with the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen.
parts.answer: Recycled back into the reactor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the source of nitrogen for the process.
parts.answer: Air

practice.stem: Many brick kilns around Lahore burn coal containing sulfur.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how sulfur dioxide is produced when coal is burned in brick kilns.
parts.answer: Sulfur impurities in the coal burn in oxygen: S + O₂ → SO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two effects of acid rain.
parts.answer: Any two: damages buildings/limestone and marble; corrodes metal structures; makes lakes acidic and kills fish; damages trees/crops.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing sulfur dioxide emissions from factories.
parts.answer: Use low-sulfur fuel / remove sulfur from fuel / react the waste gases with calcium oxide or calcium carbonate (flue-gas desulfurisation).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which catalyst is used in the Haber process?
A iron
B nickel
C platinum
D vanadium(V) oxide
parts.answer: A iron
parts.working: Iron is the catalyst for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Vanadium(V) oxide (D) is the Contact process catalyst.

practice.stem: A fertiliser factory near Daharki makes ammonia by the Haber process.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction in the Haber process, including the reversible sign.
parts.answer: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sources of the nitrogen and the hydrogen.
parts.answer: nitrogen: air; hydrogen: methane (natural gas) reacted with steam

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the typical temperature and pressure used.
parts.answer: about 450 °C and 20 000 kPa (200 atm)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest what is done with the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen.
parts.answer: They are recycled back into the reactor.

practice.stem: A fertiliser factory near Multan makes ammonium sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for making ammonium sulfate from ammonia and sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium sulfate. Give 3 significant figures. [Ar: H, 1; N, 14; O, 16; S, 32]

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why farmers add nitrogen-containing fertilisers to soil.
parts.answer: Plants need nitrogen for growth (to make proteins); it replaces nitrogen removed by crops.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The forward reaction in the Haber process is exothermic. Explain why a temperature of about 450 °C is used rather than a much lower temperature.
parts.answer: A lower temperature gives a higher yield but the rate is too slow; 450 °C is a compromise giving a reasonable yield at an acceptable rate.
parts.working: B1 low temperature too slow; B1 compromise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a pressure of about 20 000 kPa is used rather than a much higher pressure.
parts.answer: Higher pressure would give a higher yield and rate, but costs more (stronger equipment, more energy) and is more dangerous.
parts.working: B1 higher yield acknowledged; B1 cost/safety.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of the iron catalyst on the yield.
parts.answer: None; it only increases the rate.

practice.stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g); the forward reaction is exothermic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a pressure of only about 200 kPa is used in the Contact process even though higher pressure would increase the yield.
parts.answer: The equilibrium yield is already very high (over 95 %) at low pressure; higher pressure would cost more for little gain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an excess of air is used.
parts.answer: More oxygen moves the equilibrium to the right, increasing the conversion of (expensive) sulfur dioxide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two raw materials that are sources of the sulfur dioxide.
parts.answer: Sulfur (burned in air); sulfide ores (roasted in air).

practice.stem: Dilute sulfuric acid shows the typical reactions of an acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dilute sulfuric acid reacts with magnesium. Write the equation and give one observation.
parts.answer: Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂; fizzing / magnesium dissolves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Dilute sulfuric acid reacts with copper(II) oxide on warming. Write the equation and give one observation.
parts.answer: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O; black solid dissolves to give a blue solution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Dilute sulfuric acid reacts with sodium carbonate. Write the equation.
parts.answer: Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂

practice.stem: Sulfuric acid is made by the Contact process. The sulfur trioxide is first dissolved in concentrated sulfuric acid to make oleum, which is then diluted with water. [Ar: H, 1; O, 16; S, 32]

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two sources of the sulfur dioxide used.
parts.answer: burning sulfur; roasting sulfide ores

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the conversion of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide and state the catalyst, temperature and pressure used.
parts.answer: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃; vanadium(V) oxide; about 450 °C and 200 kPa (2 atm)
parts.working: B1 equation; B1 V₂O₅; B1 both conditions

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a pressure much higher than 200 kPa is not used.
parts.answer: The yield is already high at low pressure, so higher pressure would add cost for little gain.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sulfuric acid, in tonnes, made from 16 tonnes of sulfur if the overall yield is 96%.
parts.answer: 47.0 tonnes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ammonia that could be made from 140 tonnes of nitrogen. N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃  [Ar: H, 1; N, 14]
parts.answer: 170 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: In one pass through the reactor only 15 % of the nitrogen is converted. Calculate the mass of ammonia made in one pass.
parts.answer: 25.5 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the overall conversion in the plant is much greater than 15 %.
parts.answer: Unreacted gases are recycled through the reactor many times.

practice.stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen needed to react with 480 dm³ of sulfur dioxide (both at r.t.p.).
parts.answer: 240 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sulfur trioxide formed from 64 kg of sulfur dioxide if the conversion is 98 %. [Mr: SO₂, 64; SO₃, 80]
parts.working: M1 1000 mol SO₂ → 1000 mol SO₃ = 80 kg; A1 × 0.98 = 78.4 kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sulfur trioxide is not added directly to water. Explain why.
parts.answer: The reaction is very exothermic and forms a mist of acid droplets that is hard to collect (so it is dissolved in concentrated sulfuric acid instead).

practice.stem: For the Contact process reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) (forward reaction exothermic), state and explain the effect of each change on the rate of reaction and on the equilibrium yield of sulfur trioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Higher temperature (above 450 °C).
parts.answer: Rate increases; yield decreases (exothermic forward reaction, equilibrium moves left).
parts.working: B1 rate; B1 yield with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Higher pressure.
parts.answer: Rate increases; yield increases (fewer moles of gas on the right).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Removing the catalyst.
parts.answer: Rate decreases (much slower); yield unchanged.

practice.stem: Sulfur dioxide is added to dried apricots from Gilgit as a preservative.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of sulfur in SO₂ and in SO₄²⁻.
parts.answer: +4 and +6

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sulfur dioxide decolourises acidified potassium manganate(VII). State whether sulfur dioxide acts as an oxidising agent or a reducing agent, and explain.
parts.answer: Reducing agent; it is oxidised to sulfate (S: +4 → +6) and reduces the manganate(VII).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the ability of sulfur dioxide to act as a preservative in dried apricots may be linked to this property.
parts.answer: It removes oxygen/acts as a reducing agent, stopping oxidation (and kills bacteria).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each change as physical or chemical: (i) ice melting in a glass of water; (ii) LPG burning in a stove; (iii) an iron gate rusting; (iv) sugar dissolving in tea.
parts.answer: (i) physical; (ii) chemical; (iii) chemical; (iv) physical
parts.working: B2 all four correct; B1 for three

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features that show a change is chemical.
parts.answer: A new substance is formed; it is usually not easily reversed; there is often an energy change (heat/light), colour change or gas given off.

practice.stem: State whether each change in a kitchen is physical or chemical and give a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ghee melting in a hot pan.
parts.answer: Physical; no new substance, it solidifies again on cooling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An egg being fried.
parts.answer: Chemical; new substances form and it cannot be reversed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Water boiling in a kettle.
parts.answer: Physical; only a change of state.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Gas burning on a stove.
parts.answer: Chemical; new substances (CO₂ and water) form and heat is given out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether dissolving sugar in tea is a physical or chemical change.
parts.answer: Physical

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how you could show that the sugar is still present and unchanged.
parts.answer: Evaporate the water from a sugar solution; the sugar is left behind (and tastes the same).

parts.label: c
parts.text: 10 g of sugar is dissolved in 200 g of water. State the mass of the solution.

practice.stem: During load-shedding a family in Quetta lights a candle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one physical change that takes place when a candle burns.
parts.answer: Wax melts (and solidifies again as it runs down / vaporises).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the chemical change and name two products.
parts.answer: Wax vapour burns (combustion); carbon dioxide and water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the candle gets shorter even though melted wax is not lost.
parts.answer: Wax is burned and changed into gases that escape.

practice.stem: A student heats four substances. Classify each change as physical or chemical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Change P: ice is warmed and melts.
parts.answer: Physical

parts.label: b
parts.text: Change Q: green copper(II) carbonate is heated; it turns black and gives off a gas that turns limewater milky.
parts.answer: Chemical

parts.label: c
parts.text: Change R: wax is warmed and melts, then sets again on cooling.
parts.answer: Physical

parts.label: d
parts.text: Change S: magnesium ribbon is heated and burns to form a white powder.
parts.answer: Chemical

parts.label: e
parts.text: Give one piece of evidence from change Q that shows it is chemical.
parts.answer: Colour change to a new black solid / a new gas (CO₂) is formed.

practice.stem: Classify each change as physical or chemical and give one reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Milk turning into yoghurt (dahi).
parts.answer: Chemical; new substances form (lactic acid) and the taste changes permanently.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Water freezing to make ice blocks.
parts.answer: Physical; change of state only.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A firework exploding at a wedding.
parts.answer: Chemical; new substances, heat and light produced.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Crushing sugar cane to extract the juice.
parts.answer: Physical; no new substance, the juice was already present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why rusting is a chemical change.
parts.answer: A new substance (hydrated iron(III) oxide) forms with different properties; it cannot easily be reversed.
parts.working: B1 new substance; B1 different properties/not easily reversed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An iron gate weighs more after rusting. Explain why.
parts.answer: Iron combines with oxygen (and water) from the air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why iron gates near the sea in Karachi rust faster than those in Islamabad.
parts.answer: Salt in the sea air speeds up rusting (and air is more humid).

parts.label: a
parts.text: When ammonium nitrate dissolves in water the temperature falls. When magnesium reacts with acid the temperature rises. A student says 'both are chemical changes because there is an energy change'. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Energy changes happen in physical changes too (dissolving, melting, boiling); a chemical change is identified by formation of a new substance.
parts.working: B1 physical changes also have energy changes; B1 new substance is the test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one observation from the magnesium reaction that does show a chemical change.
parts.answer: Bubbles of a new gas (hydrogen) / magnesium disappears to form a new substance.

practice.stem: 3.20 g of pink-brown copper powder is heated in air in an open crucible until its mass is constant. 4.00 g of black solid is formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen that combined with the copper.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the masses to show that the formula of the black solid is CuO. [Ar: O, 16; Cu, 64]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two pieces of evidence that a chemical change has taken place.
parts.answer: Colour change from pink-brown to black; mass increases because oxygen combines (new substance).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Boiling water gives steam. Electrolysis of water gives hydrogen and oxygen. State which is a chemical change and explain.
parts.answer: Electrolysis; new substances (hydrogen and oxygen) with different properties form; boiling only changes state.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe tests on the gases that would show that new substances have formed in electrolysis.
parts.answer: Hydrogen pops with a lighted splint; oxygen relights a glowing splint.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what happens to the steam from boiling water if it touches a cold surface.
parts.answer: It condenses back to water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Vinegar and baking soda react in an open beaker on a balance. Explain why the reading falls.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide gas escapes into the air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The experiment is repeated in a flask sealed with a balloon. State what happens to the reading and explain.
parts.answer: It stays the same; no atoms are lost, the gas is trapped (mass is conserved).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ice in a sealed plastic bag melts. State what happens to the mass and whether the change is physical or chemical.
parts.answer: Mass unchanged; physical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Heating ammonium chloride gives ammonia and hydrogen chloride, which recombine on cooling. Explain why this is a chemical change even though it is reversed.
parts.answer: New substances (ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases) are formed; bonds are broken and made.
parts.working: B1 new substances; B1 bonds broken/made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate turns white when heated and blue again when water is added. Explain why this is also a chemical change.
parts.answer: Water of crystallisation is removed and a new substance (anhydrous CuSO₄) forms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use these examples to comment on the statement 'all reversible changes are physical'.
parts.answer: The statement is false: some chemical changes are reversible; the test is whether new substances form.

practice.stem: A student mixes iron filings and powdered sulfur.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a magnet could show that the iron in the mixture has not combined.
parts.answer: The magnet attracts the iron filings out of the mixture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When heated, the mixture glows red and a black solid forms that is not attracted by a magnet. Explain why this shows a chemical change.
parts.answer: A new substance (iron(II) sulfide) has formed with different properties (not magnetic); heat given out.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iron(II) sulfide formed from 5.6 g of iron and 3.2 g of sulfur. Fe + S → FeS  [Ar: S, 32; Fe, 56]

parts.label: d
parts.text: The experiment is repeated with 7.0 g of iron and 3.2 g of sulfur. Calculate the mass of iron left over.
parts.working: M1 3.2 g S (0.10 mol) reacts with 5.6 g Fe; A1 7.0 − 5.6 = 1.4 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium chloride dissolves in water. Explain, in terms of particles, why this is a physical change.
parts.answer: The ions separate and spread among water molecules, but no new substance forms; evaporating the water gives back sodium chloride.
parts.working: B1 ions separate, no new substance; B1 can be recovered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sodium also 'disappears' when added to water. Explain why this is a chemical change, with an equation.
parts.answer: Sodium reacts to form new substances, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe one test that shows the solution from sodium is different from the salt solution.
parts.answer: Add universal indicator: the sodium solution is alkaline (purple/blue), the salt solution is neutral (green).

practice.stem:
Four solids are added to water.
A: dissolves, temperature falls by 5 °C; evaporation gives back the same white solid.
B: fizzes; the gas pops with a lighted splint; the solution turns universal indicator purple; evaporation leaves a different white solid.
C: dissolves to give a blue solution; evaporation gives back the same blue crystals.
D: added to aqueous silver nitrate instead of water, a white precipitate forms immediately.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each solid, state whether a physical or a chemical change took place, giving evidence.
parts.answer: A physical: it dissolves and the same solid is recovered. B chemical: a new gas (hydrogen) forms, the solution is alkaline and a different solid is left. C physical: the same blue crystals are recovered. D chemical: a new insoluble substance (the precipitate) forms.
parts.working: 1 mark each for A, B, C and D, each with correct evidence (A and C: same solid recovered; B: new gas, alkaline solution, different solid; D: new insoluble substance).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify solid B, given that it gives an orange-red flame colour, and write the equation.
parts.answer: Calcium; Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ ions and nitrogen forms N³⁻ ions. What is the formula of magnesium nitride?
A Mg₃N₂
B Mg₂N₃
C MgN
D Mg₂N
parts.answer: A Mg₃N₂
parts.working: Charges must balance: 3 × (+2) = +6 and 2 × (−3) = −6, so Mg₃N₂. Mg₂N₃ (B) simply swaps the numbers the wrong way and gives +4 and −9.

practice.stem: Sodium chloride is obtained from rock salt mined at Khewra in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The electronic configuration of a sodium atom is 2,8,1 and of a chlorine atom is 2,8,7. Describe what happens to the electrons when sodium reacts with chlorine to form sodium chloride.
parts.answer: Each sodium atom transfers (loses) its one outer electron to a chlorine atom, which gains it; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions form.
parts.working: B1 one electron transferred from Na to Cl; B1 Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions formed (both with full outer shells).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of the sodium ion and of the chloride ion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which ion has the electronic configuration 2,8?
A Na⁺
B K⁺
C Cl⁻
D Li⁺
parts.answer: A Na⁺
parts.working: Sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to give Na⁺, 2,8. K⁺ (B) is 2,8,8 because potassium is 2,8,8,1; Cl⁻ is 2,8,8; Li⁺ is 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an ion.
parts.answer: An atom or group of atoms that has lost or gained electrons, so it has an electrical charge.
parts.working: B1 charged particle formed by loss or gain of electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the charge on the ion formed by an element in each of these groups of the Periodic Table: (i) Group I (ii) Group II (iii) Group III (iv) Group VI (v) Group VII.
parts.working: 3 marks all five; 2 marks four; 1 mark two or three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why positive ions are formed by metals.
parts.answer: Metal atoms have few outer-shell electrons, which they lose to gain a full outer shell; losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons.
parts.working: B1 metals lose (outer) electrons, so protons outnumber electrons.

practice.stem: Magnesium fluoride is used to coat camera lenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Magnesium (2,8,2) reacts with fluorine (2,7). Describe the transfer of electrons that takes place.
parts.answer: Each magnesium atom loses its two outer electrons, one to each of two fluorine atoms.
parts.working: B1 magnesium loses two electrons. B1 each fluorine atom gains one electron (two fluorine atoms per magnesium).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formula and electronic configuration of each ion formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the formula of magnesium fluoride.
parts.answer: MgF₂

practice.stem: Calcium oxide (quicklime) is made in lime kilns and used in cement and to treat acidic soil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for calcium oxide. Show the outer-shell electrons and the charges on the ions.
parts.answer: Calcium transfers two electrons to oxygen. Ca²⁺ has 8 electrons in its outer shell (2,8,8) and O²⁻ has 8 electrons in its outer shell (2,8), shown as 6 dots + 2 crosses; charges 2+ and 2−.
