parts.working: B1 two electrons transferred from Ca to O; B1 both ions shown with 8 outer electrons (O²⁻: 6 of its own + 2 from Ca); B1 charges Ca²⁺ and O²⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calcium oxide melts at about 2600 °C. Explain why it has such a high melting point.
parts.answer: It is a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, so a lot of energy is needed to overcome these forces.
parts.working: B1 giant lattice / many strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions; B1 much energy needed to overcome them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. Suggest why calcium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride.
parts.answer: The ions in calcium oxide have larger charges (2+ and 2−) so the attraction between them is stronger.
parts.working: B1 higher charges on ions → stronger attraction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Use the ions K⁺, Al³⁺, Fe³⁺, O²⁻, OH⁻, NO₃⁻ and SO₄²⁻ to write the formulae of:
(i) potassium oxide
(ii) aluminium sulfate
(iii) iron(III) hydroxide
(iv) aluminium nitrate
parts.answer: (i) K₂O  (ii) Al₂(SO₄)₃  (iii) Fe(OH)₃  (iv) Al(NO₃)₃
parts.working: B1 each. Brackets are needed around SO₄, OH and NO₃ when there is more than one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solid potassium bromide does not conduct electricity, but molten potassium bromide does. Explain this difference.
parts.answer: Conduction needs mobile charged particles. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move; when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 ions present in both; B1 ions fixed / cannot move in solid; B1 ions mobile in molten (or aqueous) state.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other condition in which potassium bromide conducts electricity.
parts.answer: When dissolved in water (aqueous solution).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of elements forms an ionic compound with the formula XY₂, where X is the metal?
A calcium and chlorine
B sodium and oxygen
C aluminium and fluorine
D magnesium and oxygen
parts.answer: A calcium and chlorine
parts.working: Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ give CaCl₂ (XY₂). Sodium and oxygen give Na₂O (X₂Y), aluminium and fluorine give AlF₃, magnesium and oxygen give MgO.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for potassium sulfide. Show only the outer shells and the charges on the ions.
parts.answer: Two potassium atoms each give one electron (shown as a cross) to a sulfur atom, which has six outer electrons (shown as dots). The result is two K⁺ ions (1+ each, with no outer electrons) and one S²⁻ ion in square brackets with eight outer electrons (charge 2−).
parts.working: B1 two K⁺ ions each 1+ with no outer electrons. B1 sulfide ion in brackets with 8 outer electrons. B1 charge 2− on S, with two electrons transferred from the two K atoms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula of potassium sulfide.
parts.answer: K₂S

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of the sulfide ion and name the noble gas that has the same configuration.
parts.answer: 2,8,8; argon

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of solid sodium chloride.
parts.answer: A giant lattice of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
parts.working: B1 giant lattice / regular arrangement of positive and negative ions. B1 strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (in all directions).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Magnesium oxide melts at 2852 °C, but sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. Both are ionic. Suggest why magnesium oxide has the much higher melting point.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions have larger charges (2+ and 2−) than Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (1+ and 1−), so the attraction between the ions is stronger and needs more energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 ions in MgO have higher charges. B1 stronger electrostatic attraction / more energy needed to separate ions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Magnesium oxide is used to line furnaces. Give the property that makes it suitable.
parts.answer: very high melting point
parts.working: B1 high melting point (does not melt at furnace temperatures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lithium (2,1) reacts with nitrogen (2,5) to form the ionic compound lithium nitride, Li₃N. Explain, in terms of electron transfer, why the formula is Li₃N.
parts.answer: Each lithium atom loses one electron to form Li⁺. A nitrogen atom needs to gain three electrons to form N³⁻ (2,8). So three lithium atoms are needed for each nitrogen atom.
parts.working: B1 Li loses 1 e⁻ → Li⁺; B1 N gains 3 e⁻ → N³⁻; B1 three Li needed per N so charges balance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of protons and electrons in (i) a lithium ion, Li⁺ (ii) a nitride ion, N³⁻. (Proton numbers: Li = 3, N = 7.)
parts.answer: (i) 3 protons, 2 electrons  (ii) 7 protons, 10 electrons
parts.working: B1 each pair. Electrons = protons − charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An ion X²⁻ contains 18 electrons and 16 neutrons. Deduce the proton number and nucleon (mass) number of X, and identify X.
parts.answer: Proton number 16; nucleon number 32; X is sulfur (the ion is S²⁻).
parts.working: M1 protons = 18 − 2 = 16; A1 nucleon number = 16 + 16 = 32; B1 sulfur.

parts.label: b
parts.text: X forms an ionic compound with aluminium. Write its formula.
parts.answer: Al₂S₃

parts.label: c
parts.text: The ion X²⁻ has the same electronic configuration as an argon atom. Suggest why its chemical properties are different from those of argon.
parts.answer: Both have 2,8,8, but the ion has only 16 protons and a 2− charge; it is attracted to positive ions and can lose electrons (be oxidised), whereas argon is a neutral atom.
parts.working: B1 same configuration 2,8,8; B1 different number of protons / ion is charged, so attracts positive ions or can be oxidised.

practice.stem:
The table shows the numbers of protons and electrons in five particles.
Particle | protons | electrons
A | 12 | 10
B | 9 | 10
C | 18 | 18
D | 13 | 10
E | 16 | 18

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which particles are positive ions, which are negative ions and which are atoms.
parts.answer: positive ions: A and D; negative ions: B and E; atom: C
parts.working: B1 positive: A (12p,10e), D (13p,10e). B1 negative: B (9p,10e), E (16p,18e). B1 atom: C (equal protons and electrons).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the element of particle C.
parts.answer: argon

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formulae of the ionic compounds formed by (i) A and B (ii) D and E.
parts.answer: (i) MgF₂ (ii) Al₂S₃
parts.working: B1 MgF₂ (Mg²⁺, F⁻). B1 Al₂S₃ (Al³⁺, S²⁻).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A crystal of calcium fluoride is hit with a hammer and shatters. Explain why, in terms of the arrangement of the ions.
parts.answer: The force shifts one layer of ions relative to the next, so ions of the same charge come next to each other; they repel strongly and the crystal splits apart.
parts.working: B1 layers of ions are displaced. B1 like charges are brought side by side. B1 repulsion makes the crystal break (brittle).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calcium chloride is soluble in water. Explain why an aqueous solution of calcium chloride conducts electricity, but solid calcium chloride does not.
parts.answer: In the solution the ions are free to move and carry charge; in the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice.
parts.working: B1 ions free to move in solution. B1 ions fixed in lattice in the solid (no mobile charge carriers).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why calcium chloride solution conducts electricity but copper conducts by a different kind of particle.
parts.answer: In the solution the charge is carried by moving ions (Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻); in copper it is carried by delocalised electrons.
parts.working: B1 ions in solution. B1 delocalised electrons in the metal.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. Which statement about this atom is correct?
A Its nucleon number is 23 and it has 11 electrons.
B Its nucleon number is 12 and it has 11 electrons.
C Its nucleon number is 23 and it has 12 electrons.
D Its proton number is 23 and it has 11 electrons.
parts.answer: A Its nucleon number is 23 and it has 11 electrons.
parts.working: Nucleon number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23; a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons (11). C wrongly uses the neutron number for electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An atom of potassium is shown as ³⁹₁₉K. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in this atom.
parts.answer: 19 protons, 20 neutrons, 19 electrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of the potassium atom.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine has two isotopes, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. State what is meant by the term isotopes.
parts.answer: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
parts.working: B1 same proton number / same element; B1 different number of neutrons (different nucleon number).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both isotopes of chlorine have the same chemical properties.
parts.answer: They have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration (7 outer electrons).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of neutrons in an atom of chlorine-37. (Proton number of Cl = 17.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the relative mass and relative charge of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
parts.answer: proton: mass 1, charge +1; neutron: mass 1, charge 0; electron: mass 1/1840 (negligible), charge −1
parts.working: 1 mark for each particle with both mass and charge correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in an atom the protons, the neutrons and the electrons are found.
parts.answer: protons and neutrons in the nucleus; electrons in shells around the nucleus

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phosphorus is used in the heads of safety matches. An atom of phosphorus is ³¹₁₅P. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons.
parts.answer: 15 protons, 16 neutrons, 15 electrons
parts.working: B1 15 protons and 15 electrons. B1 16 neutrons (31 − 15).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of phosphorus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the electronic configuration to state the group and the period of phosphorus in the Periodic Table.
parts.answer: Group V, Period 3
parts.working: B1 Group V (5 outer electrons). B1 Period 3 (3 shells).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by (i) proton number (ii) nucleon number.
parts.answer: (i) the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom (ii) the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are two isotopes of carbon. Carbon-14 is used to find the age of old wood and bones. State the number of neutrons in each isotope.
parts.answer: carbon-12: 6; carbon-14: 8
parts.working: B1 each (proton number of carbon is 6).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why carbon-14 atoms take part in the same chemical reactions as carbon-12 atoms.
parts.answer: They have the same number of electrons (same electronic configuration, 2,4).
parts.working: B1 same number of outer electrons.

practice.stem: Boron compounds are used to make heat-resistant glassware for laboratories.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Boron has two isotopes: boron-10 (abundance 19.9 %) and boron-11 (abundance 80.1 %). Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of neutrons in each isotope. (Proton number of B = 5.)
parts.answer: boron-10: 5; boron-11: 6

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of magnesium contains 79.0 % magnesium-24, 10.0 % magnesium-25 and 11.0 % magnesium-26. Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in the ion ²⁶Mg²⁺. (Proton number of Mg = 12.)
parts.answer: 12 protons, 14 neutrons, 10 electrons
parts.working: B1 neutrons 14; B1 protons 12 and electrons 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which two particles are isotopes of the same element?
Particle P: 8 protons, 8 neutrons
Particle Q: 8 protons, 10 neutrons
Particle R: 9 protons, 10 neutrons
Particle S: 10 protons, 8 neutrons
A P and Q
B P and S
C Q and R
D R and S
parts.answer: A P and Q
parts.working: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons: P and Q both have 8 protons (oxygen). Q and R (C) have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons, so they are different elements.

practice.stem: Copper is used in Pakistan for electrical wiring and for brass utensils. Natural copper contains 69.2 % copper-63 and 30.8 % copper-65.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative atomic mass of copper. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of neutrons in an atom of copper-65. (Proton number of copper = 29)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the relative atomic mass of copper is closer to 63 than to 65.
parts.answer: Copper-63 is more abundant than copper-65.

practice.stem: An atom of element R has a nucleon number of 27 and contains 14 neutrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify element R. Explain how you worked this out.
parts.answer: aluminium; proton number = 27 − 14 = 13

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of an atom of R.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Another atom has the same proton number as R but a nucleon number of 26. State the number of neutrons in this atom and the term used for the relationship between the two atoms.
parts.answer: 13 neutrons; isotopes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gallium has two isotopes, gallium-69 and gallium-71. The relative atomic mass of gallium is 69.72. Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope.
parts.answer: gallium-69: 64 %; gallium-71: 36 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the relative atomic mass of gallium is closer to 69 than to 71.
parts.answer: Gallium-69 is the more abundant isotope.

practice.stem:
Four particles are described below.
W: 17 protons, 18 neutrons, 17 electrons
X: 17 protons, 20 neutrons, 17 electrons
Y: 18 protons, 22 neutrons, 18 electrons
Z: 17 protons, 18 neutrons, 18 electrons

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which two particles are isotopes of the same element. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: W and X: both have 17 protons but different numbers of neutrons (18 and 20).
parts.working: B1 W and X; B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which particle is a negative ion. Give its symbol with charge.
parts.answer: Z; Cl⁻ (17 protons, 18 electrons)
parts.working: B1 Z; B1 Cl⁻ (one more electron than protons).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the nucleon number of Y and explain why Y is unreactive.
parts.answer: 40; Y is argon with configuration 2,8,8 — a full outer shell, so it does not need to gain, lose or share electrons.
parts.working: B1 18 + 22 = 40; B1 full outer shell / stable configuration.

practice.stem: Silicon, used in solar cells, has three natural isotopes: silicon-28 (92.2 %), silicon-29 (4.7 %) and silicon-30 (3.1 %).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative atomic mass of silicon. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of neutrons in each isotope. (Proton number of silicon = 14)
parts.answer: silicon-28: 14; silicon-29: 15; silicon-30: 16

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why relative atomic masses are usually not whole numbers, even though each isotope has a whole-number nucleon number.
parts.answer: They are weighted averages of the masses of the isotopes in their natural abundances.

practice.stem: Bromine has two isotopes, bromine-79 and bromine-81. The relative atomic mass of bromine is 79.9.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope.
parts.answer: bromine-79: 55 %; bromine-81: 45 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Bromine exists as Br₂ molecules. State the three possible relative masses of a Br₂ molecule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which of these three molecules is the most common. Explain.
parts.answer: Mass 160 (one Br-79 and one Br-81): it can form in two ways (79+81 or 81+79), and the two isotopes have similar abundances.
parts.working: B1 160. B1 two combinations give it / probability 2 × 0.55 × 0.45 = 0.495 is largest.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which molecule contains a triple covalent bond?
A O₂
B N₂
C Cl₂
D CH₄
parts.answer: B N₂
parts.working: N₂ has N≡N (three shared pairs) so each N has 8 outer electrons. O₂ (A) has a double bond, Cl₂ a single bond, CH₄ four single bonds.

practice.stem: Natural gas, which is mainly methane, is piped to many homes for cooking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the bonding in a molecule of methane, CH₄. Include the number of shared pairs and the number of outer-shell electrons around each atom.
parts.answer: Carbon shares one pair of electrons with each of four hydrogen atoms: four single covalent bonds (4 shared pairs). Carbon then has 8 outer electrons and each hydrogen has 2.
parts.working: B1 covalent bond = shared pair of electrons; B1 four shared pairs / single bonds; B1 C has 8 and each H has 2 outer electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Methane boils at −162 °C. Explain why its boiling point is so low.
parts.answer: Methane is a simple molecular substance; the intermolecular forces between molecules are weak, so little energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.working: B1 weak intermolecular forces (not covalent bonds broken); B1 little energy needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a covalent bond.
parts.answer: A pair of electrons shared between two atoms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ammonia, NH₃, is used to make fertilisers at plants in Pakistan. Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram of an ammonia molecule. Show only outer-shell electrons.
parts.answer: The nitrogen atom shares one pair of electrons with each of three hydrogen atoms (each pair = one dot and one cross). Nitrogen also has one non-bonding pair, so it has 8 outer electrons; each hydrogen has 2.
parts.working: B1 three shared pairs, one N–H each. B1 one lone pair on N. B1 N has 8 and each H has 2 electrons in outer shell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paraffin wax used in candles is made of simple covalent molecules. Give two physical properties you would expect it to have.
parts.answer: Any two: low melting point; does not conduct electricity (solid or molten); insoluble in water; soft.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the wax melts easily even though the covalent bonds inside its molecules are strong.
parts.answer: Melting only overcomes the weak forces between the molecules (intermolecular forces); the covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break.
parts.working: B1 weak intermolecular forces are overcome. B1 covalent bonds within molecules are not broken.

practice.stem: Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, is used in hand sanitisers. Its structure is CH₃–CH₂–O–H, with every bond a single covalent bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of covalent bonds in one molecule of ethanol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of electrons shared in one molecule of ethanol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of non-bonding pairs of electrons on the oxygen atom.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for a molecule of carbon dioxide, CO₂. Show only outer-shell electrons.
parts.answer: Carbon in the centre forms a double bond (two shared pairs) with each oxygen atom. Each oxygen also has two non-bonding (lone) pairs. Every atom has 8 outer electrons.
parts.working: B1 two double bonds / four shared pairs; B1 two lone pairs on each O; B1 8 electrons around each atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of electrons that are shared in one CO₂ molecule.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Methanol has the structural formula CH₃OH. State the number of covalent bonds (bonding pairs) in one molecule and the number of non-bonding pairs on the oxygen atom.
parts.answer: 5 bonding pairs; 2 non-bonding pairs on oxygen
parts.working: B1 5 (three C–H, one C–O, one O–H); B1 2 lone pairs (O has 6 outer electrons, 2 used in bonds).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrogen chloride is a covalent gas. Explain why pure hydrogen chloride does not conduct electricity.
parts.answer: It is made of neutral molecules; there are no ions or delocalised electrons free to move and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 molecules / no ions; B1 no mobile charged particles.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many pairs of outer-shell electrons on the oxygen atom in a water molecule are NOT used in bonding?
A 0
B 1
C 2
D 3
parts.answer: C 2
parts.working: Oxygen has 6 outer electrons: 2 are shared in the two O–H bonds and 4 remain as 2 non-bonding (lone) pairs. 1 (B) is the number for nitrogen in ammonia.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for a molecule of carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄. Show outer-shell electrons only.
parts.answer: The carbon atom shares one pair of electrons with each of the four chlorine atoms (four single C–Cl bonds). Each chlorine has three non-bonding pairs plus the shared pair, so every chlorine has 8 outer electrons; carbon also has 8 outer electrons.
parts.working: B1 four C–Cl single bonds, one shared pair each. B1 each Cl has three non-bonding pairs. B1 C and each Cl have 8 outer electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of non-bonding electrons in one molecule of CCl₄.
parts.working: Each Cl has 3 non-bonding pairs = 6 electrons; 4 × 6 = 24. Carbon has no non-bonding pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the bonding in an oxygen molecule, O₂.
parts.answer: The two oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons (a double covalent bond); each also has two non-bonding pairs.
parts.working: B1 double bond / two shared pairs. B1 each O has 8 outer electrons (two lone pairs).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Oxygen boils at −183 °C. Explain why oxygen is a gas at room temperature.
parts.answer: It is made of small molecules with only weak forces between them, so little energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.working: B1 simple molecules / weak intermolecular forces. B1 little energy needed, so low boiling point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phosphorus trichloride, PCl₃, is a covalent liquid. Describe the arrangement of outer-shell electrons in one molecule in words.
parts.answer: Phosphorus shares one pair of electrons with each of the three chlorine atoms and keeps one non-bonding pair. Each chlorine has three non-bonding pairs and the shared pair, so every atom has 8 outer electrons.
parts.working: B1 three P–Cl single bonds. B1 one lone pair on P. B1 three lone pairs on each Cl / every atom has 8.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of non-bonding pairs of electrons in one molecule of PCl₃.

practice.stem:
Melting and boiling points of three halogens:
chlorine, Cl₂: m.p. −101 °C, b.p. −34 °C
bromine, Br₂: m.p. −7 °C, b.p. 59 °C
iodine, I₂: m.p. 114 °C, b.p. 184 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the physical state of each substance at 25 °C.
parts.answer: chlorine: gas; bromine: liquid; iodine: solid
parts.working: 2 marks for all three correct, 1 mark for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the trend in boiling points from chlorine to iodine.
parts.answer: The molecules get larger (more electrons), so the intermolecular forces get stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.working: B1 larger molecules down the group; B1 stronger intermolecular forces need more energy to overcome.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says 'when bromine boils, the Br–Br bonds break'. Explain why this is wrong.
parts.answer: Boiling only separates whole Br₂ molecules by overcoming weak intermolecular forces; the strong covalent Br–Br bond inside each molecule stays intact.
parts.working: B1 intermolecular forces overcome; B1 covalent bonds within molecules not broken (Br₂ molecules remain).

practice.stem:
Boiling points of four alkanes.
Alkane | formula | boiling point / °C
methane | CH₄ | −162
ethane | C₂H₆ | −89
propane | C₃H₈ | −42
butane | C₄H₁₀ | −1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the trend in boiling points.
parts.answer: Boiling point increases as the molecules get larger, because the intermolecular forces become stronger with larger molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them.
parts.working: B1 b.p. increases with number of carbon atoms / size. B1 stronger forces between molecules. B1 more energy to overcome.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which of these alkanes are gases on a winter morning in Quetta at −5 °C.
parts.answer: methane, ethane and propane (butane is a liquid below −1 °C)

parts.label: c
parts.text: LPG cylinders contain butane. Suggest why some cooks find that the burner gives a weak flame on very cold mornings.
parts.answer: At low temperature less butane boils / turns to gas, because its boiling point (−1 °C) is close to or above the temperature.
parts.working: B1 butane does not vaporise easily below its boiling point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student writes: 'When water boils, the covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen atoms break, so the bubbles are hydrogen and oxygen gas.' Explain what is wrong with this statement.
parts.answer: Boiling is a physical change: only the weak forces between water molecules are overcome. The O–H covalent bonds stay intact, so the bubbles are water molecules (steam), not hydrogen and oxygen.
parts.working: B1 intermolecular forces overcome, not covalent bonds. B1 O–H bonds remain unbroken. B1 bubbles contain H₂O (steam).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why much more energy is needed to split water into hydrogen and oxygen than to boil it.
parts.answer: Splitting water means breaking strong covalent bonds, which are much stronger than the forces between molecules.
parts.working: B1 covalent bonds much stronger than intermolecular forces.

practice.stem: Nitrogen gas, N₂, makes up about 78 % of clean, dry air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the bonding in one molecule of nitrogen, N₂, in words. Outer-shell electrons only.
parts.answer: The two nitrogen atoms share three pairs of electrons (a triple covalent bond). Each nitrogen atom also has one non-bonding pair, so each has 8 outer electrons.
parts.working: B1 triple bond = three shared pairs between the two N atoms. B1 one lone pair on each N; 8 outer electrons each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of shared electrons in one N₂ molecule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Compare N₂ with O₂, which has a double bond. State the number of shared pairs in each molecule and say which covalent bond needs more energy to break.
parts.answer: N₂ has 3 shared pairs and O₂ has 2. The N≡N triple bond needs more energy to break than the O=O double bond, so it is the stronger bond.
parts.working: B1 N₂ 3 shared pairs, O₂ 2 shared pairs. B1 triple bond is stronger / needs more energy to break.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure and bonding in a metal such as copper.
parts.answer: A giant lattice of positive metal ions in a 'sea' of delocalised electrons; the bonding is the electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
parts.working: B1 lattice of positive ions; B1 delocalised electrons / attraction between ions and electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why copper conducts electricity when solid.
parts.answer: The delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure and carry charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe metallic bonding.
parts.answer: A lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons; the bonding is the electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
parts.working: B1 positive ions in a regular lattice. B1 delocalised (mobile) electrons. B1 attraction between positive ions and electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cooking pots (degchis) are often made of aluminium or steel. Explain why metals are good conductors of heat.
parts.answer: The delocalised electrons can move through the metal and carry energy quickly; the closely packed ions also pass on vibrations.
parts.working: B1 delocalised / mobile electrons. B1 move and transfer energy through the structure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the handle of a degchi is often covered with plastic or wood.
parts.answer: Plastic and wood are poor conductors of heat, so the handle stays cool enough to hold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe in words what a labelled diagram of the structure of solid magnesium would show.
parts.answer: Rows/layers of Mg²⁺ ions in a regular, closely packed arrangement, with delocalised electrons shown between and around the ions; labels 'magnesium ion, Mg²⁺' and 'delocalised electron'.
parts.working: B1 regular arrangement of positive ions in layers, close together. B1 delocalised electrons between ions. B1 correct labels with 2+ charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many electrons each magnesium atom gives to the 'sea' of delocalised electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the sentences.
In a metal, the particles in the lattice are ____ ions. They are surrounded by ____ electrons, which are free to move. The metal is held together by the attraction between the ions and the ____.
parts.answer: positive; delocalised; electrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the sentences to explain why a metal can conduct electricity when a voltage is applied.
parts.answer: The delocalised electrons move through the metal, carrying charge.

practice.stem: Electricians in Faisalabad use copper wire for house wiring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper is drawn into thin wires for electrical cables. Explain, in terms of structure, why metals can be bent and drawn into wires without breaking.
parts.answer: The positive ions are arranged in layers. When a force is applied the layers slide over each other. The delocalised electrons move with them, so the metallic bonding is not broken.
parts.working: B1 layers of ions; B1 layers slide over one another; B1 bonding remains because electrons are delocalised (attraction kept in new positions).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Silver is beaten into very thin sheets (varq) that are used to decorate sweets. Explain, in terms of structure, why silver can be hammered into thin sheets without breaking.
parts.answer: Silver ions are arranged in layers that can slide over one another when a force is applied. The delocalised electrons move with the ions, so the attraction between ions and electrons holds the metal together in its new shape.
parts.working: B1 layers of ions. B1 layers slide over each other. B1 metallic bonding is not broken because the electrons are delocalised / bonding is not directional.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name of this property.
parts.answer: malleable (malleability)

practice.stem:
Data for three Period 3 metals.
Metal | melting point / °C | relative electrical conductivity
sodium | 98 | 21
magnesium | 650 | 23
aluminium | 660 | 38

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the number of delocalised electrons provided by each atom of Na, Mg and Al.
parts.answer: Na 1; Mg 2; Al 3
parts.working: B1 all three (equal to the number of outer electrons).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend in electrical conductivity across the three metals and suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: Conductivity increases from Na to Al, because each atom provides more delocalised electrons, so more charge carriers are available.
parts.working: B1 increases Na → Al. B1 more delocalised electrons per atom.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why aluminium has a higher melting point than sodium.
parts.answer: Aluminium ions have a 3+ charge and there are more delocalised electrons, so the attraction between ions and electrons is stronger than in sodium (1+ ions).
parts.working: B1 higher charge on ions (Al³⁺ vs Na⁺). B1 more delocalised electrons / stronger metallic bonding, more energy to overcome.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a metal still conducts electricity when it is molten.
parts.answer: The delocalised electrons are still present and free to move in the liquid metal, so they can carry charge.
parts.working: B1 delocalised electrons still present. B1 they move / carry charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Lead(II) bromide is ionic. It does not conduct when solid but does conduct when molten. Explain why its behaviour is different from a metal's.
parts.answer: In lead(II) bromide the charge carriers are ions, which are fixed in the solid and free only when molten; a metal has mobile electrons in both states.
parts.working: B1 ions are the charge carriers in lead(II) bromide and are fixed when solid. B1 metals have mobile electrons whether solid or liquid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Potassium melts at 63 °C and calcium melts at 842 °C. Both are in Period 4. Explain the difference in melting points in terms of metallic bonding.
parts.answer: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ ions and provides two delocalised electrons per atom, whereas potassium forms K⁺ ions and provides one; the attraction between the ions and the electrons is stronger in calcium, so more energy is needed to melt it.
parts.working: B1 Ca²⁺ vs K⁺ (higher charge). B1 two vs one delocalised electron per atom. B1 stronger attraction → more energy needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Potassium is soft enough to cut with a knife. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Its metallic bonding is weak, so its layers of ions are easily pushed apart / slide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium melts at 98 °C and magnesium melts at 650 °C. Both are metals in Period 3. Suggest why magnesium has the higher melting point.
parts.answer: Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ ions and gives two delocalised electrons per atom, while sodium forms Na⁺ and gives one. So the attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger in magnesium and more energy is needed to break it.
parts.working: B1 Mg²⁺ vs Na⁺ (higher charge); B1 more delocalised electrons per atom in Mg; B1 stronger metallic bonding / more energy needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity even though solid sodium does.
parts.answer: Sodium has delocalised electrons that can move; in solid sodium chloride the ions are fixed in the lattice and there are no free electrons.
parts.working: B1 metal: mobile delocalised electrons; B1 ionic solid: ions cannot move.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare how electric charge is carried in a copper wire and in aqueous copper(II) sulfate.
parts.answer: In copper wire, delocalised electrons move through the metal. In copper(II) sulfate solution, Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions move to the electrodes.
parts.working: B1 electrons in metal. B1 ions in solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When a current passes through copper(II) sulfate solution, new substances form at the electrodes. When a current passes through a copper wire, the wire is unchanged. Explain the difference.
parts.answer: In the wire, electrons enter at one end and the same number leave at the other, so no chemical change happens. In the solution, ions gain or lose electrons at the electrodes, so they are changed into new substances (electrolysis).
parts.working: B1 metal: electrons simply flow through; no reaction. B1 solution: ions discharged at electrodes / chemical change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a copper rod bends when hit with a hammer, but a crystal of sodium chloride shatters.
parts.answer: In copper the layers of positive ions slide over each other and the delocalised electrons keep holding the ions together whatever their position, so the metal changes shape. In sodium chloride, sliding brings ions of the same charge next to each other; they repel, and the crystal breaks.
parts.working: B1 metal: layers of ions slide. B1 metallic bonding is non-directional / electrons still attract ions in new positions. B1 ionic: layers shift so like charges meet. B1 repulsion → crystal splits.

practice.stem: Relative electrical conductivities: sodium 21, aluminium 38. Sodium is 2,8,1 and aluminium is 2,8,3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the conductivity of aluminium to that of sodium. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the number of delocalised electrons per atom in aluminium to that in sodium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says: 'Conductivity is directly proportional to the number of delocalised electrons per atom.' Use your answers to (a) and (b) to comment on this statement.
parts.answer: The statement is not supported: aluminium has three times as many delocalised electrons per atom but only about 1.8 times the conductivity, so other factors also matter.
parts.working: B1 not proportional (1.8 is not 3). B1 conductivity increases with more electrons, but not in proportion / other factors affect it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student writes: 'In a metal, each electron belongs to one atom and the bonding is a shared pair between two atoms, like in a covalent bond.' Explain what is wrong with this description.
parts.answer: In metallic bonding the outer electrons are not attached to particular atoms; they are delocalised over the whole structure. The atoms become positive ions, and the bonding is the attraction between all the ions and the sea of electrons, not a shared pair between two atoms.
parts.working: B1 electrons are delocalised / not owned by one atom. B1 particles are positive ions. B1 attraction between ions and sea of electrons, not localised shared pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the correct model to explain why metals have high melting points.
parts.answer: There is strong attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons throughout the giant structure, which needs a lot of energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 strong electrostatic attraction in a giant lattice.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance conducts electricity when molten but not when solid?
A sugar
B potassium chloride
C copper
D iodine
parts.answer: B potassium chloride
parts.working: Potassium chloride is ionic: its ions are fixed in the solid but free to move when molten. Copper (C) conducts both as a solid and when molten.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of structure of each substance: (i) diamond (ii) sodium chloride (iii) iodine (iv) aluminium.
parts.answer: (i) giant covalent (ii) giant ionic (iii) simple molecular (simple covalent) (iv) giant metallic

parts.label: a
parts.text: Table salt melts at 801 °C. Sugar (sucrose) is a covalent compound made of molecules; it melts at about 186 °C. Explain why salt has a much higher melting point.
parts.answer: Salt is a giant ionic lattice with strong attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout; sugar is made of molecules with only weak forces between them, which need much less energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 salt: giant ionic, strong attraction between ions. B1 sugar: simple molecules / weak intermolecular forces. B1 more energy needed to separate ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table.
Type of structure | particles present | does it conduct when solid?
giant ionic | ____ | ____
simple molecular | ____ | ____
giant covalent (diamond) | ____ | ____
giant metallic | ____ | ____
parts.answer: giant ionic: positive and negative ions, no; simple molecular: molecules, no; diamond: atoms, no; metallic: positive ions and delocalised electrons, yes

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table gives properties of four substances.
substance: melting point / conducts when solid / conducts when molten
P: 1710 °C / no / no
Q: 801 °C / no / yes
R: −95 °C / no / no
S: 1085 °C / yes / yes
Which substance has a giant ionic structure?
A P
B Q
C R
D S
parts.answer: B Q
parts.working: Q: high melting point, conducts only when molten (ions become mobile). P (A) has a high melting point but never conducts, so it is giant covalent.

practice.stem:
A student in Peshawar tests four substances.
W: m.p. 660 °C; conducts as a solid and when molten; insoluble in water
X: m.p. 80 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water
Y: m.p. 770 °C; does not conduct as a solid; conducts when molten and when dissolved in water
Z: m.p. 3550 °C; does not conduct as a solid; insoluble in water

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the type of structure of each of W, X, Y and Z. Choose from: giant ionic, giant covalent, simple molecular, metallic.
parts.answer: W: metallic; X: simple molecular; Y: giant ionic; Z: giant covalent
parts.working: B1 each. W conducts as solid; X low m.p. and non-conductor; Y conducts only molten/dissolved; Z very high m.p., insoluble, non-conductor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Y conducts electricity when dissolved in water but not when solid.
parts.answer: In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice; in solution the ions are free to move and carry charge.

practice.stem:
Properties of four substances.
Substance | melting point / °C | conducts as solid | conducts when molten | solubility in water
J | 1538 | yes | yes | insoluble
K | 44 | no | no | insoluble
L | 772 | no | yes | soluble
M | 3550 | no | no | insoluble

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the type of structure of each substance, J to M. Give a reason for each.
parts.answer: J: giant metallic (conducts as solid); K: simple molecular (low m.p., does not conduct); L: giant ionic (conducts when molten or dissolved, not as solid); M: giant covalent (very high m.p., no conduction, insoluble)
parts.working: 1 mark each for structure with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why molten sodium chloride conducts electricity but molten sulfur does not.
parts.answer: Molten sodium chloride contains ions that are free to move; molten sulfur is made of molecules, which have no charge, so there are no mobile charged particles.
parts.working: B1 NaCl: mobile ions. B1 sulfur: neutral molecules / no ions or free electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sulfur melts at 115 °C. Explain why its melting point is low.
parts.answer: Only weak forces between the sulfur molecules have to be overcome.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Electrical cables have a copper core inside a coating of PVC (a polymer made of long covalent molecules). Explain, in terms of structure, why copper is used for the core.
parts.answer: Copper has delocalised electrons that are free to move and carry charge, and its layers of ions slide so it can be drawn into wires.
parts.working: B1 delocalised electrons conduct. B1 ductile because layers slide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why PVC is used for the coating.
parts.answer: PVC is made of covalent molecules with no free electrons or ions, so it does not conduct electricity (it insulates); it is also flexible.
parts.working: B1 no mobile charged particles. B1 so it is an insulator (prevents shocks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mothballs are made of naphthalene, which has simple molecules. You can smell a mothball in a cupboard, but you cannot smell salt. Explain this difference.
parts.answer: Naphthalene molecules have only weak forces between them, so some escape from the solid as vapour at room temperature and reach your nose. In salt, the ions are held by strong attraction in a giant lattice, so no particles escape.
parts.working: B1 naphthalene: weak intermolecular forces. B1 volatile / turns to vapour (sublimes) at room temperature. B1 salt: strong ionic bonds, not volatile.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Silicon(IV) oxide melts at about 1700 °C but carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature. Both are oxides of Group IV elements. Explain the difference in terms of structure and bonding.
parts.answer: SiO₂ is a giant covalent structure: melting requires breaking many strong covalent bonds, needing a lot of energy. CO₂ is simple molecular: only weak intermolecular forces between molecules must be overcome.
parts.working: B1 SiO₂ giant covalent with many strong covalent bonds broken; B1 CO₂ simple molecules; B1 weak intermolecular forces need little energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Graphite and copper both conduct electricity. Compare how the charge is carried in each.
parts.answer: Both by delocalised electrons: in graphite each carbon atom has one delocalised electron, which moves along the layers; in copper the delocalised electrons move throughout the lattice of positive ions.
parts.working: B1 graphite: delocalised electrons (one per C, move along layers); B1 copper: sea of delocalised electrons around positive ions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why magnesium oxide is used to line furnaces but sodium chloride is not.
parts.answer: MgO has a much higher melting point (stronger attraction between 2+ and 2− ions), so it does not melt at furnace temperatures.

practice.stem:
Melting points of chlorides of Period 3 elements.
Chloride | NaCl | MgCl₂ | AlCl₃ | SiCl₄ | PCl₃
Melting point / °C | 801 | 714 | 178 (turns to vapour) | −69 | −94

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the change in melting point across the series, in terms of structure and bonding.
parts.answer: NaCl and MgCl₂ have high melting points because they are giant ionic lattices with strong attraction between ions. AlCl₃, SiCl₄ and PCl₃ have low melting points because they are made of simple molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces.
parts.working: B1 NaCl, MgCl₂ high m.p. B1 giant ionic / strong electrostatic forces. B1 AlCl₃, SiCl₄, PCl₃ low m.p. B1 simple molecular / weak forces between molecules.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether liquid SiCl₄ conducts electricity. Explain.
parts.answer: No: it consists of molecules, with no ions or free electrons.

practice.stem: Three unlabelled jars each contain a white powder. One is sodium chloride, one is silicon(IV) oxide (fine sand) and one is glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a series of simple tests that would identify which jar contains which substance. Give the expected result for each substance.
parts.answer: Add a small sample of each to water: glucose and sodium chloride dissolve, silicon(IV) oxide does not (so it is identified). Test each solution for conductivity with a battery, bulb and two electrodes: sodium chloride solution conducts (bulb lights); glucose solution does not, so it is identified.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 5: add to water and observe solubility; silicon(IV) oxide is insoluble; conductivity test on the solutions; sodium chloride solution conducts; glucose solution does not conduct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the result for sodium chloride solution in terms of particles.
parts.answer: It contains ions that are free to move and carry charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these substances in order of melting point, lowest first: magnesium, magnesium oxide, oxygen, silicon(IV) oxide. (Melting points: 650 °C, 2852 °C, −218 °C, 1710 °C.)
parts.answer: oxygen, magnesium, silicon(IV) oxide, magnesium oxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each substance, name the type of force or bond that must be overcome when it melts.
parts.answer: oxygen: weak intermolecular forces; magnesium: metallic bonding (attraction between Mg²⁺ ions and delocalised electrons); silicon(IV) oxide: covalent bonds; magnesium oxide: ionic bonding (attraction between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Graphite and aluminium both conduct electricity. Explain how each conducts.
parts.answer: Both have delocalised electrons that can move: in aluminium they come from every atom in the metallic lattice; in graphite each carbon has one electron not used in covalent bonding, delocalised along the layers.
parts.working: B1 aluminium: sea of delocalised electrons. B1 graphite: one free electron per carbon, delocalised between layers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aluminium can be rolled into foil but graphite crumbles. Explain this difference in terms of structure.
parts.answer: In aluminium, layers of ions slide but metallic bonding holds them together. In graphite, the layers slide apart easily because only weak forces hold them, but within each layer strong covalent bonds cannot bend, so graphite breaks into flakes rather than changing shape.
parts.working: B1 metal: layers slide, bonding remains. B1 graphite: weak forces between layers → layers separate / brittle.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why diamond is used in drill tips for cutting rock?
A Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a rigid giant structure.
B Diamond has delocalised electrons between layers.
C Diamond is made of small molecules with strong bonds.
D Diamond has weak forces between layers.
parts.answer: A Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a rigid giant structure.
parts.working: Four strong covalent bonds per atom in a 3-D giant lattice make diamond very hard. B and D describe graphite.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of diamond.
parts.answer: Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a giant three-dimensional lattice (tetrahedral arrangement).
parts.working: B1 each C bonded to four others. B1 giant 3D structure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why diamond has a very high melting point.
parts.answer: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken throughout the giant structure, which needs a lot of energy.
parts.working: B1 strong covalent bonds. B1 many must be broken / lots of energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why diamond does not conduct electricity.
parts.answer: All four outer electrons of each carbon atom are used in covalent bonds, so there are no delocalised electrons (and no ions) to carry charge.
parts.working: B1 all outer electrons in bonds. B1 no mobile electrons/ions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one use of diamond and the property it depends on.
parts.answer: cutting tools / drill bits (very hard) or jewellery (sparkles / hard-wearing)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three substances that have giant covalent structures.
parts.answer: diamond, graphite, silicon(IV) oxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two physical properties shared by most giant covalent substances.
parts.answer: Any two: very high melting point; insoluble in water; hard (except graphite); do not conduct (except graphite).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The 'lead' in a pencil is graphite mixed with clay. Explain, in terms of structure, why graphite leaves a mark when it is rubbed on paper.
parts.answer: Graphite is made of layers held together by weak forces, so layers easily slide off and are left on the paper.
parts.working: B1 layers with weak forces between them. B1 layers slide / flake off onto the paper.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Within each layer, the carbon atoms are held together strongly. State the type of bonding within a layer.
parts.answer: covalent bonding

practice.stem: Graphite is used as a dry lubricant in locks and as electrodes in electrolysis cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of graphite.
parts.answer: Layers of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons; each carbon is covalently bonded to three others; weak forces between the layers.
parts.working: B1 layers of hexagonal rings, each C bonded to 3 others; B1 weak forces between layers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the structure to explain why graphite (i) is used as a lubricant (ii) is used for electrodes.
parts.answer: (i) The layers can slide over each other because forces between layers are weak. (ii) Each carbon has one delocalised electron that can move and carry charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In graphite, how many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom covalently bonded to?
A 2
B 3
C 4
D 6
parts.answer: B 3
parts.working: Each carbon in graphite bonds to three others in a hexagonal layer, leaving one electron delocalised. 4 (C) is the number in diamond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sandpaper is coated with grains of silicon(IV) oxide. Explain why silicon(IV) oxide is hard enough to scratch wood and paint.
parts.answer: It is a giant covalent structure in which every atom is held by strong covalent bonds in three dimensions, so it is very difficult to break or scratch.
parts.working: B1 giant covalent lattice. B1 many strong covalent bonds in 3D.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of oxygen atoms bonded to each silicon atom and the number of silicon atoms bonded to each oxygen atom.
parts.answer: 4 oxygen atoms per silicon; 2 silicon atoms per oxygen

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why silicon(IV) oxide is used to line furnaces.
parts.answer: very high melting point (strong covalent bonds)

practice.stem: Substance Z is colourless and extremely hard. It does not melt below 3500 °C, does not conduct electricity and is insoluble in water. When strongly heated in oxygen, it burns to form carbon dioxide only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify Z. Explain how the information supports your answer.
parts.answer: Diamond. Very high melting point and no conduction show a giant covalent structure without delocalised electrons; burning to give only carbon dioxide shows it is pure carbon.
parts.working: B1 diamond. B1 m.p. and non-conductor → giant covalent, all electrons used in bonding. B1 only CO₂ formed → element carbon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Graphite also burns to give only carbon dioxide. Give one simple test that would distinguish graphite from Z.
parts.answer: Test conductivity: graphite conducts, diamond does not (or graphite is soft and marks paper).

practice.stem:
A student connects a 6 V battery, a bulb and two crocodile clips in series. She touches the clips on to each of three samples in turn.
Sample | Does the bulb light?
graphite rod | yes
small diamond crystal | no
lump of quartz (silicon(IV) oxide) | no

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which substance conducts. Explain this result.
parts.answer: Graphite; each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that can move along the layers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the diamond is tested as a single crystal and not crushed.
parts.answer: Crushing a diamond is very difficult (it is extremely hard); a single crystal makes a fair test.
parts.working: B1 too hard to crush / diamond is hardest substance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why neither silicon(IV) oxide nor diamond conducts.
parts.answer: All outer electrons are used in covalent bonds; there are no ions or free electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of silicon(IV) oxide, SiO₂.
parts.answer: A giant covalent lattice in which each silicon atom is covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms.
parts.working: B1 giant covalent / 3-D lattice; B1 each Si bonded to 4 O and each O to 2 Si.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to (a) to show that the formula is SiO₂.
parts.answer: Each Si has 4 bonds to O, but each O is shared between 2 Si, so each Si 'owns' 4 ÷ 2 = 2 O atoms; ratio Si : O = 1 : 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sand (mainly silicon(IV) oxide) is used to make glass. Explain why sand does not conduct electricity and has a high melting point.
parts.answer: No ions or delocalised electrons are free to move; many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it, needing much energy.
parts.working: B1 no mobile charged particles; B1 many strong covalent bonds.

practice.stem: The density of diamond is 3.51 g/cm³ and the density of graphite is 2.26 g/cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 1.00 g of diamond and of 1.00 g of graphite. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: diamond 0.285 cm³; graphite 0.442 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest, in terms of structure, why graphite has a lower density than diamond.
parts.answer: Graphite's layers are relatively far apart, with large spaces between them; in diamond the atoms are packed closely in all three directions.
parts.working: B1 large gaps between layers in graphite. B1 diamond atoms tightly bonded in 3D.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Both are forms of carbon. Explain why graphite is soft but diamond is hard.
parts.answer: In graphite the layers slide over each other because only weak forces act between them; in diamond every atom is held by four strong covalent bonds in three dimensions.
parts.working: B1 graphite: weak forces between layers. B1 diamond: rigid 3D network of covalent bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In diamond, each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds, and each bond is shared between two atoms. Calculate the number of C–C bonds in 12 g of diamond (1 mole of carbon atoms, 6.02 × 10²³ atoms).

parts.label: b
parts.text: In graphite, each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds. Calculate the number of C–C bonds in 12 g of graphite.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Graphite has fewer covalent bonds per atom, yet its melting point is very similar to diamond's. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To melt graphite, the strong covalent bonds within the layers must still be broken; the weak forces between layers are not the main barrier.
parts.working: B1 melting graphite needs strong covalent bonds within layers to break.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Graphite is used as the electrodes in the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide. Give two properties of graphite that make it suitable and explain each in terms of structure.
parts.answer: Conducts electricity (delocalised electrons in each layer); very high melting point, so it does not melt in the hot electrolyte (strong covalent bonds within layers must be broken).
parts.working: B1 conducts. B1 delocalised electrons. B1 high melting point. B1 many strong covalent bonds. (Accept fairly unreactive / cheap as a property if explained.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The graphite anodes slowly wear away and must be replaced. Explain why.
parts.answer: Oxygen is formed at the hot anode and reacts with the carbon to make carbon dioxide, so the anode burns away.
parts.working: B1 oxygen produced at anode. B1 reacts with carbon to form CO₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Diamond and iodine both contain only covalent bonds between their atoms. Diamond does not melt below 3500 °C, but iodine melts at 114 °C. Explain this difference.
parts.answer: Iodine consists of separate I₂ molecules: melting only overcomes the weak forces between the molecules, and the I–I covalent bonds are not broken. Diamond is a giant covalent lattice with no separate molecules: melting requires breaking a huge number of strong C–C covalent bonds.
parts.working: B1 iodine: simple molecules. B1 weak intermolecular forces overcome (covalent bonds not broken). B1 diamond: giant covalent structure. B1 many strong covalent bonds must break.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a mixture?
A air
B water
C sodium chloride
D copper
parts.answer: A air
parts.working: Air contains nitrogen, oxygen and other gases not chemically combined, in variable proportions. Water (B) is a compound with a fixed composition.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these substances is a compound?
A air
B brass
C carbon dioxide
D sulfur
parts.answer: C carbon dioxide
parts.working: Carbon dioxide contains carbon and oxygen chemically joined in a fixed ratio. Brass (B) is an alloy, a mixture of copper and zinc that are not chemically combined.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by (i) an element (ii) a compound.
parts.answer: (i) a substance made of only one type of atom (ii) a substance containing two or more elements chemically bonded together in a fixed proportion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of each from substances found in a kitchen.
parts.answer: element: e.g. aluminium (foil), copper, oxygen; compound: e.g. water, sodium chloride (salt), sugar, carbon dioxide

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student mixes iron filings and powdered sulfur. Describe how she could separate the iron from the mixture.
parts.answer: Use a magnet; the iron is attracted and the sulfur is left behind.

parts.label: b
parts.text: She heats another sample of the mixture. It glows red and forms a black solid, iron(II) sulfide. Explain why a magnet no longer separates the iron.
parts.answer: The iron has chemically combined with sulfur to form a new compound with different properties; iron(II) sulfide is not magnetic like iron.
parts.working: B1 chemical reaction / new compound formed. B1 compound has different properties from its elements.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one other difference between the mixture and the compound.
parts.answer: e.g. the mixture can have any proportions but the compound has a fixed ratio Fe:S; making the compound releases energy; the compound's colour is different.

practice.stem:
Four boxes of particles are described.
Box W: single atoms, all of the same kind, not joined.
Box X: molecules each made of two identical atoms joined together.
Box Y: identical molecules, each made of one atom of one kind joined to two atoms of a different kind.
Box Z: some molecules made of two identical atoms and some molecules made of two different atoms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify the contents of each box as an element, a compound or a mixture.
parts.answer: W: element; X: element; Y: compound; Z: mixture
parts.working: 1 mark each. X is an element because both atoms in each molecule are the same kind.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether each change is physical or chemical: (i) dissolving sugar in water (ii) burning magnesium ribbon (iii) melting candle wax (iv) a silver spoon turning black in air.
parts.answer: (i) physical (ii) chemical (iii) physical (iv) chemical

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one sign that a chemical change has taken place.
parts.answer: e.g. a new substance forms; colour change; gas given off; energy released; difficult to reverse

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each of the following as an element, a compound or a mixture: nitrogen, glucose, sea water, magnesium oxide, mercury, brass.
parts.answer: elements: nitrogen, mercury; compounds: glucose, magnesium oxide; mixtures: sea water, brass
parts.working: 3 marks for all six correct; 2 marks for 4–5; 1 mark for 2–3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two differences between a compound and a mixture.
parts.answer: A compound has a fixed composition and its elements are chemically bonded (can only be separated by chemical reactions); a mixture has variable composition, its components are not chemically bonded and can be separated by physical methods. A compound's properties differ from those of its elements.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: fixed vs variable composition; chemically combined vs not; separated by chemical vs physical means; properties of compound different from its elements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each substance as an element, a compound or a mixture: tap water, distilled water, steel, ozone (O₃), ammonia, petrol, glucose, neon.
parts.answer: elements: ozone, neon; compounds: distilled water, ammonia, glucose; mixtures: tap water, steel, petrol
parts.working: 4 marks all correct; 3 marks 6–7; 2 marks 4–5; 1 mark 2–3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ozone, O₃, is an element even though it is made of molecules.
parts.answer: Each molecule contains only one type of atom (oxygen).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of magnesium in magnesium oxide, MgO. (Ar: Mg, 24; O, 16)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student burns 1.2 g, 2.4 g and 3.6 g of magnesium. State the mass of magnesium oxide formed each time.
parts.working: M1 mass of MgO = mass of Mg ÷ 0.60. A1 all three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how these results show that magnesium oxide is a compound and not a mixture.
parts.answer: The percentage of magnesium is always the same (fixed composition), whereas a mixture can have any proportions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distilled water boils at 100 °C. A sample of river water from the Indus starts to boil at 100.3 °C and the temperature slowly rises as it boils. Explain these observations.
parts.answer: Distilled water is a pure compound, so it boils at a fixed temperature. River water is a mixture containing dissolved substances, so it boils above 100 °C and over a range of temperatures.
parts.working: B1 pure substance has a fixed boiling point. B1 mixture / impurities raise b.p. and give a range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a method to obtain pure water from the river water.
parts.answer: distillation

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium is a soft, very reactive metal. Chlorine is a poisonous green gas. They react to form sodium chloride, which we eat in food. Explain why the compound has such different properties from its elements.
parts.answer: In a compound the elements are chemically bonded (here as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions), so it is a new substance with its own properties, not a mixture of the elements' properties.
parts.working: B1 chemical bonding forms a new substance. B1 properties of compound differ from those of its elements (atoms changed to ions).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gases explodes when lit, forming water. Give two ways in which water is different from the mixture of gases.
parts.answer: Any two: water is a liquid at room temperature; it does not burn / explode; it has a fixed composition (H:O = 2:1 atoms); separating it needs a chemical reaction (e.g. electrolysis).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of different elements and the total number of atoms shown in each formula: (i) Ca(OH)₂ (ii) (NH₄)₂SO₄ (iii) CuSO₄·5H₂O
parts.answer: (i) 3 elements, 5 atoms (ii) 4 elements, 15 atoms (iii) 4 elements, 21 atoms
parts.working: 1 mark each for both numbers correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ammonium sulfate is used as a fertiliser. Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in it. (Ar: N, 14; H, 1; S, 32; O, 16) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem:
Two students heat iron with sulfur.
Experiment 1: 5.6 g iron + 3.2 g sulfur → 8.8 g iron(II) sulfide, nothing left over.
Experiment 2: 5.6 g iron + 4.0 g sulfur → 8.8 g iron(II) sulfide and 0.8 g of sulfur left over.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the mass of iron(II) sulfide is the same in both experiments.
parts.answer: Iron and sulfur always combine in a fixed ratio; 5.6 g of iron can only combine with 3.2 g of sulfur, so the extra 0.8 g of sulfur in experiment 2 is left unreacted.
parts.working: B1 fixed ratio in a compound. B1 excess sulfur does not react.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in iron(II) sulfide. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the mass of sulfur needed to react exactly with 14.0 g of iron.

practice.stem: Boiling points: nitrogen −196 °C, argon −186 °C, oxygen −183 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two pieces of evidence that air is a mixture and not a compound.
parts.answer: Any two: its composition varies (e.g. water vapour, CO₂ levels); its components can be separated by a physical method (fractional distillation of liquid air); each gas keeps its own properties; there is no fixed formula; liquid air boils over a range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Liquid air at −200 °C is allowed to warm slowly. Use the data to state which gas boils off first and which last. Explain.
parts.answer: Nitrogen first (lowest boiling point, −196 °C); oxygen last (highest, −183 °C).
parts.working: B1 nitrogen first. B1 oxygen last because it has the highest boiling point.

practice.stem: A student heats 10.0 g of a white solid strongly in a crucible until its mass stops changing. A gas is given off and 5.6 g of white residue remains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the original mass that is lost on heating.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the result shows that the white solid is a compound and not an element.
parts.answer: It breaks down on heating into a gas and a different solid, so it must contain more than one element; an element cannot be split into simpler substances.
parts.working: B1 it decomposes into two (simpler) substances. B1 elements cannot be broken down by chemical means.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The gas turns limewater milky. Identify the gas and suggest the identity of the white solid.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide; calcium carbonate (residue calcium oxide)
parts.working: B1 CO₂. B1 calcium carbonate (accept any carbonate consistent with 44 % loss: CaCO₃).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which metal is extracted from its oxide by electrolysis rather than by heating with carbon?
A aluminium
B iron
C zinc
D copper
parts.answer: A aluminium
parts.working: Aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide. Iron (B) is below carbon and is extracted with carbon (as carbon monoxide) in the blast furnace.

practice.stem: Iron is made in a blast furnace from hematite, coke, limestone and hot air.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the purpose of each raw material:
(i) coke
(ii) limestone
(iii) hot air
parts.answer: (i) burns to provide heat and forms carbon monoxide, the reducing agent (ii) removes acidic impurities such as silicon(IV) oxide, forming slag (iii) provides oxygen for the coke to burn

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the main ore of iron used.
parts.answer: hematite (iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write equations for: (i) the formation of carbon monoxide from coke in two steps (ii) the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide.
parts.answer: (i) C + O₂ → CO₂ then CO₂ + C → 2CO (ii) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
parts.working: B1 C + O₂ → CO₂; B1 CO₂ + C → 2CO; B1 balanced reduction equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In the reaction in (a)(ii), name the substance that is reduced and the reducing agent.
parts.answer: iron(III) oxide is reduced; carbon monoxide is the reducing agent

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Zinc can be extracted by heating zinc oxide with carbon, but magnesium cannot be extracted by heating magnesium oxide with carbon. Why?
A Carbon is more reactive than zinc but less reactive than magnesium.
B Carbon is less reactive than zinc but more reactive than magnesium.
C Magnesium oxide has a lower melting point than zinc oxide.
D Zinc is more reactive than magnesium.
parts.answer: A Carbon is more reactive than zinc but less reactive than magnesium.
parts.working: Carbon can only remove oxygen from oxides of metals below it in the reactivity series: zinc is below carbon, magnesium is above it. B reverses the order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an ore.
parts.answer: A rock (naturally occurring mineral) from which a metal can be extracted profitably.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the main ore of (i) iron (ii) aluminium.
parts.answer: (i) hematite (ii) bauxite

parts.label: c
parts.text: Gold is found in rivers in northern Pakistan as the metal itself, not as a compound. Explain why.
parts.answer: Gold is very unreactive, so it does not react with oxygen, water or other substances in the ground.
parts.working: B1 very low in reactivity series / unreactive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Limestone decomposes in the furnace. Write the equation.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calcium oxide reacts with silicon(IV) oxide (sand) to form slag. Write the equation and name the slag.
parts.answer: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃; calcium silicate

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain this reaction in terms of the types of oxide involved.
parts.answer: Calcium oxide is a basic oxide and silicon(IV) oxide is an acidic oxide, so they react (neutralise) to form a salt.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how the slag and the molten iron are removed separately.
parts.answer: Slag is less dense, so it floats on the molten iron and is tapped off at a higher level.

practice.stem: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of aluminium oxide (from bauxite) dissolved in molten cryolite, using carbon electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite rather than melted on its own.
parts.answer: Aluminium oxide has a very high melting point (over 2000 °C); the solution in molten cryolite works at a much lower temperature (about 950 °C), saving energy and cost.
parts.working: B1 lowers the operating temperature; B1 saves energy / cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equations for the reactions at the cathode and at the anode.
parts.answer: cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al; anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the carbon anodes must be replaced regularly.
parts.answer: The oxygen produced at the hot anodes reacts with the carbon to form carbon dioxide, so the anodes burn away.
parts.working: B1 oxygen reacts with carbon; B1 forms CO₂ / anodes wear away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict which of these oxides can be reduced by heating with carbon: magnesium oxide, zinc oxide, copper(II) oxide, aluminium oxide. Explain your choice.
parts.answer: zinc oxide and copper(II) oxide; zinc and copper are less reactive than carbon, so carbon can remove the oxygen. Magnesium and aluminium are more reactive than carbon.
parts.working: B1 zinc oxide; B1 copper(II) oxide (and no others); B1 reason based on position relative to carbon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student heats black copper(II) oxide with carbon powder in a crucible. Write the balanced equation and state what is seen at the end.
parts.answer: 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂; pink-brown (orange-brown) solid copper forms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a method of extraction for each metal: potassium, zinc, iron, copper, silver. Choose from: electrolysis of a molten compound; heating the oxide with carbon; found uncombined or by simple heating.
parts.answer: potassium: electrolysis; zinc: heating with carbon; iron: heating with carbon; copper: heating with carbon; silver: found uncombined (native) / simple heating
parts.working: 3 marks all five; 2 marks four; 1 mark three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the link between the position of a metal in the reactivity series and how difficult it is to extract.
parts.answer: The more reactive the metal, the more stable its compounds and the harder it is to extract; the most reactive need electrolysis, which uses a lot of electricity and is expensive.
parts.working: B1 more reactive → more difficult to extract / compounds more stable. B1 metals above carbon need electrolysis.

practice.stem: Zinc is used to galvanise steel. In one method of extraction, zinc oxide is heated with carbon in a furnace.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of zinc oxide with carbon to form zinc and carbon monoxide.
parts.answer: ZnO + C → Zn + CO

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the substance that is reduced and the reducing agent. Explain your answer in terms of oxygen.
parts.answer: Zinc oxide is reduced (it loses oxygen); carbon is the reducing agent (it removes oxygen and is oxidised).
parts.working: B1 ZnO reduced. B1 carbon reducing agent, gains oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Zinc boils at 907 °C and the furnace works at about 1100 °C. Suggest how the zinc is collected.
parts.answer: The zinc leaves the furnace as a vapour and is condensed (cooled) to liquid/solid zinc.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Iron from the blast furnace contains about 4 % carbon. State one property that makes this iron unsuitable for most uses.
parts.answer: It is brittle (hard but breaks easily).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how this iron is converted into steel.
parts.answer: Oxygen is blown through the molten iron, which oxidises carbon (and other impurities) to gases such as carbon dioxide; calcium oxide (a basic oxide) is added to react with acidic oxides such as silicon dioxide, forming slag, which is removed.
parts.working: B1 oxygen blown through molten iron. B1 carbon removed as CO/CO₂. B1 basic oxide (CaO) added to remove acidic impurities as slag.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of iron that can be obtained from 800 tonnes of iron(III) oxide. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)
parts.answer: 560 tonnes
parts.working: M1 Mr Fe₂O₃ = 160 and 112 t Fe in every 160 t; A1 800 × 112 ÷ 160 = 560 t.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of hematite ore is 90 % iron(III) oxide by mass. Calculate the maximum mass of iron from 1000 tonnes of this ore.
parts.answer: 630 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the actual mass of iron produced is less than this.
parts.answer: Not all the iron oxide is reduced / some iron is lost in the slag.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The overall reaction is 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. Calculate the mass of aluminium produced from 51 tonnes of aluminium oxide. (Ar: Al = 27, O = 16)
parts.answer: 27 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen produced at the same time.
parts.answer: 24 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why recycling aluminium cans is better than extracting new aluminium.
parts.answer: Recycling uses much less electrical energy; it conserves bauxite ore; it reduces waste in landfill; less mining and land damage.

practice.stem:
Zinc blende, ZnS, is roasted in air and the zinc oxide is then reduced with carbon.
2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂
ZnO + C → Zn + CO

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of zinc sulfide, ZnS. (Ar: Zn, 65; S, 32)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of zinc, in tonnes, that can be obtained from 1.94 tonnes of zinc sulfide.
parts.answer: 1.30 tonnes
parts.working: M1 1 mol ZnS → 1 mol Zn, so mass = 1.94 × 65 ÷ 97. A1 1.30 t.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the sulfur dioxide produced must not be released into the air, and one way it can be used.
parts.answer: Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain (and harms breathing); it can be converted into sulfuric acid (Contact process).
parts.working: B1 acid rain / toxic. B1 used to make sulfuric acid.

practice.stem: In the blast furnace: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of iron in 1.12 kg of iron. (Ar: Fe, 56)
parts.answer: 20 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon monoxide, measured at room temperature and pressure, needed to produce 1.12 kg of iron. (1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.)
parts.answer: 720 dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: The carbon dioxide formed reacts with hot coke higher up the furnace. Write the equation and explain why this is useful.
parts.answer: CO₂ + C → 2CO; it regenerates carbon monoxide, the reducing agent, so more iron oxide can be reduced.
parts.working: B1 equation. B1 makes more CO for reduction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copper is used for electrical wiring in houses. Which two properties make it suitable?
A good electrical conductor and ductile
B high density and brittle
C low melting point and hard
D reacts with water and conducts heat
parts.answer: A good electrical conductor and ductile
parts.working: Wiring needs a metal that conducts electricity well and can be drawn into wires (ductile). B is wrong: copper is not brittle, and density is not the reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three physical properties that are typical of metals.
parts.answer: Any three of: good conductors of electricity; good conductors of heat; malleable; ductile; shiny when freshly cut; high melting and boiling points; high density; sonorous.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one chemical property that is typical of metals.
parts.answer: Metals form basic oxides / form positive ions / reactive metals produce hydrogen with dilute acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property is NOT typical of metals?
