A high density
B forms acidic oxides
C malleable
D good conductor of heat
parts.answer: B forms acidic oxides
parts.working: Metal oxides are basic (or amphoteric); acidic oxides are typical of non-metals. High density (A) is typical of most metals, even though a few are light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper is heated strongly in air. Describe the colour change seen.
parts.answer: pink-brown (orange-brown) to black

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO

parts.label: c
parts.text: Copper(II) oxide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid but not with sodium hydroxide solution. State what this shows about copper(II) oxide.
parts.answer: It is a basic oxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each use, give one property of the metal that makes it suitable.
(i) aluminium foil used to wrap naan
(ii) gold used for jewellery
(iii) steel girders used in buildings
parts.answer: (i) malleable / non-toxic / does not corrode (ii) shiny / does not corrode or tarnish / malleable (iii) strong

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why aluminium is used for overhead power cables. Give two properties.
parts.answer: Good electrical conductor; low density (light, so pylons can support it); resistant to corrosion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why aluminium is used to make aircraft bodies.
parts.answer: Low density (strong but light, especially as an alloy) and resistant to corrosion because of its oxide layer.
parts.working: B1 low density; B1 corrosion resistance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why copper is used for water pipes.
parts.answer: It does not react with water / is unreactive and does not corrode easily; it is easy to bend (malleable).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid, and give one observation.
parts.answer: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂; effervescence (bubbles) / magnesium disappears / mixture gets warm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calcium reacts with cold water. Write the balanced equation and describe a test for the gas produced.
parts.answer: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂; a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
parts.working: B1 formulae; B1 balanced; B1 test and result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is seen when copper is added to dilute hydrochloric acid, and explain.
parts.answer: No reaction (no bubbles), because copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of zinc with dilute sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the test for the gas produced.
parts.answer: A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of gas, at room temperature and pressure, formed when 1.30 g of zinc reacts completely. (Ar: Zn, 65; 1 mol of gas occupies 24 000 cm³ at r.t.p.)
parts.answer: 480 cm³

practice.stem:
Element X: shiny grey solid; conducts electricity; its oxide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form a salt and water.
Element Y: dull yellow solid that breaks into powder when hit; does not conduct; its oxide dissolves in water to give a solution of pH 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the information to classify elements X and Y as metals or non-metals. Give two pieces of evidence for each.
parts.answer: X is a metal: it is shiny, conducts electricity and its oxide is basic (reacts with acid to form a salt). Y is a non-metal: it is a dull, brittle solid that does not conduct, and its oxide is acidic (pH 2).
parts.working: B1 X metal. B1 two pieces of evidence. B1 Y non-metal. B1 two pieces of evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper is used for cooking pots. Explain, using the reactivity series, why copper does not react with water or with dilute acids to give off hydrogen.
parts.answer: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it is less reactive than hydrogen and cannot displace hydrogen from water or from acid.
parts.working: B1 copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series. B1 so it cannot displace hydrogen (no reaction).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one other property of copper that makes it suitable for a cooking pot.
parts.answer: e.g. high melting point; unreactive with water/food; malleable to shape

parts.label: c
parts.text: Aluminium is used for overhead power cables rather than copper, although copper is a better conductor. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Aluminium has a much lower density, so the cables are lighter and need fewer/lighter pylons; aluminium is also cheaper.
parts.working: B1 low density / lighter. B1 cheaper (or resists corrosion).

practice.stem:
Data for four metals:
metal: density / g/cm³, relative electrical conductivity, cost, resistance to corrosion
W: 2.7, 61, low, good
X: 8.9, 100, high, good
Y: 7.9, 17, low, poor
Z: 19.3, 73, very high, excellent

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which metal is best for overhead power cables? Use the data to explain.
parts.answer: W: low density with good conductivity, low cost and good corrosion resistance.
parts.working: B1 W; B1 two supporting data points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative conductivity divided by density for W and for X. Give your answers to 3 significant figures and explain what they show.
parts.answer: W: 22.6; X: 11.2. W conducts about twice as well as X for the same mass of cable.
parts.working: M1 61 ÷ 2.7; A1 22.6 and 11.2; B1 W better per unit mass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why Y is not used for a bridge near the sea in Gwadar unless it is protected.
parts.answer: Y has poor corrosion resistance; it would corrode (rust) quickly in moist, salty air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series but aluminium cooking pots do not react with water. Explain why.
parts.answer: Aluminium is covered by a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide that sticks to the surface and stops water reaching the metal.
parts.working: B1 oxide layer; B1 layer protects / prevents further reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A piece of aluminium foil is placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. At first nothing happens; after a few minutes bubbles appear quickly. Suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: The acid first reacts with / removes the oxide layer (no gas). Once the metal is exposed, the reactive aluminium reacts with the acid, giving hydrogen.
parts.working: B1 oxide layer removed by acid first; B1 then Al reacts producing hydrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: A 0.36 g piece of magnesium ribbon reacts completely with excess acid. Calculate the volume of hydrogen formed at r.t.p. (Ar: Mg, 24; 1 mol of gas = 24 000 cm³)
parts.answer: 360 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of magnesium chloride formed. (Ar: Cl, 35.5) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem: A metal M forms M²⁺ ions. 0.65 g of M reacts completely with excess dilute hydrochloric acid: M + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂. The hydrogen formed has a volume of 240 cm³ at r.t.p. (1 mol of gas = 24 000 cm³)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of hydrogen produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative atomic mass of M and identify M.
parts.answer: 65; zinc

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is important that all the metal reacts and that the acid is in excess.
parts.answer: So that the volume of hydrogen corresponds to the whole mass of metal; otherwise the moles (and Ar) would be wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Most metal oxides are basic. State what is meant by a basic oxide and give an example.
parts.answer: An oxide that reacts with an acid to form a salt and water (and does not react with alkalis); e.g. magnesium oxide, copper(II) oxide, calcium oxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aluminium oxide and zinc oxide are amphoteric. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: They react with both acids and alkalis (to form salts).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how you could show that zinc oxide is amphoteric, using reagents found in a school laboratory.
parts.answer: Add zinc oxide to dilute hydrochloric acid: it dissolves (forms zinc chloride). Add zinc oxide to warm aqueous sodium hydroxide: it also dissolves.
parts.working: B1 dissolves in acid. B1 dissolves in alkali (NaOH).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mixture reacts?
A copper and aqueous zinc sulfate
B iron and aqueous copper(II) sulfate
C silver and aqueous iron(II) sulfate
D copper and aqueous magnesium chloride
parts.answer: B iron and aqueous copper(II) sulfate
parts.working: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from solution. In A, copper is less reactive than zinc, so there is no reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A piece of magnesium ribbon is placed in blue aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Give two observations.
parts.answer: The blue colour fades; a pink-brown solid (copper) forms on the magnesium; the solution gets warm; the magnesium gets smaller.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced equation and the ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Mg + CuSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Cu; Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this is called a displacement reaction.
parts.answer: The more reactive magnesium takes the place of (displaces) the less reactive copper from its compound.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Metal X displaces copper from aqueous copper(II) sulfate but does not displace zinc from aqueous zinc sulfate. What could X be?
A iron
B magnesium
C silver
D gold
parts.answer: A iron
parts.working: X must be more reactive than copper but less reactive than zinc: iron fits. Magnesium (B) would displace both copper and zinc.

practice.stem:
Equal-sized pieces of four metals are put in dilute hydrochloric acid.
magnesium: rapid fizzing, metal disappears quickly
zinc: steady fizzing
iron: slow bubbling
copper: no change

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the observations to put the metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first.
parts.answer: magnesium, zinc, iron, copper

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the salt formed when zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: zinc chloride

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which of these metals react with dilute hydrochloric acid? silver, zinc, copper, magnesium, iron
parts.answer: zinc, magnesium and iron
parts.working: 2 marks all three and no others; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas given off in these reactions and state the test for it.
parts.answer: hydrogen; squeaky pop with a lighted splint

practice.stem:
A student places small pieces of metals P, Q and R in solutions of their nitrates and records whether a reaction happens (✓) or not (✗).
P in Q nitrate: ✓   P in R nitrate: ✓
Q in P nitrate: ✗   Q in R nitrate: ✓
R in P nitrate: ✗   R in Q nitrate: ✗

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put the metals P, Q and R in order of reactivity, most reactive first. Explain how you decided.
parts.answer: P > Q > R. P displaces both Q and R; Q displaces only R; R displaces neither.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether R would react with dilute hydrochloric acid if R is copper. Explain.
parts.answer: No; copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one safety precaution and one way to make the comparison fair.
parts.answer: Wear eye protection; use the same size / mass of each metal and the same volume and concentration of solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how potassium, calcium and copper react (if at all) with cold water.
parts.answer: Potassium: reacts violently, melts, moves around and the hydrogen burns with a lilac flame. Calcium: reacts steadily with bubbling, forming a cloudy solution. Copper: no reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water but reacts with steam. Write the equation for the reaction with steam.
parts.answer: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the order of reactivity in terms of the tendency to form positive ions.
parts.answer: The more reactive the metal, the more easily its atoms lose electrons to form positive ions.

practice.stem:
A student adds 1 g of each metal powder (an excess) to 25 cm³ of the same aqueous copper(II) sulfate in a polystyrene cup, stirs, and records the highest temperature.
Metal | starting temperature / °C | highest temperature / °C
magnesium | 22.0 | 47.5
zinc | 22.5 | 34.0
iron | 21.5 | 28.0
copper | 22.0 | 22.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise for each metal.
parts.answer: magnesium 25.5 °C; zinc 11.5 °C; iron 6.5 °C; copper 0 °C
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the results to put the metals in order of reactivity. Explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: magnesium > zinc > iron > copper; the bigger the temperature rise, the more reactive the metal compared with copper (more energy released).
parts.working: B1 order. B1 larger rise = more reactive / bigger difference in reactivity from copper.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why there is no temperature change with copper.
parts.answer: Copper cannot displace itself, so no reaction takes place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give two variables that must be kept the same to make this a fair test.
parts.answer: Any two: volume and concentration of copper(II) sulfate; mass/moles of metal (in excess); particle size (powder); same insulated cup; stirring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A coil of copper wire is placed in colourless aqueous silver nitrate. Give two observations.
parts.answer: Grey/silver crystals form on the wire; the solution turns blue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic equation and use it to explain which species is oxidised.
parts.answer: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag; copper is oxidised because it loses electrons.
parts.working: B1 ionic equation. B1 Cu loses electrons → oxidised.

practice.stem: A student plans to put pieces of magnesium, iron and copper separately into aqueous magnesium sulfate, iron(II) sulfate and copper(II) sulfate (nine combinations).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict which of the nine combinations react.
parts.answer: magnesium + iron(II) sulfate; magnesium + copper(II) sulfate; iron + copper(II) sulfate
parts.working: 2 marks all three and no others; 1 mark two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For the reaction between iron and copper(II) sulfate, describe what is seen.
parts.answer: A pink-brown coating of copper forms on the iron; the blue solution fades (to pale green).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the total number of reactions predicted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The thermite reaction is used to weld railway lines: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe. Explain why this reaction happens.
parts.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than iron, so it removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.
parts.answer: oxidising agent: iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃); reducing agent: aluminium

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iron formed from 5.4 g of aluminium. (Ar: Al = 27, Fe = 56)

practice.stem:
A metal M is tested.
M in aqueous zinc sulfate: no change
M in aqueous copper(II) sulfate: brown coating forms, solution fades
M in dilute sulfuric acid: slow bubbling

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to place M in the reactivity series relative to zinc, copper and hydrogen.
parts.answer: Below zinc, above copper and above hydrogen.
parts.working: B1 between zinc and copper; B1 above hydrogen (reacts with acid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: M forms M²⁺ ions. Write an ionic equation for the reaction of M with copper(II) ions.
parts.answer: M + Cu²⁺ → M²⁺ + Cu

parts.label: c
parts.text: Plan an experiment using temperature changes to check whether M is more reactive than iron. Give the measurements and how you would decide.
parts.answer: Add equal masses of powdered M and powdered iron separately to equal volumes of the same copper(II) sulfate solution in an insulated cup; measure the starting and highest temperatures; the metal giving the larger temperature rise is more reactive.
parts.working: B1 same mass/particle size and volume/concentration of CuSO₄; B1 measure initial and maximum temperature; B1 larger rise = more reactive.

practice.stem: An iron nail of mass 5.60 g is left in excess aqueous copper(II) sulfate. 1.12 g of iron reacts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. Calculate the mass of copper formed when 1.12 g of iron reacts. (Ar: Fe, 56; Cu, 64)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming all the copper sticks to the nail, calculate the final mass of the nail.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mass of the nail increases even though iron is lost from it.
parts.answer: Each iron atom (Ar 56) is replaced by a copper atom of greater mass (Ar 64).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mixture of magnesium powder and copper(II) oxide is heated. A vigorous reaction takes place. Write the equation and explain why the reaction happens.
parts.answer: Mg + CuO → MgO + Cu; magnesium is more reactive than copper, so it takes the oxygen from copper(II) oxide.
parts.working: B1 equation. B1 Mg more reactive than Cu.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of copper formed from 0.48 g of magnesium with excess copper(II) oxide. (Ar: Mg, 24; Cu, 64)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict whether zinc powder reacts when heated with magnesium oxide. Explain.
parts.answer: No: zinc is less reactive than magnesium, so it cannot remove oxygen from magnesium oxide.

practice.stem:
A student makes simple cells by dipping a strip of copper and a strip of another metal into the same salt solution and measuring the voltage. A positive reading means the other metal is the negative electrode.
Other metal | voltage / V
magnesium | +2.7
zinc | +1.1
iron | +0.8
silver | −0.46

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to put the metals magnesium, zinc, iron, copper and silver in order of reactivity, most reactive first. Explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: magnesium, zinc, iron, copper, silver; the bigger the voltage with copper, the further the metal is above copper; silver gives a reversed (negative) reading because it is less reactive than copper.
parts.working: B1 order. B1 reasoning based on size and sign of voltage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the voltage of a cell made with magnesium and zinc electrodes in the same electrolyte.
parts.answer: about 1.6 V

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which metal would form the negative electrode in the magnesium–zinc cell. Explain.
parts.answer: Magnesium: it is more reactive, so it loses electrons more readily.

practice.stem:
A student sets up four test tubes, each containing an iron nail, and leaves them for one week.
A: nail in tap water, open to the air
B: nail in boiled water with a layer of oil on top
C: nail in dry air with anhydrous calcium chloride, tube stoppered
D: nail in salt water, open to the air

parts.label: a
parts.text: In which tubes does the nail rust?
parts.answer: A and D

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of boiling the water and adding a layer of oil in tube B.
parts.answer: Boiling removes dissolved air (oxygen); the oil stops air dissolving back into the water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What do the results show is needed for iron to rust?
parts.answer: Both water and oxygen (air).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest which tube rusts fastest and why.
parts.answer: D: salt water speeds up rusting.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which method protects a steel ship's hull by sacrificial protection?
A painting the hull
B coating the hull with oil
C attaching blocks of zinc to the hull
D covering the hull with plastic
parts.answer: C attaching blocks of zinc to the hull
parts.working: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes instead of the steel. A, B and D are barrier methods and stop protecting if the coating is damaged.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Suggest the most suitable method of rust prevention for each object, and give a reason.
(i) the body of a car
(ii) the gears in a machine
(iii) a steel garden fence
(iv) an underground steel gas pipe
parts.answer: (i) paint – barrier, looks good; (ii) oil/grease – barrier that also lubricates moving parts; (iii) paint, plastic coating or galvanising – barrier; (iv) sacrificial protection with blocks of magnesium/zinc – pipe cannot be painted again once buried
parts.working: 1 mark each for a sensible method with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water. Explain why rusting is an oxidation reaction.
parts.answer: Iron gains oxygen (and iron atoms lose electrons to form Fe³⁺ ions).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the chemical name of rust.
parts.answer: hydrated iron(III) oxide

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the appearance of a rusted iron nail compared with a new one.
parts.answer: Orange-brown and flaky instead of grey and shiny.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the sentences.
Rusting of iron needs both ____ and ____. Coating iron with grease prevents rusting because it acts as a ____ that keeps these substances away from the iron.
parts.answer: water; oxygen (air); barrier

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why painting a bicycle chain would not be a good way to stop it rusting.
parts.answer: The paint would crack or rub off as the chain moves/bends, exposing the iron.

practice.stem: Galvanised steel sheets are widely used for roofs of sheds and cattle shelters in rural Punjab.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by galvanising.
parts.answer: Coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A galvanised steel roof sheet is scratched, exposing the steel. Explain why the steel still does not rust.
parts.answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so zinc loses electrons (is oxidised) in preference to iron. The zinc corrodes instead of the iron (sacrificial protection).
parts.working: B1 zinc more reactive; B1 zinc oxidised / loses electrons instead of iron; B1 iron protected even where exposed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a painted steel gate starts to rust when the paint is chipped.
parts.answer: Paint is only a barrier; once broken, water and oxygen reach the iron.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the chemical name of rust and write a word equation for its formation.
parts.answer: hydrated iron(III) oxide; iron + water + oxygen → hydrated iron(III) oxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why cars in Karachi rust faster than cars in a dry inland city.
parts.answer: Karachi is coastal: the air is humid and contains salt, and salt (an electrolyte) speeds up rusting.
parts.working: B1 more moisture; B1 salt speeds up rusting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two barrier methods for preventing rusting of a bicycle and say which part each is used for.
parts.answer: Paint for the frame; oil or grease for the chain; plastic coating for the basket / handlebars.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two matched methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which iron object will rust fastest?
A a painted gate in a dry desert town
B an iron nail in salt water, open to the air
C an iron nail in boiled water under a layer of oil
D a greased bicycle chain kept indoors
parts.answer: B an iron nail in salt water, open to the air
parts.working: Rusting needs water and oxygen, and dissolved salt speeds it up. In C the boiled water has had dissolved air removed and the oil stops air re-entering, so there is almost no oxygen.

practice.stem: Blocks of magnesium are attached by wires to steel water pipes buried underground in Islamabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the magnesium blocks stop the steel pipe from rusting.
parts.answer: Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it is oxidised (loses electrons) instead of the iron. The electrons flow to the steel, so iron does not form ions; the magnesium corrodes rather than the steel.
parts.working: B1 Mg more reactive than iron. B1 Mg oxidised / loses electrons in preference. B1 iron is protected (does not lose electrons).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the blocks must be replaced every few years.
parts.answer: The magnesium is used up as it corrodes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why copper blocks would not protect the pipe.
parts.answer: Copper is less reactive than iron, so the iron would corrode instead (faster).

practice.stem:
A student puts three cleaned iron nails in each of three conditions for one week and records the gain in mass of each nail.
Condition | nail 1 / g | nail 2 / g | nail 3 / g
distilled water, open to air | 0.011 | 0.013 | 0.012
salt water, open to air | 0.031 | 0.029 | 0.033
boiled water with a layer of oil | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean mass gain for each condition.
parts.answer: distilled water 0.012 g; salt water 0.031 g; boiled water + oil 0.000 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two conclusions from the results.
parts.answer: Iron rusts in water and air; salt water speeds up rusting; without oxygen (boiled water under oil) no rusting occurs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the nails are rubbed with sandpaper before the experiment.
parts.answer: To remove any oil, paint or existing rust/oxide so all nails start with clean surfaces (fair test).

practice.stem: A fishing boat at Gwadar has a 5.0 kg zinc block fixed to its steel hull. The block loses 1.3 kg each year by corrosion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many years it takes until only 20 % of the original mass of the block is left. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.1 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why zinc is used rather than painting the hull below the water line only.
parts.answer: Paint can be scratched or damaged, exposing steel; zinc protects the steel even where it is exposed, because zinc is more reactive and corrodes instead.
parts.working: B1 paint can be damaged. B1 zinc gives sacrificial protection even at scratches.

practice.stem: A student pushes damp iron wool into the bottom of a measuring cylinder and turns it upside down in a trough of water. The volume of air trapped is 100.0 cm³ at the start. After eight days, when the reading has stopped changing, the volume is 79.2 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the air used up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas that was used up and explain why the water level rose.
parts.answer: Oxygen; it reacted with the iron to form rust, so the volume of gas fell and water moved up to take its place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student waited until the reading stopped changing.
parts.answer: To make sure all the oxygen had reacted.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one source of error and one improvement.
parts.answer: Error: temperature or pressure changes alter the gas volume; reading not at eye level / meniscus. Improvement: keep at constant temperature and read at the same temperature; use more iron wool (or wet it) so all the oxygen reacts; repeat and average.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tin is less reactive than iron. Food cans are made of steel coated with tin. Explain why a scratched tin can rusts quickly at the scratch.
parts.answer: Once the steel is exposed, the iron is more reactive than tin, so the iron corrodes (loses electrons) in preference; the tin offers no sacrificial protection and may even speed up rusting.
parts.working: B1 iron more reactive than tin. B1 iron corrodes instead of tin / no sacrificial protection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a scratched galvanised (zinc-coated) bucket does not rust at the scratch.
parts.answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes instead of the exposed iron (sacrificial protection).
parts.working: B1 zinc more reactive. B1 zinc oxidised instead of iron.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why food cans are coated with tin rather than zinc.
parts.answer: Zinc would react with acids in food (zinc compounds could get into food); tin is less reactive.

practice.stem: Assume that iron rusts according to the equation 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iron(III) oxide formed from 2.8 g of iron. (Ar: Fe, 56; O, 16)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen, in cm³ at r.t.p., used in this reaction. (1 mol of gas = 24 000 cm³)
parts.answer: 900 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the mass of rust actually formed is larger than your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide; it also contains water.

practice.stem:
A student wants to show that both water and oxygen are needed for rusting.
Tube A: iron nail in tap water, open to the air.
Tube B: iron nail held above some anhydrous calcium chloride (a drying agent); the tube is left open.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After a week, the nail in tube B has rusted slightly. Suggest two reasons why.
parts.answer: Water vapour from the air can enter because the tube is not sealed; the anhydrous calcium chloride may already be partly used up / not enough to absorb all water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student should change the experiment so that it shows that water is needed for rusting.
parts.answer: Seal tube B with a stopper (and use fresh anhydrous calcium chloride); keep everything else the same as tube A.
parts.working: B1 seal tube. B1 fresh/enough drying agent (control other variables).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a further tube she could set up to show that oxygen is needed.
parts.answer: A nail in water that has been boiled (to remove dissolved air), covered with a layer of oil.

practice.stem: Sialkot is known for making surgical instruments and cutlery from stainless steel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an alloy.
parts.answer: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually metals).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the two metals in brass.
parts.answer: copper and zinc

parts.label: c
parts.text: Stainless steel contains iron, chromium and nickel. Give one use of stainless steel and the property that makes it suitable.
parts.answer: Cutlery / kitchen sinks / surgical instruments; it is hard and resists rusting.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why is an alloy usually harder than the pure metal it is made from?
A Atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide easily.
B The alloy contains covalent bonds between the atoms.
C The alloy has no delocalised electrons.
D The atoms in an alloy are all the same size and packed more tightly.
parts.answer: A Atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide easily.
parts.working: Different-sized atoms distort the layers, making it harder for layers to slide. B and C are wrong: alloys still have metallic bonding with delocalised electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is an alloy?
A steel
B iron(III) oxide
C cryolite
D graphite
parts.answer: A steel
parts.working: Steel is a mixture of iron with carbon (and sometimes other metals). Iron(III) oxide (B) is a compound, not a mixture of a metal with another element.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the main elements in (i) steel (ii) brass.
parts.answer: (i) iron and carbon (ii) copper and zinc

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one use of brass and one use of stainless steel.
parts.answer: brass: e.g. musical instruments, door fittings, plug pins, decorative items; stainless steel: e.g. cutlery, surgical instruments, sinks, chemical plant

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, what a labelled diagram of an alloy would show, compared with a pure metal.
parts.answer: A pure metal: identical atoms/ions in regular layers. An alloy: mostly the same atoms but with some atoms of a different size spread among them, distorting the layers.
parts.working: B1 regular layers of same-size atoms in pure metal. B1 different-sized atoms disrupt layers in alloy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to (a) to explain why steel is harder than pure iron.
parts.answer: The different-sized atoms make it harder for the layers to slide over each other.
parts.working: B1 layers cannot slide as easily. B1 so the alloy is harder/stronger.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of structure, why brass is harder than pure copper. You may describe a diagram in words.
parts.answer: In pure copper the atoms are all the same size and arranged in regular layers that slide easily. In brass the zinc atoms are a different size; they distort the layers so the layers cannot slide over each other easily, so brass is harder.
parts.working: B1 pure metal: regular layers slide easily; B1 alloy: atoms of different sizes disrupt layers; B1 layers cannot slide easily → harder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Brass is used for door handles and musical instruments. Give one reason, other than hardness, why brass is used rather than iron.
parts.answer: It does not rust / resists corrosion; attractive gold colour.

practice.stem:
A metallurgist measures the hardness of copper–zinc alloys (higher number = harder).
% zinc: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40
hardness: 40, 52, 63, 75, 86

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the hardness changes as the percentage of zinc increases.
parts.answer: Hardness increases as the percentage of zinc increases (by about 11–12 units per 10 % zinc).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the hardness of an alloy containing 25 % zinc.
parts.answer: 69 (accept 68–70)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why an alloy with 30 % zinc is better than pure copper for making screws and hinges.
parts.answer: It is much harder (75 vs 40) so it is stronger and less easily bent or worn, while still resisting corrosion.
parts.working: B1 harder / stronger; B1 data quoted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mild steel contains about 0.25 % carbon. Give one property and one use of mild steel.
parts.answer: property: strong but easily shaped (malleable); use: car bodies, machinery, nails, wire

parts.label: b
parts.text: Stainless steel contains chromium and nickel as well as iron. Give the main advantage of stainless steel over mild steel.
parts.answer: It resists corrosion / does not rust.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why mild steel, not stainless steel, is used to build most bridges.
parts.answer: Mild steel is much cheaper; it can be painted to prevent rusting.

practice.stem: The purity of gold is measured in carats: pure gold is 24 carat, so 18-carat gold is 18/24 gold by mass. Much jewellery in Pakistan is made of 21-carat gold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of gold in 21-carat gold.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of pure gold in one tola (11.66 g) of 21-carat gold. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why jewellery is usually made from gold alloyed with copper or silver rather than from pure (24-carat) gold.
parts.answer: Pure gold is very soft; the alloy is harder and more hard-wearing (and cheaper).
parts.working: B1 harder/does not bend or scratch easily.

practice.stem: One type of stainless steel contains 74 % iron, 18 % chromium and 8 % nickel by mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of each metal in a 2.50 kg stainless steel pan.
parts.answer: iron 1.85 kg; chromium 0.45 kg; nickel 0.20 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why stainless steel is described as a mixture and not a compound.
parts.answer: The metals are not chemically combined and the proportions can vary.

practice.stem: Density of an aluminium alloy used for aircraft = 2800 kg/m³; density of steel = 7900 kg/m³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of a 0.50 m³ panel made of (i) the aluminium alloy (ii) steel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why aircraft bodies are made of aluminium alloy rather than steel.
parts.answer: The alloy panel is about 2550 kg lighter, so the aircraft uses less fuel / can carry more load.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an aluminium alloy is used instead of pure aluminium.
parts.answer: Pure aluminium is too soft/weak; the alloy is stronger.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 250 g sample of brass contains 64 % copper by mass. Calculate the masses of copper and zinc in the sample.
parts.answer: copper 160 g; zinc 90 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of copper atoms to zinc atoms. Give your answer as x : 1 to 3 significant figures. (Ar: Cu = 64, Zn = 65)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why brass is described as a mixture and not a compound.
parts.answer: The metals are not chemically combined in a fixed ratio; the composition of brass can vary (and it keeps the metallic properties of its components).
parts.working: B1 not chemically bonded / no fixed formula; B1 variable composition.

practice.stem: An aluminium alloy used in aircraft contains 95.6 % aluminium and 4.4 % copper by mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of aluminium atoms to copper atoms in this alloy. Give your answer as x : 1, with x to 3 significant figures. (Ar: Al, 27; Cu, 64)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Even though there is only about one copper atom for every fifty aluminium atoms, the alloy is much stronger than pure aluminium. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Each copper atom is a different size and distorts the regular layers around it, so layers cannot slide easily; many slip planes are blocked by relatively few atoms.
parts.working: B1 copper atoms different size / distort layers. B1 layers slide less easily → stronger.

practice.stem:
A student compares the hardness of copper and brass. She places a steel ball bearing on a sheet of each metal and drops a 1 kg mass onto it from 50 cm. She measures the diameter of the dent made.
Metal | dent 1 / mm | dent 2 / mm | dent 3 / mm
copper | 3.2 | 3.4 | 3.3
brass | 2.1 | 2.3 | 2.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean dent diameter for each metal.
parts.answer: copper 3.3 mm; brass 2.2 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which metal is harder. Explain how the results show this.
parts.answer: Brass: it has the smaller dent, so it resisted the impact more.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two variables that must be kept the same.
parts.answer: Any two: mass of the weight; height of drop; size of ball bearing; thickness of the metal sheets; same surface underneath.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to make the measurement of the dent diameter more accurate.
parts.answer: Use a magnifying glass/travelling microscope or vernier calipers; measure two diameters at right angles and average.

practice.stem: 100 tonnes of molten iron from the blast furnace contains 4.0 % carbon by mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon that must be removed to make steel containing 0.50 % carbon. Assume only carbon is removed. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.52 tonnes
parts.working: M1 iron (non-carbon) = 96.0 t, carbon = 4.0 t. M1 carbon left x: x ÷ (96.0 + x) = 0.0050, x = 0.482 t. A1 removed = 4.0 − 0.482 = 3.52 t.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why changing the percentage of carbon changes the properties of steel.
parts.answer: Carbon atoms are a different size from iron atoms and disrupt the layers; more carbon makes the steel harder and stronger but more brittle, less carbon makes it softer and more malleable.
parts.working: B1 carbon atoms disrupt layers. B1 more carbon → harder/more brittle (or less carbon → more malleable).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term electrolysis.
parts.answer: The decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by the passage of an electric current.
parts.working: Breakdown/decomposition of ionic compound (molten or aqueous) by electricity B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Explain why.
parts.answer: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move; when molten the ions are free to move and carry the charge.
parts.working: Ions cannot move in solid B1; ions free to move when molten B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the electrode at which sodium is produced and state its charge.
parts.answer: the cathode, negative

practice.stem: Molten lead(II) bromide, PbBr₂, is electrolysed using graphite electrodes in a fume cupboard.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen at the anode (positive electrode).
parts.answer: red-brown vapour/gas (bromine)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product at the cathode and describe its appearance.
parts.answer: lead; silvery/grey liquid metal (collects as beads at the bottom)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write ionic half-equations for the reactions at the cathode and at the anode.
parts.answer:
Cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb
Anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the electrolysis is done in a fume cupboard.
parts.answer: Bromine (and lead vapour) are toxic.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What are the products?
A sodium at the cathode, chlorine at the anode
B hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode
C hydrogen at the cathode, oxygen at the anode
D sodium at the cathode, oxygen at the anode
parts.answer: B hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode
parts.working: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions (from water) are discharged at the cathode; at high concentration Cl⁻ is discharged at the anode. A would only happen with molten sodium chloride.

practice.stem: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed using platinum electrodes. The gases are collected in two test-tubes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gas formed at the cathode and the gas formed at the anode.
parts.answer: cathode: hydrogen; anode: oxygen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a test for each gas and the result.
parts.answer: Hydrogen: lighted splint gives a squeaky pop. Oxygen: relights a glowing splint.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the ratio of the volume of gas at the cathode to the volume at the anode.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In electrolysis, which electrode do positive ions move towards? Name this electrode.
parts.answer: the negative electrode, the cathode

parts.label: b
parts.text: Molten calcium bromide, CaBr₂, is electrolysed. Name the products at the cathode and at the anode.
parts.answer: cathode: calcium; anode: bromine

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the ions are oxidised or reduced at each electrode.
parts.answer: Calcium ions are reduced (gain electrons) at the cathode; bromide ions are oxidised (lose electrons) at the anode.
parts.working: Reduction at cathode B1; oxidation at anode B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance conducts electricity and is decomposed by it?
A copper
B molten zinc chloride
C solid sodium chloride
D liquid ethanol
parts.answer: B molten zinc chloride
parts.working: Molten zinc chloride is an ionic compound with mobile ions, so it is an electrolyte. Copper conducts but is not decomposed; solid NaCl has fixed ions; ethanol is covalent with no ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Molten potassium iodide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Name the product at each electrode.
parts.answer: cathode: potassium; anode: iodine

parts.label: b
parts.text: Electrons flow in the external wires. In which direction do they flow: from the anode to the cathode, or from the cathode to the anode?
parts.answer: from the anode to the cathode (through the external circuit)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the particles that carry the current through the molten potassium iodide.
parts.answer: ions (K⁺ and I⁻)

practice.stem: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using carbon (graphite) electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen at the cathode and at the anode.
parts.answer: cathode: pink-brown solid (copper) forms; anode: bubbles of colourless gas (oxygen)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.
parts.answer: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the anode.
parts.answer: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ (or 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻)

parts.label: d
parts.text: The blue colour of the solution fades during the electrolysis. Explain why.
parts.answer: Cu²⁺ ions (which give the blue colour) are removed from the solution as copper metal.

practice.stem:
Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using copper electrodes. Before the experiment the anode has a mass of 15.40 g and the cathode 15.10 g. After 30 minutes the anode has a mass of 14.76 g.
[Ar: Cu, 64]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode.
parts.answer: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the mass of the cathode after 30 minutes.
parts.working: Anode lost 0.64 g; same mass gained at cathode: 15.10 + 0.64 = 15.74 B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of electrons that passed through the circuit.
parts.working: 0.64 ÷ 64 = 0.010 mol Cu M1; × 2 = 0.020 mol electrons A1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the blue colour of the solution does not change.
parts.answer: Cu²⁺ ions are added at the anode at the same rate as they are removed at the cathode.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride and very dilute aqueous sodium chloride are each electrolysed with inert electrodes. Name the gas formed at the anode in each case.
parts.answer: concentrated: chlorine; very dilute: oxygen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference.
parts.answer: In concentrated solution there are many chloride ions so Cl⁻ is discharged; in very dilute solution OH⁻ ions (from water) are discharged instead, giving oxygen.
parts.working: Concentration of Cl⁻ decides; high Cl⁻ → chlorine, low → oxygen from hydroxide/water B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the gas formed at the cathode in both cases and explain why sodium is not formed.
parts.answer: Hydrogen; sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions (from water) are discharged instead.
parts.working: Hydrogen B1; Na more reactive than H B1

practice.stem: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is electrolysed using carbon electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.
parts.answer: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the anode.
parts.answer: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test for the gas formed at the anode, with the result.
parts.answer: Damp blue litmus paper turns red and then is bleached (white).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write the overall equation for the electrolysis.
parts.answer: 2HCl → H₂ + Cl₂

practice.stem:
Each electrolyte is electrolysed with inert electrodes.
1 molten potassium bromide
2 concentrated aqueous potassium bromide
3 aqueous silver nitrate
4 concentrated aqueous copper(II) chloride

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the product at the cathode for each electrolyte.
parts.answer: 1 potassium; 2 hydrogen; 3 silver; 4 copper
parts.working: All four B2; two or three B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product at the anode for each electrolyte.
parts.answer: 1 bromine; 2 bromine; 3 oxygen; 4 chlorine
parts.working: All four B2; two or three B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the anode product for electrolyte 3 is different from the others.
parts.answer: Nitrate ions are not discharged (there is no halide ion), so hydroxide ions/water are discharged, giving oxygen.
parts.working: No halide present; OH⁻ from water discharged instead B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Aqueous sodium sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes. A few drops of universal indicator are added. What colour is seen near each electrode?
A cathode red, anode blue/purple
B cathode blue/purple, anode red
C both electrodes green
D both electrodes red
parts.answer: B cathode blue/purple, anode red
parts.working: At the cathode H⁺ is removed (H₂ forms), leaving excess OH⁻, so the solution becomes alkaline (blue/purple). At the anode OH⁻ is removed (O₂ forms), leaving excess H⁺ (red). A has the two reversed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride, the solution left behind becomes alkaline. Name the alkali formed.
parts.answer: sodium hydroxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the solution becomes alkaline.
parts.answer: H⁺ ions are removed at the cathode (as H₂) and Cl⁻ ions at the anode (as Cl₂); Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions are left in solution.
parts.working: H⁺ and Cl⁻ removed B1; Na⁺ and OH⁻ remain B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.
parts.answer: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sodium metal can be produced by electrolysing molten sodium chloride but not by electrolysing aqueous sodium chloride.
parts.answer: In aqueous solution, H⁺ ions from the water are also present; hydrogen is less reactive than sodium, so H⁺ is discharged instead of Na⁺. In the melt only Na⁺ is present at the cathode.
parts.working: Water provides H⁺ ions B1; H⁺ discharged in preference because sodium is more reactive (only Na⁺ in the melt) B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of electrons, why the reaction at the cathode is reduction.
parts.answer: The ions gain electrons at the cathode.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why electrolysis of molten compounds uses a lot of energy.
parts.answer: Energy is needed to melt the compound (high melting point) as well as to drive the current.

practice.stem:
Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed until 4.14 g of lead has formed at the cathode.
[Ar: Pb, 207; Br, 80]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of lead formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of bromine formed at the anode.
parts.working: Moles Br₂ = moles Pb = 0.020 M1; 0.020 × 160 = 3.2 g A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of electrons transferred.

practice.stem:
Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with platinum electrodes. 60 cm³ of hydrogen is collected at the cathode, measured at room temperature and pressure.
[One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the volume of oxygen formed at the anode at r.t.p.
parts.answer: 30 cm³
parts.working: Half the volume of hydrogen B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the formation of oxygen at the anode.
parts.answer: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ (or 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of electrons that passed.
parts.working: Moles H₂ = 60 ÷ 24 000 = 0.0025 M1; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ so electrons = 0.0050 mol A1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the concentration of the sulfuric acid increases during the electrolysis.
parts.answer: Water is used up (decomposed into hydrogen and oxygen), so the same amount of acid is in less water.

practice.stem:
Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using inert electrodes. 1.28 g of copper is deposited on the cathode.
[Ar: Cu, 64. One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of electrons needed to deposit this copper.
parts.working: 1.28 ÷ 64 = 0.020 mol Cu M1; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so 0.040 mol e⁻ A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: The anode reaction is 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻. Calculate the volume of oxygen formed at r.t.p., in cm³.
parts.answer: 240 cm³

practice.stem:
A jeweller electrolyses aqueous silver nitrate with inert electrodes. 2.16 g of silver forms on the cathode.
[Ar: Ag, 108. One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.
parts.answer: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen, at r.t.p., formed at the anode. Give your answer in cm³.
parts.answer: 120 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what happens to the pH of the solution during the electrolysis. Explain.
parts.answer: pH decreases (becomes acidic): OH⁻ removed at anode leaves H⁺ / nitric acid in solution.

practice.stem:
A student electrolyses dilute sulfuric acid with carbon electrodes and collects the gases in two inverted measuring cylinders full of the acid.
Time / min | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
Volume at cathode / cm³ | 8 | 16 | 24 | 32 | 40
Volume at anode / cm³ | 3 | 7 | 11 | 15 | 19

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate at which gas forms at the cathode, in cm³/min.
parts.answer: 8 cm³/min

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the volume at the anode after 5 minutes if the gases behaved exactly as the equation predicts.
parts.answer: 20 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: After the first minute, the anode volume increases by 4 cm³ each minute. Use this to show that the ratio of the rates of formation is as expected.
parts.answer: 8 : 4 = 2 : 1, the expected ratio of H₂ to O₂

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why less oxygen was collected than expected.
parts.answer: Any two of: oxygen is more soluble in water than hydrogen, so some dissolves in the acid at first; some oxygen reacts with the carbon anode to form carbon dioxide; a leak/gas lost before collection began.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: oxygen dissolves in the solution (more soluble than H₂); oxygen reacts with/oxidises the carbon anode (CO₂ formed); gas lost/leak

practice.stem: An aqueous solution of an unknown salt Z is electrolysed with carbon electrodes. A pink-brown solid forms on the cathode. A pale yellow-green gas forms at the anode; it bleaches damp litmus paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the products at each electrode.
parts.answer: cathode: copper; anode: chlorine

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the name of salt Z and state whether the solution is concentrated or dilute. Explain.
parts.answer: Copper(II) chloride, concentrated: chlorine (not oxygen) is formed, so the chloride ion concentration must be high.
parts.working: Copper(II) chloride B1; concentrated, because Cl⁻ discharged rather than OH⁻ B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Copper forms at the cathode but hydrogen does not. Explain why.
parts.answer: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so Cu²⁺ ions are discharged in preference to H⁺ ions.

practice.stem:
A student electrolyses concentrated aqueous potassium iodide with carbon electrodes in a U-tube. Observations:
cathode: bubbles of a colourless gas; a drop of phenolphthalein near this electrode turns pink
anode: the colourless solution turns yellow-brown; no gas is seen

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the product at the anode and write its half-equation.
parts.answer: iodine; 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas at the cathode and explain why the phenolphthalein turns pink.
parts.answer: Hydrogen; H⁺ ions from water are discharged, leaving OH⁻ ions (with K⁺), so the solution near the cathode becomes alkaline.
parts.working: Hydrogen B1; OH⁻ left in excess / potassium hydroxide forms B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could confirm that the yellow-brown substance is iodine.
parts.answer: Add starch solution: it turns blue-black.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aqueous sodium sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Write half-equations for the reactions at the cathode and at the anode.
parts.answer:
Cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (or 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻)
Anode: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why neither sodium nor any sulfur-containing product forms.
parts.answer: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen so H⁺ is discharged instead of Na⁺; sulfate ions are not discharged, so hydroxide ions/water are discharged instead.
parts.working: Na⁺ not discharged as Na is more reactive than H B1; SO₄²⁻ not discharged, OH⁻ discharged instead B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the total amount of sodium sulfate in the solution does not change, even though the electrolysis continues for an hour.
parts.answer: Only water is decomposed; the Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions stay in solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the overall equation for the reaction in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.
parts.answer: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of a hydrogen fuel cell car compared with a petrol car.
parts.answer: The only product is water (no CO₂, CO or oxides of nitrogen from the car).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cell cars.
parts.answer: Any one of: hydrogen is difficult/expensive to store (high pressure); few refuelling stations; hydrogen is flammable/explosive; much hydrogen is made from fossil fuels.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is produced, apart from electrical energy, in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
A carbon dioxide only
B water only
C carbon dioxide and water
D hydrogen peroxide
parts.answer: B water only
parts.working: Hydrogen combines with oxygen to form water; there is no carbon in the fuel, so no carbon dioxide is made (unlike option C, from burning a hydrocarbon).

practice.stem: A small hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell powers a weather station high in the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether hydrogen is oxidised or reduced in the fuel cell. Explain in terms of electrons.
parts.answer: Oxidised; hydrogen loses electrons (H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ / forms water).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a word equation for the overall reaction in the fuel cell.
parts.answer: hydrogen + oxygen → water

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a fuel cell is more suitable than a petrol generator for this remote weather station.
parts.answer: Any one: no exhaust fumes/pollutants; quiet; few moving parts so little maintenance; more efficient so less fuel has to be carried up.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe a chemical test that shows the liquid produced by the cell contains water, and give the result.
parts.answer: Add anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: it turns from white to blue (or anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride: blue to pink).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two reactants used in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.
parts.answer: Hydrogen and oxygen (from air)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the only chemical product.
parts.answer: Water

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the useful form of energy produced.
parts.answer: Electrical energy

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one way hydrogen for fuel cells can be produced.
parts.answer: Electrolysis of water / from methane (natural gas) and steam

practice.stem:
A transport company compares two cars.
Petrol car: refuelling time 3 minutes; range 600 km; exhaust gases carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and water vapour; thousands of filling stations in Pakistan.
Hydrogen fuel cell car: refuelling time 5 minutes; range 500 km; exhaust water vapour only; very few hydrogen filling stations in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the information to give two advantages of the fuel cell car.
parts.answer: Any two: no carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas) released; no carbon monoxide (toxic); no oxides of nitrogen (acid rain); only water vapour is produced.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two pollutants it avoids (or 'only water vapour').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the information to give two disadvantages of the fuel cell car.
parts.answer: Very few hydrogen filling stations; shorter range (500 km against 600 km) / longer refuelling time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the petrol car's exhaust contains carbon monoxide.
parts.answer: Incomplete combustion of the petrol (not enough oxygen).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one way in which a fuel cell differs from an ordinary battery (dry cell).
parts.answer: A fuel cell keeps working as long as hydrogen and oxygen are supplied; a battery runs flat when its chemicals are used up (and must be recharged or replaced).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why hydrogen is difficult to use as a fuel in cars.
parts.answer: Any two: it is a gas, so it must be stored under high pressure or as a liquid (bulky tanks); it is highly flammable/explosive with air; few refuelling stations; production often uses fossil fuels.

practice.stem: State whether each statement about a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is true or false.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Statement 1: a fuel cell produces carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: False

parts.label: b
parts.text: Statement 2: a fuel cell needs a continuous supply of fuel.
parts.answer: True

parts.label: c
parts.text: Statement 3: hydrogen loses electrons in a fuel cell.
parts.answer: True

parts.label: d
parts.text: Statement 4: a fuel cell changes electrical energy into chemical energy.
parts.answer: False (it changes chemical energy into electrical energy).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A delivery company in Islamabad is choosing between petrol vans and hydrogen fuel cell vans. Give two environmental advantages of the fuel cell vans.
parts.answer: No carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas) from the van; no carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen or particulates (less air pollution / smog).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: no CO₂; no CO; no NOₓ/SO₂; no particulates; only water produced

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using fuel cell vans may still cause some carbon dioxide emission overall.
parts.answer: The hydrogen is often made using fossil fuels (e.g. from methane) or electricity from fossil-fuel power stations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one practical disadvantage for the company.
parts.answer: Hydrogen is hard to store / few filling stations / vans more expensive.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, what happens at the electrode where oxygen is supplied?
A Hydrogen gains electrons.
B Oxygen gains electrons and is reduced.
C Oxygen loses electrons and is oxidised.
D Water is broken down into hydrogen and oxygen.
parts.answer: B Oxygen gains electrons and is reduced.
parts.working: Oxygen molecules take electrons from the external circuit, so oxygen is reduced. Hydrogen loses electrons at the other electrode; splitting water is electrolysis, the reverse of a fuel cell.

practice.stem:
In one type of fuel cell, these reactions happen:
Electrode 1: 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻
Electrode 2: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻

parts.label: a
parts.text: At which electrode is hydrogen oxidised? Explain using the half-equations.
parts.answer: Electrode 1; hydrogen loses electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Combine the half-equations to give the overall equation.
parts.answer: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
parts.working: M1 4 electrons cancel (2H₂ in electrode 1 and O₂ in electrode 2) and OH⁻ cancel; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which electrode is the negative terminal of the cell.
parts.answer: Electrode 1 (where hydrogen gives up electrons)

practice.stem: A hydrogen fuel cell car uses about 1.0 kg of hydrogen to travel 100 km.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water produced when the car uses 1.0 kg of hydrogen. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O  [Ar: H, 1; O, 16]
parts.answer: 9.0 kg
parts.working: M1 500 mol H₂ → 500 mol H₂O; A1 × 18 g = 9.0 kg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Both burning hydrogen and using it in a fuel cell release energy. State the main energy change in each.
parts.answer: Burning: chemical energy → heat (thermal) energy; fuel cell: chemical energy → electrical energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the fuel cell is more efficient than burning hydrogen in an engine.
parts.answer: Less energy is wasted as heat.

practice.stem:
A student supplies hydrogen to a small fuel cell at different rates. Air is supplied at a fixed rate. The current produced is measured.
Hydrogen supplied / cm³ per min: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
Current / mA: 32, 64, 95, 128, 128

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the current changes as the rate of hydrogen supply increases.
parts.answer: The current is (directly) proportional to the hydrogen supply up to 8 cm³/min; then it stays constant at 128 mA.
parts.working: B1 proportional/increases steadily at first; B1 constant above 8 cm³/min.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the current does not increase above 8 cm³ of hydrogen per minute.
parts.answer: Another factor now limits the reaction, e.g. the oxygen (air) supply is fixed, so extra hydrogen cannot react.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of hydrogen supplied in 30 minutes at 6 cm³ per minute. [one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one variable, other than the air supply, that must be kept the same.
parts.answer: Temperature / the same fuel cell (electrodes) / the same electrolyte.

practice.stem: Some spacecraft use hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen needed each day if the fuel cells use 2.0 kg of hydrogen per day. [Ar: H, 1; O, 16]
parts.answer: 16 kg
parts.working: M1 1000 mol H₂ needs 500 mol O₂; A1 × 32 g = 16 kg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of fuel cells for a spacecraft, apart from producing electricity.
parts.answer: The water produced can be used for drinking.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why fuel cells are preferred to petrol engines inside a spacecraft.
parts.answer: No harmful/carbon dioxide gases in a sealed cabin (and no moving parts).

practice.stem: A hydrogen filling station near Karachi makes hydrogen by the electrolysis of water, using electricity from solar panels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the decomposition of water into hydrogen and oxygen.
parts.answer: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen, at r.t.p., produced at the same time as 4.0 kg of hydrogen. [Ar: H, 1; one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a fuel cell car using this hydrogen is responsible for much less carbon dioxide than one using hydrogen made from methane.
parts.answer: The electricity comes from solar energy (renewable), so no fossil fuel is burned and no CO₂ is released in making the hydrogen.

practice.stem:
A fuel cell bus uses 0.40 kg of hydrogen on a short journey.
[Ar: H, 1; O, 16. One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of hydrogen used.
parts.answer: 200 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water produced, in kg.
parts.answer: 3.6 kg
parts.working: moles H₂O = moles H₂ = 200 M1; 200 × 18 = 3600 g = 3.6 kg A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen used, at r.t.p., in dm³.
parts.answer: 2400 dm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: In the fuel cell, hydrogen loses electrons at one electrode. State whether hydrogen is oxidised or reduced. Explain.
parts.answer: Oxidised, because it loses electrons.

practice.stem: A laboratory fuel cell uses 3.6 dm³ of hydrogen at r.t.p. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O  [one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of hydrogen in 3.6 dm³ at r.t.p.
parts.answer: 0.15 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen used at r.t.p.
parts.answer: 1.8 dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water formed. [Mr: H₂O, 18]

parts.label: d
parts.text: Each H₂ molecule gives up two electrons. Calculate the number of moles of electrons that flow through the external circuit.
parts.answer: 0.30 mol

practice.stem: Energy released when 1 mole of fuel is completely oxidised: hydrogen 286 kJ; methane 890 kJ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per gram for each fuel. Give answers to 3 significant figures. [Mr: H₂, 2; CH₄, 16]
parts.answer: Hydrogen 143 kJ/g; methane 55.6 kJ/g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrogen releases more energy per gram, yet a car's hydrogen tank is much larger than a methane (CNG) tank for the same journey. Explain.
parts.answer: Hydrogen has a very low density; even when compressed, a given volume holds much less mass/energy than methane.
parts.working: B1 low density; B1 energy per volume is small.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one environmental advantage of hydrogen over methane as a fuel.
parts.answer: It produces only water, no carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas).

practice.stem: The tank of a fuel cell car holds 5.0 kg of hydrogen gas at very high pressure. [Ar: H, 1; one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of hydrogen in the full tank.
parts.answer: 2500 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume this hydrogen would occupy at r.t.p.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each mole of hydrogen that reacts releases 286 kJ of energy. The fuel cell turns 60 % of this into electrical energy. Calculate the electrical energy from a full tank, in MJ.
parts.answer: 429 MJ

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one safety hazard of storing hydrogen at very high pressure in a car.
parts.answer: A leak (e.g. after a crash) could form an explosive mixture with air / the tank could burst.

practice.stem: A petrol car in Lahore burns octane, C₈H₁₈, as its fuel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed when 1.00 kg of octane burns completely. 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O  [Mr: C₈H₁₈, 114; CO₂, 44]. Give 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A fuel cell car produces no carbon dioxide while driving. Explain why it may still be responsible for carbon dioxide emissions.
parts.answer: The hydrogen may be made from methane/fossil fuels, releasing CO₂; or the electricity for electrolysis may come from fossil-fuel power stations.
parts.working: B1 production of hydrogen; B1 named fossil source.

practice.stem: A school kit has a small solar panel, an electrolysis unit that splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, gas storage tubes, a fuel cell and a small fan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the energy changes in the whole kit, starting with sunlight.
parts.answer: Light → electrical (solar panel) → chemical (electrolysis makes H₂ and O₂) → electrical (fuel cell) → kinetic (fan).
parts.working: B1 light → electrical → chemical; B1 chemical → electrical → kinetic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the volume of hydrogen collected is about twice the volume of oxygen.
parts.answer: Water is H₂O; 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, so 2 moles of hydrogen form for each mole of oxygen, and equal moles of gas have equal volumes.
parts.working: B1 equation/ratio; B1 equal moles occupy equal volumes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student collects 18 cm³ of hydrogen and 10 cm³ of oxygen. Calculate the volume of oxygen that is used when all the hydrogen reacts in the fuel cell, and the volume of oxygen left over.
parts.answer: 9 cm³ used; 1 cm³ left

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the fan runs for only a short time.
parts.answer: Only a very small amount of hydrogen is stored.

practice.stem: A craftsman in Peshawar electroplates a steel spoon with silver.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what should be used as the cathode and what should be used as the anode.
parts.answer: cathode: the steel spoon; anode: a piece of (pure) silver

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable electrolyte.
parts.answer: aqueous silver nitrate (a solution containing silver ions)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why metals are electroplated.
parts.answer: To improve appearance; to resist corrosion.

practice.stem: A bicycle factory in Lahore electroplates steel handlebars with nickel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is used as the cathode and as the anode.
parts.answer: Cathode: the steel handlebars; anode: nickel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable electrolyte.
parts.answer: Aqueous nickel(II) sulfate (any soluble nickel salt).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.
parts.answer: Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni

practice.stem: A student copper-plates a steel key using aqueous copper(II) sulfate and a copper anode.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen at the key and at the copper anode after some time.
parts.answer: Key: becomes coated with pink-brown copper; anode: gets thinner.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the blue colour of the electrolyte stays the same.
parts.answer: Copper ions removed at the cathode are replaced by copper ions formed at the anode.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the key must be connected to the negative terminal.
parts.answer: Positive copper ions are attracted to the negative electrode, where they gain electrons.

practice.stem: A chlor-alkali plant near Karachi electrolyses brine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three products of the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (brine).
parts.answer: Chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one use of chlorine.
parts.answer: Water treatment (killing bacteria) / making bleach / making PVC

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one use of sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Making soap / paper / bleach

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis and not by heating its oxide with carbon.
parts.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name of the ore of aluminium.
parts.answer: Bauxite

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why recycling aluminium cans saves a great deal of energy.
parts.answer: Electrolysis uses large amounts of electricity; melting scrap aluminium needs far less energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons for electroplating objects.
parts.answer: To improve appearance; to resist corrosion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of an electroplated object you might find at home.
parts.answer: Silver-plated cutlery / chromium-plated taps / gold-plated jewellery / tin-plated food cans

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the object to be plated must be cleaned before electroplating.
parts.answer: Grease/dirt would stop the metal coating sticking evenly.

practice.stem: A student copper-plates a steel paper clip using aqueous copper(II) sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which terminal of the power pack the paper clip is connected to.
parts.answer: Negative

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is seen on the paper clip.
parts.answer: A pink-brown coating of copper forms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student did not clean the paper clip. Suggest what the coating looks like.
parts.answer: Patchy / uneven / flakes off.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name a material that could be used for the anode.
parts.answer: Copper

practice.stem: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, dissolved in molten cryolite. The electrodes are made of carbon (graphite).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite.
parts.answer: It lowers the operating temperature (aluminium oxide has a very high melting point), saving energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equations for the reactions at the cathode and at the anode.
parts.answer:
Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al
Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the carbon anodes must be replaced regularly.
parts.answer: The oxygen formed reacts with the hot carbon anodes to form carbon dioxide, so the anodes burn away.
parts.working: Oxygen reacts with carbon B1; forms CO₂ so anode wears away B1

practice.stem: Copper is purified by electrolysis with an impure copper anode, a pure copper cathode and aqueous copper(II) sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why very pure copper is needed for electrical wiring.
parts.answer: Impurities increase resistance / reduce conductivity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Impure copper contains small amounts of zinc and silver. Explain what happens to each when the impure copper anode dissolves.
parts.answer: Zinc (more reactive) forms Zn²⁺ ions that stay in solution; silver (less reactive) does not dissolve and falls to the bottom as anode sludge.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the half-equation at the cathode.
parts.answer: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

practice.stem: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed industrially with inert electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode.
parts.answer: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.
parts.answer: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (or 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why sodium hydroxide is left in the solution.
parts.answer: H⁺ ions (from water) are removed as hydrogen, and Cl⁻ as chlorine; Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions remain.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the chlorine and hydrogen must be kept apart.
parts.answer: The mixture can explode / they react violently.

practice.stem:
A student plates a key with copper for 20 minutes at different currents.
Current / A: 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.80
Mass of copper deposited / g: 0.08, 0.16, 0.24, 0.32

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between current and mass of copper deposited.
parts.answer: Mass is directly proportional to current.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the mass deposited at 1.0 A in 20 minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the mass deposited at 0.40 A in 40 minutes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the key is dried before each weighing.
parts.answer: Water on the key would add to the mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of aluminium that can be made from 51 tonnes of aluminium oxide. 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂  [Ar: O, 16; Al, 27]
parts.answer: 27 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the formation of oxygen at the anode.
parts.answer: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the gas formed when oxygen reacts with the hot anode.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide

practice.stem: A jeweller in Peshawar silver-plates brass bangles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of silver-plated jewellery over solid silver jewellery.
parts.answer: Cheaper (uses much less silver).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the electrolyte used for silver plating must contain silver ions.
parts.answer: Silver ions are reduced at the cathode to form the silver coating.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the anode is made of silver.
parts.answer: Silver atoms at the anode lose electrons to form Ag⁺ ions, replacing those deposited, so the electrolyte concentration stays constant.
parts.working: B1 Ag → Ag⁺ + e⁻; B1 keeps concentration constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Match each process to the electrolyte used: (i) extraction of aluminium; (ii) purification of copper; (iii) manufacture of chlorine.
parts.answer: (i) aluminium oxide in molten cryolite; (ii) aqueous copper(II) sulfate; (iii) concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (brine)

parts.label: b
parts.text: In aluminium extraction, explain why oxide ions move to the anode.
parts.answer: They are negatively charged and attracted to the positive electrode.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the electrolyte in aluminium extraction must be molten.
parts.answer: The ions must be free to move to carry the current.

practice.stem: Impure copper is purified by electrolysis using aqueous copper(II) sulfate. In one cell the impure copper anode loses 12.8 kg and the pure copper cathode gains 12.2 kg.
