Assume all the copper that leaves the anode is deposited on the cathode, and that the impurities do not dissolve but fall to the bottom of the cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the cathode is made of at the start.
parts.answer: a thin sheet of pure copper

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode.
parts.answer: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of copper in the part of the anode that was used up. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the mass of impurities (sludge) collected below the anode.
parts.answer: 0.6 kg

parts.label: a
parts.text: 0.540 g of silver is deposited. Calculate the moles of electrons that passed. Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag  [Ar: Ag, 108]

parts.label: b
parts.text: The same quantity of electricity is passed through aqueous nickel(II) sulfate. Calculate the mass of nickel deposited. Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni  [Ar: Ni, 59]

parts.label: c
parts.text: 0.020 mol of electrons passes through each of two cells, one plating silver and one plating copper. Calculate the mass of each metal deposited. [Ar: Cu, 64]
parts.answer: Silver 2.16 g; copper 0.64 g

practice.stem: In the extraction of aluminium, oxygen formed at the hot carbon anodes reacts with them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon lost from the anodes when 96 kg of oxygen reacts completely to form carbon dioxide. C + O₂ → CO₂  [Ar: C, 12; O, 16]
parts.answer: 36 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite rather than melted on its own.
parts.answer: Aluminium oxide has a very high melting point; the solution melts at a lower temperature, saving energy/cost (and conducts better).
parts.working: B1 lower operating temperature; B1 saves energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why aluminium forms at the cathode.
parts.answer: Al³⁺ ions are attracted to the negative electrode and gain electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Overall: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂. Calculate the mass of sodium hydroxide made when 71 tonnes of chlorine is produced. [Mr: Cl₂, 71; NaOH, 40]
parts.answer: 80 tonnes
parts.working: M1 1 mol Cl₂ : 2 mol NaOH; A1 2 × 40 = 80 t.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, at r.t.p., produced with 7.1 kg of chlorine. [one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
parts.answer: 2400 dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the plant sells hydrogen as well as chlorine and sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: It is a valuable by-product (fuel / making ammonia or margarine), so less waste and more profit.

practice.stem:
A student nickel-plates a steel spoon using a nickel anode and aqueous nickel(II) sulfate.
Mass of nickel anode: before 12.43 g, after 11.84 g
Mass of spoon (cathode): before 25.10 g, after 25.65 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the moles of electrons that would be needed to dissolve the nickel lost from the anode. Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻  [Ar: Ni, 59]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass the cathode should have gained if all the nickel ions formed were deposited.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the cathode gained only 0.55 g.
parts.answer: Any two: some nickel fell off the cathode (poorly adhering); cathode not fully dried/some solid lost when rinsed; some of the current produced hydrogen at the cathode; some anode material fell off as solid rather than dissolving.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student tries to silver-plate a copper ring using aqueous sodium nitrate as the electrolyte and a silver anode. Explain why no useful silver coating forms at first, and name the gas seen at the cathode.
parts.answer: There are no silver ions in the electrolyte at the start; hydrogen (from water) is discharged at the cathode instead of sodium.
parts.working: B1 no Ag⁺ initially, H⁺/water reduced; B1 hydrogen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why aqueous silver nitrate is a better electrolyte.
parts.answer: It provides Ag⁺ ions, which are discharged in preference to H⁺ (silver is less reactive than hydrogen).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a very small current gives a better coating than a large current.
parts.answer: The metal deposits slowly and evenly, so it sticks well (a large current gives a rough, powdery coat).

practice.stem: Salts: sodium carbonate, silver chloride, barium sulfate, copper(II) nitrate, calcium carbonate, ammonium chloride, lead(II) chloride, potassium sulfate

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sort the salts into those that are soluble in water and those that are insoluble.
parts.answer: Soluble: sodium carbonate, copper(II) nitrate, ammonium chloride, potassium sulfate. Insoluble: silver chloride, barium sulfate, calcium carbonate, lead(II) chloride.
parts.working: All eight correct B3; six or seven B2; four or five B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one general rule that explains why copper(II) nitrate is soluble.
parts.answer: All nitrates are soluble.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which salt is best prepared by mixing two aqueous solutions and filtering off the solid formed?
A barium sulfate
B copper(II) sulfate
C sodium chloride
D zinc nitrate
parts.answer: A barium sulfate
parts.working: Barium sulfate is insoluble, so it forms as a precipitate that can be filtered off. The others are soluble and would stay in solution.

practice.stem: A student makes crystals of copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide (a black insoluble powder) and dilute sulfuric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: copper(II) oxide + sulfuric acid → copper(II) sulfate + water

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the steps the student should follow to obtain pure, dry crystals.
parts.answer: Warm the acid and add copper(II) oxide a little at a time until some is left over (excess); filter to remove the excess oxide; heat the filtrate to evaporate some water until crystallisation point (crystals form on a cold glass rod); leave to cool and crystallise, then filter/pick out the crystals and dry them between filter papers.
parts.working: Add excess CuO to (warm) acid B1; filter B1; heat filtrate to crystallisation point / evaporate some water B1; cool, filter and dry crystals (e.g. on filter paper) B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the salt formed in each reaction.
(i) zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid
(ii) potassium hydroxide and dilute nitric acid
(iii) magnesium carbonate and dilute sulfuric acid
parts.answer: (i) zinc chloride (ii) potassium nitrate (iii) magnesium sulfate

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the other two products of reaction (iii).
parts.answer: water and carbon dioxide

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each pair of aqueous solutions, state whether a precipitate forms. If it does, name the precipitate.
(i) sodium carbonate and calcium nitrate
(ii) potassium chloride and sodium nitrate
(iii) lead(II) nitrate and sodium chloride
parts.answer: (i) yes, calcium carbonate (ii) no precipitate (iii) yes, lead(II) chloride
parts.working: B1 each. All sodium, potassium and nitrate salts are soluble; carbonates are insoluble except Na, K, NH₄⁺; chlorides are soluble except Ag⁺ and Pb²⁺.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction in (a)(i).
parts.answer: Ca²⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → CaCO₃(s)
parts.working: B1 correct ions and formula; B1 state symbols.

practice.stem: Sodium sulfate is made by titrating aqueous sodium hydroxide with dilute sulfuric acid. A few drops of indicator are used in the first titration to find the volume of acid needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a titration is used to make sodium sulfate, instead of adding an excess of the base and filtering.
parts.answer: Sodium hydroxide is soluble, so excess cannot be filtered off; the exact volumes must be used so the product is not contaminated with excess alkali or acid.
parts.working: NaOH (base) soluble so excess cannot be removed by filtering B1; exact neutralisation needed for a pure salt B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: After finding the volume of acid, the student repeats the titration with the same volumes but without the indicator. Explain why.
parts.answer: So that the salt is not contaminated by the indicator.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O

practice.stem: A student wants to make a dry sample of barium sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two aqueous solutions she could mix.
parts.answer: e.g. barium chloride (or barium nitrate) and sodium sulfate (or dilute sulfuric acid)
parts.working: Soluble barium salt B1; soluble sulfate B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction.
parts.answer: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how she should obtain a pure, dry sample of the solid after mixing.
parts.answer: Filter; wash the residue with distilled water; dry it in a warm oven or between filter papers.
parts.working: Filter B1; wash with distilled water and dry B1

practice.stem:
Zinc sulfate crystals, ZnSO₄·7H₂O, are made from zinc oxide: ZnO + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂O. One mole of ZnSO₄ in solution gives one mole of ZnSO₄·7H₂O crystals.
[Ar: H, 1; O, 16; S, 32; Zn, 65]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative formula mass of ZnSO₄·7H₂O.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student reacts 4.05 g of zinc oxide with excess acid. Calculate the maximum mass of crystals that can form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: She obtains 11.5 g of crystals. Calculate the percentage yield to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the yield is less than 100 %.
parts.answer: Some salt stays dissolved in the solution left after crystallising (or losses on filtering/transfer).

parts.label: a
parts.text: When making magnesium sulfate from magnesium carbonate and dilute sulfuric acid, the carbonate is added in excess. Explain why.
parts.answer: To make sure all the acid is used up, so the salt is not contaminated with acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two observations that show the magnesium carbonate is in excess.
parts.answer: Fizzing/effervescence stops; some solid remains undissolved.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the balanced equation, with state symbols, for the reaction.
parts.answer: MgCO₃(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
parts.working: Balanced equation B1; state symbols B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student wants to prepare pure crystals of potassium nitrate. Which method is most suitable?
A Add excess potassium metal to dilute nitric acid and filter.
B Titrate aqueous potassium hydroxide with dilute nitric acid using an indicator, repeat without indicator, then crystallise.
C Mix aqueous potassium chloride with aqueous silver nitrate and filter off the potassium nitrate.
D Add excess solid potassium carbonate to dilute nitric acid and filter off the excess.
parts.answer: B Titrate aqueous potassium hydroxide with dilute nitric acid using an indicator, repeat without indicator, then crystallise.
parts.working: Potassium nitrate is soluble and both reactants (KOH and HNO₃) are soluble, so a titration is needed to find the exact volumes, then the reaction is repeated without indicator. D is wrong because potassium carbonate is soluble, so the excess cannot be filtered off and would contaminate the salt. A is dangerous (K reacts violently); in C the potassium nitrate stays in solution and the precipitate is silver chloride.

practice.stem: Three salts are needed for a school display: silver chloride, ammonium nitrate and zinc sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each salt, name the method of preparation (precipitation, titration, or excess insoluble base/metal/carbonate with acid) and name suitable starting materials.
parts.answer: Silver chloride: precipitation, e.g. silver nitrate solution + sodium chloride solution. Ammonium nitrate: titration, aqueous ammonia + dilute nitric acid. Zinc sulfate: excess zinc oxide (or zinc carbonate / zinc) + dilute sulfuric acid, then filter and crystallise.
parts.working: Each salt with correct method and reagents B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why your method for ammonium nitrate must be titration.
parts.answer: Both reactants are soluble (aqueous ammonia is a soluble base) so the excess cannot be filtered off.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an ionic equation for the formation of silver chloride.
parts.answer: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)

practice.stem:
25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide is exactly neutralised by 0.100 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid.
2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
[Ar: O, 16; Na, 23; S, 32]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of sulfuric acid needed.
parts.answer: 25.0 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium sulfate in the neutral solution.

practice.stem:
50.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ barium chloride is mixed with excess aqueous sodium sulfate.
[Ar: O, 16; S, 32; Ba, 137]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2NaCl

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of barium sulfate formed. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The dried solid has a mass of 1.31 g. Suggest why it is greater than your answer to (b).
parts.answer: The solid was not completely dry / sodium chloride (soluble impurity) was not washed out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student makes copper(II) sulfate solution correctly but then heats it in an evaporating basin until all the water has gone. He obtains a white powder instead of blue crystals. Explain why.
parts.answer: Heating to dryness drove off the water of crystallisation; the white powder is anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
parts.working: Water of crystallisation removed B1; anhydrous CuSO₄ is white B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how he should have heated the solution, and how he could tell when to stop.
parts.answer: Heat gently to evaporate only part of the water; stop at the crystallisation point, when a drop on a cold glass rod forms crystals (or crystals appear at the edge); then leave to cool.
parts.working: Evaporate only some of the water / heat to crystallisation point B1; test with a glass rod or see crystals form, then cool B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could turn his white powder back into a blue solid.
parts.answer: Add water (a few drops).

practice.stem:
A student adds excess copper(II) carbonate to 40.0 cm³ of 1.50 mol/dm³ nitric acid. The excess carbonate is filtered off and the blue solution is crystallised to give copper(II) nitrate crystals, Cu(NO₃)₂·3H₂O.
[Ar: H, 1; N, 14; O, 16; Cu, 64. One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: CuCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of nitric acid used.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide given off, in dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of crystals of Cu(NO₃)₂·3H₂O that could be obtained.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The student obtains 5.08 g of crystals. Calculate the percentage yield and suggest one reason why it is less than 100 %.
parts.answer: 70.0 %; some salt stays dissolved in the solution left after crystallisation (or losses on transfer/filter paper)

practice.stem:
Five solutions are tested with universal indicator.
Solution | pH
V | 1
W | 4
X | 7
Y | 9
Z | 14

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which solution is neutral?
parts.answer: X

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which solution could be a weak alkali such as aqueous ammonia?
parts.answer: Y

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which solution has the highest concentration of hydrogen ions?
parts.answer: V

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the colour of universal indicator in solution V and in solution Z.
parts.answer: V red; Z purple (violet)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which acid is a weak acid?
A ethanoic acid
B hydrochloric acid
C nitric acid
D sulfuric acid
parts.answer: A ethanoic acid
parts.working: Ethanoic acid is only partly ionised in water, so it is a weak acid. The other three are strong acids that are fully ionised.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does 0.1 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid have a higher pH than 0.1 mol/dm³ nitric acid?
A Ethanoic acid is only partially ionised (dissociated) in water.
B Ethanoic acid is more dilute than nitric acid.
C Ethanoic acid contains fewer hydrogen atoms per molecule.
D Ethanoic acid is an organic compound, so it does not form ions.
parts.answer: A Ethanoic acid is only partially ionised (dissociated) in water.
parts.working: Both acids have the same concentration, but ethanoic acid only partly ionises, so the concentration of H⁺ ions is lower and the pH higher. B is wrong: the concentrations are equal. D is wrong: ethanoic acid does form some ions.

practice.stem:
A student in Hyderabad tests some household liquids.
Liquid | pH
lemon juice | 2
boiled tap water (cooled) | 7
soap solution | 10
oven cleaner | 13

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how she can find the pH of the lemon juice using universal indicator paper.
parts.answer: Put a drop of juice on the paper (with a clean glass rod); compare the colour with the pH colour chart.
parts.working: B1 drop on paper / dip paper; B1 match colour with chart.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour of universal indicator in (i) the lemon juice and (ii) the oven cleaner.
parts.answer: (i) red (or orange-red) (ii) purple (or violet)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which liquid is (i) neutral, (ii) the most strongly alkaline?
parts.answer: (i) water (ii) oven cleaner

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which liquid contains the highest concentration of hydrogen ions?
parts.answer: lemon juice
parts.working: Lowest pH means highest H⁺ concentration.

practice.stem: Indicators are used to tell acids from alkalis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour of methyl orange in (i) a solution of pH 2 and (ii) a solution of pH 12.
parts.answer: (i) red (ii) yellow

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour of thymolphthalein in (i) a solution of pH 2 and (ii) a solution of pH 12.
parts.answer: (i) colourless (ii) blue

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour of red litmus in an alkaline solution.
parts.answer: blue

practice.stem: A student compares 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid with 1.0 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict which acid has the lower pH.
parts.answer: hydrochloric acid

parts.label: b
parts.text: Equal pieces of magnesium ribbon are added to equal volumes of each acid. Describe and explain the difference in what is seen.
parts.answer: Faster fizzing with hydrochloric acid; HCl is fully ionised but ethanoic acid is only partly ionised; so HCl has a higher concentration of H⁺ ions and more frequent collisions.
parts.working: HCl fizzes faster B1; HCl fully / ethanoic acid partially ionised B1; higher H⁺ concentration in HCl B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two acids can have the same concentration but different pH values.
parts.answer: Concentration is the amount of acid dissolved; pH depends on the concentration of H⁺ ions, which depends on how much the acid ionises.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an acid and a base in terms of proton transfer.
parts.answer: An acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a base is a proton acceptor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrogen chloride gas reacts with ammonia gas: HCl + NH₃ → NH₄Cl (which contains NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻ ions). Identify the acid and the base in this reaction. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: HCl is the acid: it donates a proton (H⁺) to NH₃; NH₃ is the base: it accepts the proton to form NH₄⁺.
parts.working: HCl acid, donates H⁺ B1; NH₃ base, accepts H⁺ B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation to show hydrochloric acid ionising in water and an equation to show ethanoic acid ionising in water.
parts.answer:
HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻
CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺
parts.working: Each B1 (⇌ needed for ethanoic acid)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the arrows in your two equations.
parts.answer: The single arrow shows HCl is completely ionised (strong); the reversible arrow shows ethanoic acid is only partly ionised (weak).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference between a dilute solution of a strong acid and a concentrated solution of a weak acid.
parts.answer: Dilute/concentrated refers to how much acid is dissolved per dm³; strong/weak refers to how fully the acid ionises.
parts.working: Concentration = amount per volume B1; strength = degree of ionisation B1

practice.stem: Aqueous ammonia is used in some glass cleaners. Ammonia is a weak base.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a weak base.
parts.answer: A base that is only partially ionised / reacts only partially with water to form hydroxide ions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation to show how ammonia produces hydroxide ions in water. Use the correct type of arrow.
parts.answer: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict how the pH of 0.1 mol/dm³ aqueous ammonia compares with the pH of 0.1 mol/dm³ aqueous sodium hydroxide. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Ammonia has a lower pH (about 11, NaOH about 13) because it produces a lower concentration of OH⁻ ions.
parts.working: B1 ammonia lower pH; B1 lower [OH⁻] because partially ionised while NaOH is fully ionised.

practice.stem:
A student uses a pH meter to measure the pH of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid at different concentrations.
Concentration / mol/dm³ | 0.100 | 0.010 | 0.001
pH of hydrochloric acid | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0
pH of ethanoic acid | 2.9 | 3.4 | 3.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of diluting each acid on its pH.
parts.answer: pH increases as each acid is diluted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the results to show which acid is the weaker acid. Explain.
parts.answer: Ethanoic acid; at the same concentration its pH is higher (e.g. 2.9 compared with 1.0 at 0.100 mol/dm³).
parts.working: B1 ethanoic; B1 comparison at equal concentration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of using a pH meter instead of universal indicator paper.
parts.answer: More precise (reads to 0.1 pH unit) / not affected by judging colour.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The student rinses the electrode with distilled water between readings. Explain why.
parts.answer: To remove solution from the previous test so it does not contaminate/change the next reading.

practice.stem:
A student measures the electrical conductivity of 25.0 cm³ samples of two acids, each of concentration 0.10 mol/dm³.
Acid | conductivity reading (arbitrary units)
hydrochloric acid | 39
ethanoic acid | 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference in conductivity between the two acids.
parts.answer: Hydrochloric acid is fully ionised so it has more ions (free to move) in solution; ethanoic acid is only partly ionised, so fewer ions.
parts.working: B1 HCl fully ionised / strong; B1 more mobile ions carry charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the conductivity reading for 0.10 mol/dm³ nitric acid. Give a reason.
parts.answer: About the same as hydrochloric acid (high), because nitric acid is also a strong, monobasic acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Both acids need the same volume of 0.10 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide for neutralisation. Explain why, even though ethanoic acid is weak.
parts.answer: Both contain the same number of moles of acid and both are monobasic; as OH⁻ removes H⁺, more ethanoic acid ionises until all of it has reacted.
parts.working: B1 same moles, monobasic; B1 equilibrium shifts / more ethanoic acid ionises as H⁺ is removed.

practice.stem:
Excess magnesium ribbon is added to 50.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. In a second flask, excess magnesium is added to 50.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid. Both acids are monobasic.
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
[One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, at r.t.p., produced in the first flask. Give your answer in cm³.
parts.answer: 300 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the final volume of hydrogen from the ethanoic acid, and how the time taken compares. Explain.
parts.answer: Also 300 cm³, but it takes longer; the same number of moles of acid is present, and as H⁺ ions react the ethanoic acid keeps ionising until all of it has reacted; but the H⁺ concentration at any time is lower, so the reaction is slower.
parts.working: Same volume, 300 cm³ B1; takes longer B1; same moles of acid / all eventually ionises, but lower H⁺ concentration so slower B1

practice.stem:
A student adds 0.10 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide from a burette to 20.0 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid and measures the pH with a pH meter.
Volume of NaOH / cm³ | 0 | 5.0 | 10.0 | 15.0 | 19.0 | 20.0 | 21.0 | 25.0
pH | 1.0 | 1.2 | 1.5 | 1.8 | 2.6 | 7.0 | 11.4 | 12.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the volume of sodium hydroxide needed to neutralise the acid.
parts.answer: 20.0 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the pH changes as the alkali is added.
parts.answer: pH rises slowly at first, then rises very sharply (from about 2.6 to 11.4) close to the neutral point, then rises slowly again.
parts.working: Slow rise at first B1; sudden large rise around 20 cm³ then levelling off B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid in mol/dm³.
parts.answer: 0.10 mol/dm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation.
parts.answer: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define an acid and a base in terms of proton transfer.
parts.answer: Acid: proton (H⁺) donor. Base: proton (H⁺) acceptor.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Reaction 1: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻
Reaction 2: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻
State the role of water in each reaction. Explain your answers.
parts.answer: Reaction 1: water is a base (it accepts a proton from HCl). Reaction 2: water is an acid (it donates a proton to NH₃).
parts.working: B1 base in 1; B1 acid in 2; B1 explanation in terms of gaining/losing H⁺.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In the reaction CH₃COOH + NH₃ → CH₃COO⁻ + NH₄⁺, identify the base.
parts.answer: NH₃ (ammonia)
parts.working: It accepts H⁺ to become NH₄⁺.

practice.stem:
2.50 g of powdered calcium carbonate is added to an excess of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid in one flask. Another 2.50 g is added to an excess of 1.0 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid in a second flask.
[Mr: CaCO₃ = 100. One mole of gas occupies 24 000 cm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide, in cm³ at r.t.p., produced in each flask.
parts.answer: 600 cm³ in each flask

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both flasks give the same final volume of gas.
parts.answer: The acid is in excess in both, so the amount of CaCO₃ (the same) decides the amount of CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe and explain how the rate of reaction differs between the two flasks.
parts.answer: Faster with hydrochloric acid. HCl is a strong acid, fully ionised, so higher concentration of H⁺ ions; more frequent collisions of H⁺ with the carbonate.
parts.working: B1 faster in HCl; B1 HCl fully ionised / ethanoic partially; B1 higher H⁺ concentration so more frequent collisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the products when dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with:
(i) magnesium
(ii) calcium carbonate
(iii) sodium hydroxide
parts.answer: (i) magnesium chloride + hydrogen (ii) calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide (iii) sodium chloride + water

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of a dilute acid on blue litmus paper and on methyl orange.
parts.answer: Blue litmus turns red; methyl orange turns red.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Sodium carbonate powder is added to dilute nitric acid. Which gas is given off?
A carbon dioxide
B hydrogen
C nitrogen dioxide
D oxygen
parts.answer: A carbon dioxide
parts.working: Acids react with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Hydrogen is given off when an acid reacts with a metal, not a carbonate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. State two observations.
parts.answer: Bubbles/fizzing; magnesium gets smaller and disappears (the solution warms).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sodium carbonate powder is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Name the gas given off and give a test for it.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide; turns limewater milky.
parts.working: B1 gas; B1 test and result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Black copper(II) oxide is warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid. Describe what is seen and name the salt formed.
parts.answer: The black solid dissolves and a blue(-green) solution forms; copper(II) chloride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a base.
parts.answer: A substance that neutralises an acid to form a salt and water (a proton acceptor).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by an alkali.
parts.answer: A base that is soluble in water (forms OH⁻ ions in solution).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the name of one base that is not an alkali.
parts.answer: copper(II) oxide (or any insoluble metal oxide/hydroxide, e.g. iron(III) oxide)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the ion present in all aqueous alkalis.
parts.answer: hydroxide ion, OH⁻

practice.stem: Many crops grow best in soil with a pH close to 7. A farmer near Mardan finds that his soil is acidic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of reaction that happens when calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) is added to acidic soil.
parts.answer: neutralisation

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the salt formed when calcium hydroxide reacts with nitric acid in the soil.
parts.answer: calcium nitrate

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one other everyday example of neutralisation.
parts.answer: Indigestion tablets neutralising stomach acid / toothpaste neutralising acid in the mouth / treating acidic lake water with lime.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the farmer should not add too much calcium hydroxide.
parts.answer: The soil would become alkaline, which also harms many crops.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write balanced equations for:
(i) zinc reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid
(ii) copper(II) carbonate reacting with dilute sulfuric acid
parts.answer:
(i) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
(ii) CuCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of any acid with any alkali.
parts.answer: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the ion present in all aqueous alkalis and state the pH range of alkaline solutions.
parts.answer: hydroxide ion, OH⁻; pH above 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solid ammonium sulfate is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. A gas is given off. Name the gas and give a test for it.
parts.answer: ammonia; turns damp red litmus paper blue
parts.working: Name B1; test with result B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the word equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: ammonium sulfate + sodium hydroxide → sodium sulfate + ammonia + water

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use this reaction to explain why a farmer should not spread slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) on a field at the same time as an ammonium fertiliser.
parts.answer: The base reacts with the ammonium salt and nitrogen is lost as ammonia gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance does NOT react with dilute sulfuric acid to form copper(II) sulfate?
A copper
B copper(II) oxide
C copper(II) carbonate
D copper(II) hydroxide
parts.answer: A copper
parts.working: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not react with dilute acids. The oxide and hydroxide are bases and the carbonate reacts to give the salt, water and carbon dioxide.

practice.stem: A technician has three unlabelled bottles. One contains dilute hydrochloric acid, one aqueous sodium hydroxide and one distilled water. She has only red litmus paper and magnesium ribbon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how she can use red litmus paper to identify the sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Dip red litmus in each; the one that turns it blue is sodium hydroxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how she can then use magnesium ribbon to tell the remaining two liquids apart. Give the results.
parts.answer: Add a piece of magnesium to each; fizzing (hydrogen) with the acid; no reaction with water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the gas formed in (b) and give a test for it.
parts.answer: Hydrogen; lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
parts.working: B1 gas; B1 test and result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of aluminium with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: 2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂(g)
parts.working: B1 formulae and balancing; B1 state symbols.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of calcium hydroxide with dilute nitric acid.
parts.answer: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of a carbonate with an acid.
parts.answer: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O

practice.stem:
A student adds equal-sized pieces of four metals to separate test-tubes, each containing 5 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid.
Metal | observation
iron | slow bubbling
copper | no bubbles
magnesium | very fast bubbling, tube gets hot
zinc | steady bubbling

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put the four metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first.
parts.answer: magnesium, zinc, iron, copper

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the salt formed when zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: zinc chloride

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why copper gives no bubbles.
parts.answer: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen (below hydrogen in the reactivity series).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept the same to make this a fair test.
parts.answer: Any two: volume of acid; concentration of acid; size/mass/surface area of metal pieces; temperature.

practice.stem:
Rain and decomposing plant matter have made the soil in a field acidic. A farmer neutralises the acidity with calcium hydroxide. Treat the acidity as equivalent to 4.9 kg of sulfuric acid.
Ca(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + 2H₂O
[Ar: H, 1; O, 16; S, 32; Ca, 40]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of sulfuric acid in 4.9 kg.
parts.answer: 50 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of calcium hydroxide needed, in kg.
parts.answer: 3.7 kg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the farmer uses calcium hydroxide instead of sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Calcium hydroxide is cheaper and only slightly soluble, so it is less likely to make the soil too alkaline / it is less corrosive.

practice.stem:
An antacid tablet contains 0.29 g of magnesium hydroxide, which neutralises excess stomach acid.
Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O
[Ar: H, 1; O, 16; Mg, 24]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of magnesium hydroxide in one tablet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 0.10 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid that one tablet can neutralise, in cm³.
parts.answer: 100 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Magnesium hydroxide is a base but not an alkali. Explain why.
parts.answer: It is insoluble in water (an alkali is a soluble base).

practice.stem:
The inside of a kettle in Quetta is coated with 1.25 g of limescale (calcium carbonate). It is removed with dilute hydrochloric acid.
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
[Mr: CaCO₃ = 100. One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of calcium carbonate in the limescale.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum volume of 0.50 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid needed to remove it, in cm³.
parts.answer: 50.0 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed, in dm³ at r.t.p.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the kettle must be rinsed well before it is used again.
parts.answer: To remove left-over acid (and calcium chloride), which is corrosive / harmful if drunk.

practice.stem:
Two indigestion remedies neutralise excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach. One contains sodium hydrogencarbonate, the other magnesium hydroxide.
NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂
[Mr: NaHCO₃ = 84; Mg(OH)₂ = 58. One mole of gas occupies 24 000 cm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide, in cm³ at r.t.p., formed when 0.84 g of sodium hydrogencarbonate reacts completely.
parts.answer: 240 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O
Show by calculation which antacid neutralises more acid per gram, and by what factor. Give the factor to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Magnesium hydroxide, about 2.90 times as much acid per gram
parts.working: M1 Mg(OH)₂: 2 ÷ 58 = 0.0345 mol HCl per g; M1 NaHCO₃: 1 ÷ 84 = 0.0119 mol HCl per g; A1 ratio 2.90.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of sodium hydrogencarbonate as an antacid.
parts.answer: It produces carbon dioxide gas, causing wind/bloating (or it adds sodium to the diet).

practice.stem: Oxides: sulfur dioxide, magnesium oxide, aluminium oxide, carbon monoxide, calcium oxide, carbon dioxide

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each oxide as acidic, basic, amphoteric or neutral.
parts.answer: Acidic: sulfur dioxide, carbon dioxide. Basic: magnesium oxide, calcium oxide. Amphoteric: aluminium oxide. Neutral: carbon monoxide.
parts.working: All six correct B3; four or five B2; two or three B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the general type of element that forms (i) acidic oxides and (ii) basic oxides.
parts.answer: (i) non-metals (ii) metals

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which oxide reacts with both dilute hydrochloric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide?
A copper(II) oxide
B sulfur dioxide
C sodium oxide
D zinc oxide
parts.answer: D zinc oxide
parts.working: Zinc oxide is amphoteric, so it reacts with both acids and alkalis. Copper(II) oxide is basic and reacts only with acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which oxide dissolves in water to give a solution with a pH below 7?
A sodium oxide
B magnesium oxide
C nitrogen dioxide
D copper(II) oxide
parts.answer: C nitrogen dioxide
parts.working: Nitrogen dioxide is the oxide of a non-metal and is acidic, so its solution is acidic. Sodium and magnesium oxides are basic and give alkaline solutions; copper(II) oxide is insoluble.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each oxide as acidic, basic, amphoteric or neutral:
potassium oxide, phosphorus(V) oxide, nitrogen monoxide, copper(II) oxide, zinc oxide
parts.answer: potassium oxide – basic; phosphorus(V) oxide – acidic; nitrogen monoxide – neutral; copper(II) oxide – basic; zinc oxide – amphoteric

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which of these oxides would react with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
parts.answer: phosphorus(V) oxide and zinc oxide

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium burns in oxygen with a yellow flame to form sodium oxide. Write a balanced equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sodium oxide is added to water. Name the product and state the pH of the solution formed.
parts.answer: sodium hydroxide; pH about 13–14

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether sodium oxide is an acidic or a basic oxide.
parts.answer: basic

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium oxide is an amphoteric oxide. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: It reacts with both acids and bases (alkalis) to form salts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of aluminium oxide with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a simple experiment to show that aluminium oxide is amphoteric.
parts.answer: Add some aluminium oxide powder to warm dilute hydrochloric acid and some to warm aqueous sodium hydroxide; it dissolves (reacts) in both.
parts.working: Add to an acid and to an alkali B1; dissolves in both B1

practice.stem: A student burns small samples of magnesium, sulfur and carbon separately in jars of oxygen. Water and a few drops of universal indicator are then shaken in each jar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the colour of the indicator in each jar and explain.
parts.answer: Magnesium: blue/purple — magnesium oxide is basic (forms an alkaline solution). Sulfur: red — sulfur dioxide is acidic. Carbon: yellow/orange — carbon dioxide forms a weakly acidic solution.
parts.working: Each correct colour with reason B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the burning of magnesium.
parts.answer: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one safety precaution when burning sulfur.
parts.answer: Use a fume cupboard (sulfur dioxide is toxic).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of sulfur dioxide with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form sodium sulfite, Na₂SO₃.
parts.answer: SO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₃ + H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of calcium oxide with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: CaO + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Zinc oxide reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form sodium zincate, Na₂ZnO₂, and water. Write the equation and state what this reaction shows about zinc oxide.
parts.answer: ZnO + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂O; zinc oxide is amphoteric (it also reacts with acids).

practice.stem: A white powder is either zinc oxide or magnesium oxide. Both are insoluble in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment, using dilute hydrochloric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide, to find out which oxide the powder is. Give the results you would expect for each oxide.
parts.answer: Add a spatula of powder to dilute HCl and, separately, to aqueous NaOH (warm if needed). Zinc oxide dissolves in both; magnesium oxide dissolves only in the acid.
parts.working: B1 test with acid; B1 test with alkali; B1 same small mass and volume / warm gently; B1 correct expected results for both oxides.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of oxide that magnesium oxide is.
parts.answer: basic

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a simple observation, made while heating, that would also identify zinc oxide.
parts.answer: Zinc oxide turns yellow when hot and white again when cold.

practice.stem: Limestone is quarried in the Salt Range and heated in lime kilns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the thermal decomposition of limestone to make quicklime.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of quicklime with water to make slaked lime.
parts.answer: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why calcium oxide is classified as a basic oxide.
parts.answer: It is a metal oxide that reacts with acids to form a salt and water.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give two uses of calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Any two: neutralising acidic soil; neutralising acidic industrial waste/lakes; flue gas desulfurisation; making cement/mortar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mixture of carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide is bubbled through excess aqueous sodium hydroxide. Name the gas that comes out and explain why.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide; it is a neutral oxide so it does not react with the alkali, whereas acidic carbon dioxide is absorbed.
parts.working: B1 CO; B1 CO neutral / CO₂ acidic reacts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of carbon dioxide with sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: CO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one other neutral oxide.
parts.answer: nitrogen monoxide, NO (or water, H₂O / dinitrogen oxide, N₂O)

practice.stem:
Four oxides, W, X, Y and Z, are tested.
Oxide | effect of water | reacts with dilute HCl? | reacts with aqueous NaOH?
W | dissolves, pH 13 | yes | no
X | insoluble | yes | yes
Y | dissolves, pH 2 | no | yes
Z | insoluble | no | no

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each oxide as acidic, basic, amphoteric or neutral.
parts.answer: W basic; X amphoteric; Y acidic; Z neutral
parts.working: All four B2; two or three B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a possible identity for each of W, X, Y and Z from: aluminium oxide, carbon monoxide, sodium oxide, sulfur trioxide.
parts.answer: W sodium oxide; X aluminium oxide; Y sulfur trioxide; Z carbon monoxide
parts.working: All four B2; two or three B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of oxide W with water.
parts.answer: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH

practice.stem: The oxides of the Period 3 elements are Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀ and SO₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the nature of the oxides changes across Period 3 from sodium oxide to sulfur trioxide.
parts.answer: Basic (Na₂O, MgO) → amphoteric (Al₂O₃) → acidic (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃).
parts.working: B1 basic to acidic; B1 aluminium oxide amphoteric.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Relate this change to the type of element.
parts.answer: Metals (left) form basic oxides; non-metals (right) form acidic oxides; character changes from metallic to non-metallic.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the pH of the mixture formed when each oxide is added to water: sodium oxide, aluminium oxide, sulfur trioxide. Explain the value for aluminium oxide.
parts.answer: Na₂O about 13–14; Al₂O₃ 7; SO₃ about 1. Aluminium oxide is insoluble in water, so the water stays neutral.
parts.working: B1 Na₂O high; B1 SO₃ low; B1 Al₂O₃ 7 because insoluble.

practice.stem:
In a school fume cupboard, sulfur dioxide from an experiment is absorbed by aqueous sodium hydroxide. 1.92 g of sulfur dioxide is absorbed.
SO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₃ + H₂O
[Ar: O, 16; Na, 23; S, 32]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of sulfur dioxide absorbed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum volume of 0.50 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide needed, in cm³.
parts.answer: 120 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium sulfite formed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the types of oxide, why sodium hydroxide can absorb sulfur dioxide.
parts.answer: Sulfur dioxide is an acidic oxide, so it reacts with (is neutralised by) an alkali.

practice.stem:
A white solid X is an oxide of a metal.
• X is insoluble in water.
• X dissolves in dilute nitric acid to give a colourless solution.
• X dissolves in warm aqueous sodium hydroxide to give a colourless solution.
• X turns yellow when heated strongly and white again when it cools.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify X.
parts.answer: zinc oxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the reactions with acid and alkali show about X.
parts.answer: X is amphoteric: it reacts with both acids and bases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Aluminium saucepans are protected by a thin layer of aluminium oxide. Suggest why they should not be cleaned with strongly alkaline oven cleaner.
parts.answer: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric, so it reacts with/dissolves in the alkali; the protective layer is removed and the metal underneath is attacked.
parts.working: B1 oxide amphoteric reacts with alkali; B1 protection lost / metal corroded.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name one other metal oxide that is amphoteric.
parts.answer: aluminium oxide

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State one source of each pollutant.
(i) carbon monoxide
(ii) sulfur dioxide
(iii) oxides of nitrogen
(iv) methane
parts.answer: (i) incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels (ii) burning fossil fuels that contain sulfur compounds (iii) reaction of nitrogen and oxygen in hot car engines (iv) decomposition of vegetation / waste gases from digestion in animals (livestock)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one adverse effect of particulates (soot) in the air.
parts.answer: Increased risk of respiratory problems (and cancer).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A faulty gas heater in a closed room produces a colourless, odourless, toxic gas. What is the gas?
A carbon dioxide
B carbon monoxide
C nitrogen dioxide
D sulfur dioxide
parts.answer: B carbon monoxide
parts.working: Incomplete combustion of the fuel in a shortage of oxygen gives carbon monoxide, which is toxic and has no colour or smell. Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide are toxic but have strong smells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sulfur dioxide from a coal-fired power station dissolves in rainwater. Name the environmental problem this causes.
parts.answer: acid rain

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two effects of this problem.
parts.answer: Any two of: damages/corrodes buildings and statues made of limestone or marble; corrodes metal structures; kills fish and other life in lakes; damages trees/plants.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing the sulfur dioxide released by power stations.
parts.answer: Remove sulfur from the fuel / use low-sulfur fuel / flue gas desulfurisation (react SO₂ with calcium oxide).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how oxides of nitrogen are formed in a car engine.
parts.answer: Nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together at the very high temperature inside the engine.
parts.working: Nitrogen and oxygen (from air) react B1; high temperature B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the formation of nitrogen monoxide, NO.
parts.answer: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two adverse effects of oxides of nitrogen.
parts.answer: Acid rain; photochemical smog; respiratory problems.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Black smoke from an old diesel lorry contains a pollutant made of tiny solid particles of carbon. What is this pollutant called?
A particulates
B methane
C nitrogen dioxide
D sulfur dioxide
parts.answer: A particulates
parts.working: Particulates (soot) are fine solid carbon particles from incomplete combustion. The other three are gases.

practice.stem: Modern cars have catalytic converters in their exhaust systems.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete and balance the equation for the removal of carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide in a catalytic converter.
__CO + __NO → __CO₂ + __
parts.answer: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂
parts.working: N₂ as product B1; balancing B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the substance that is oxidised in this reaction. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide; it gains oxygen (oxidation number of C increases from +2 to +4).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one other type of pollutant removed in the catalytic converter and state what it is converted to.
parts.answer: Unburned hydrocarbons; oxidised to carbon dioxide and water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In flue gas desulfurisation, waste gases from a power station pass through calcium oxide. Write the equation for the reaction of calcium oxide with sulfur dioxide.
parts.answer: CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the types of oxide, why this reaction happens.
parts.answer: Calcium oxide is a basic oxide and sulfur dioxide is an acidic oxide, so they react (neutralise) to form a salt.
parts.working: CaO basic B1; SO₂ acidic, so neutralisation B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Powdered calcium carbonate can be used instead. Suggest one advantage of using calcium carbonate.
parts.answer: It is cheap and plentiful (limestone), and is safer to handle than calcium oxide.

practice.stem: During winter, Lahore often has thick smog. Measurements show high levels of particulates and oxides of nitrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two sources of the particulates.
parts.answer: Any two of: diesel vehicle exhausts; burning crop stubble; brick kilns/industry burning coal or waste; burning rubbish.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why smog is harmful to people.
parts.answer: Particulates and NOₓ irritate the lungs and cause or worsen respiratory problems such as asthma.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions that would reduce smog.
parts.answer: Any two of: use catalytic converters; more public transport/electric vehicles; stop crop burning; cleaner kilns/filters on factory chimneys; low-sulfur fuels.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which gas in car exhaust is NOT removed by a catalytic converter?
A carbon dioxide
B carbon monoxide
C nitrogen monoxide
D unburned hydrocarbons
parts.answer: A carbon dioxide
parts.working: The converter changes CO, NO and unburned hydrocarbons into CO₂, N₂ and H₂O, so it removes B, C and D but actually produces more carbon dioxide. CO is removed by oxidation to CO₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pollutant is correctly matched with one of its adverse effects?
A carbon monoxide – acid rain
B methane – toxic because it combines with haemoglobin
C sulfur dioxide – acid rain
D particulates – depletion of oxygen in rivers
parts.answer: C sulfur dioxide – acid rain
parts.working: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain. Carbon monoxide is toxic (it combines with haemoglobin) but does not cause acid rain; methane is a greenhouse gas; particulates cause respiratory problems and cancer.

practice.stem: In winter, some families in northern Pakistan heat their rooms with charcoal stoves (angeethi) with the windows closed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why burning charcoal indoors with poor ventilation produces carbon monoxide.
parts.answer: There is not enough oxygen, so combustion is incomplete.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the incomplete combustion of carbon to carbon monoxide.
parts.answer: 2C + O₂ → 2CO

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why carbon monoxide is toxic.
parts.answer: It combines with haemoglobin in the blood, so the blood carries less oxygen around the body.
parts.working: B1 haemoglobin; B1 reduces oxygen transport.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name one other pollutant produced by the stove and give one effect on health.
parts.answer: Particulates (soot); respiratory problems / lung disease / cancer.

practice.stem:
A brick kiln burns 1000 kg of coal that contains 1.6 % sulfur by mass. All the sulfur is converted to sulfur dioxide: S + O₂ → SO₂
[Ar: O, 16; S, 32; Ca, 40]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sulfur in the coal.
parts.answer: 16 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sulfur dioxide produced.
parts.answer: 32 kg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of calcium oxide needed to remove all of this sulfur dioxide (CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃).
parts.answer: 28 kg

practice.stem:
An air-quality monitor next to a busy road records the average concentration of carbon monoxide each day for one week.
Day | Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat | Sun
CO / µg per m³ | 1850 | 1920 | 1780 | 1890 | 2100 | 1150 | 860

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean concentration for Monday to Friday. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 1908 µg per m³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease from Friday to Sunday, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a reason for the lower values at the weekend.
parts.answer: Less traffic (fewer people driving to work/school).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why carbon monoxide is dangerous to health.
parts.answer: It is toxic: it reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When petrol (octane, C₈H₁₈) burns in a limited supply of air, carbon monoxide and water are formed. Write a balanced equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: 2C₈H₁₈ + 17O₂ → 16CO + 18H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a car engine running in a closed garage is particularly dangerous.
parts.answer: The oxygen in the garage gets used up, so combustion becomes more incomplete and more carbon monoxide forms; carbon monoxide is toxic and builds up in the closed space.
parts.working: Less oxygen → more incomplete combustion/CO B1; CO toxic and accumulates B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of octane.
parts.answer: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O

practice.stem:
Without a catalytic converter, a car engine releases 0.60 g of carbon monoxide per kilometre. In a catalytic converter carbon monoxide reacts with nitrogen monoxide:
2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂
[Ar: C, 12; N, 14; O, 16]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of carbon monoxide in 0.60 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of nitrogen monoxide that would react exactly with 0.60 g of carbon monoxide. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: With a working converter, 90 % of the carbon monoxide is removed. Calculate the mass of carbon monoxide emitted on a 25 km journey.
parts.working: M1 without converter 0.60 × 25 = 15 g; A1 10 % of 15 = 1.5 g.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Identify the reducing agent in the reaction and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide; it gains oxygen (is oxidised to CO₂) and removes oxygen from NO.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a chemical test for water, giving the result.
parts.answer: Add to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: it turns from white to blue. (Or: cobalt(II) chloride paper turns from blue to pink.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a physical test to show that a sample of water is pure.
parts.answer: Measure its boiling point (100 °C) or melting point (0 °C); pure water boils at exactly 100 °C / melts at exactly 0 °C.
parts.working: Measure boiling or melting point B1; correct value B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which stage of drinking-water treatment kills harmful microbes?
A chlorination
B filtration
C sedimentation
D treatment with carbon
parts.answer: A chlorination
parts.working: Chlorine kills bacteria and other microbes. Filtration removes insoluble particles but does not kill microbes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is used at a water works to remove unpleasant tastes and smells from water?
A carbon (activated charcoal)
B chlorine
C sand
D sodium chloride
parts.answer: A carbon (activated charcoal)
parts.working: Carbon adsorbs substances that cause tastes and odours. Chlorine kills microbes; sand filters out insoluble particles.

practice.stem:
These stages of treatment at a water works are in the wrong order:
chlorination, sedimentation, treatment with carbon, filtration

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put the stages in the correct order.
parts.answer: sedimentation → filtration → treatment with carbon → chlorination
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 if chlorination last but one other error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why filtration does not remove dissolved salts.
parts.answer: Dissolved substances pass through the filter (particles are far too small to be trapped).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why chlorination is done near the end of the process.
parts.answer: So the water stays free of microbes as it is piped to homes / chlorine kills microbes that remain.

practice.stem:
A student heats two water samples and records the temperature at which each boils steadily at normal atmospheric pressure.
Sample | boiling temperature / °C
A (from a laboratory still) | 100.0
B (from a well) | 101.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the boiling point of pure water at normal atmospheric pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the results to decide whether each sample is pure water. Explain.
parts.answer: Sample A is pure – it boils at 100 °C exactly; sample B is impure – it boils above 100 °C (dissolved substances raise the boiling point).
parts.working: B1 A pure; B1 B impure with reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a chemical test to show that sample B contains water, giving the result.
parts.answer: Add anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: white turns blue (or anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride: blue turns pink).

practice.stem: Water from the Indus is treated before it is supplied to homes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the purpose of each stage:
(i) sedimentation and filtration
(ii) treatment with carbon
(iii) chlorination
parts.answer: (i) remove insoluble solids (ii) remove tastes and odours (iii) kill microbes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Even after treatment, tap water is not pure water. Explain why.
parts.answer: It still contains dissolved substances (salts/minerals and some chlorine).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Water from natural sources contains many substances. Name two substances in river water that are beneficial and explain why.
parts.answer: Dissolved oxygen, which is needed by aquatic life; some mineral salts/metal compounds that provide essential minerals for life.
parts.working: Dissolved oxygen for fish/aquatic life B1; mineral salts as essential minerals B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name three substances found in polluted water that are harmful, and give one effect of one of them.
parts.answer: Any three of: some metal compounds (toxic); plastics (harm wildlife); sewage (contains harmful microbes, causes disease); harmful microbes; nitrates/phosphates from fertilisers (deoxygenation, damage to aquatic life). Effect e.g. sewage microbes cause diseases such as cholera.
parts.working: Any three harmful substances B2 (two B1); one correct effect B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Excess nitrate fertiliser washes from farmland into a lake. Describe how this can lead to the death of fish.
parts.answer: Nitrates cause rapid growth of algae (algal bloom) on the surface; algae block light so plants below die; algae and plants die and are decomposed by bacteria; the bacteria use up dissolved oxygen, so fish die (deoxygenation).
parts.working: Algae grow rapidly B1; plants/algae die B1; bacteria decompose them using oxygen B1; less dissolved oxygen so fish die B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one other type of compound from fertilisers or detergents that causes the same problem.
parts.answer: phosphates

practice.stem: Leather tanneries in some industrial towns release waste water containing chromium compounds into nearby drains and rivers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why metal compounds in river water are harmful.
parts.answer: Many are toxic; they poison fish/aquatic life and can harm people who drink the water or eat the fish.
parts.working: B1 toxic; B1 effect on organisms/people.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two other types of pollutant that may be found in river water near a city, and give one source of each.
parts.answer: Any two with sources, e.g. sewage – from homes (contains harmful microbes); plastics – litter (harm aquatic life); nitrates/phosphates – fertiliser run-off/detergents.
parts.working: B1 each pollutant; B1 each source.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing the amount of metal compounds reaching the river.
parts.answer: Treat the waste water at the tannery before release (e.g. precipitate the metal compounds and remove them).

practice.stem:
Water from a drain carrying fertiliser run-off enters a river at 0 m. The dissolved oxygen is measured at different distances downstream.
Distance downstream / m | 0 | 200 | 500 | 1000 | 2000
Dissolved oxygen / mg per dm³ | 8.5 | 7.9 | 4.2 | 2.1 | 6.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in dissolved oxygen downstream from the drain.
parts.answer: It falls from 8.5 to a minimum of 2.1 mg/dm³ at 1000 m, then rises again to 6.8 mg/dm³ at 2000 m.
parts.working: B1 fall; B1 then rise (with data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dissolved oxygen falls.
parts.answer: Nitrates cause rapid growth of algae (algal bloom); algae die and are decomposed by bacteria; the bacteria use up dissolved oxygen.
parts.working: B1 algal growth; B1 death and decomposition; B1 bacteria use oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why fish are rarely found at 1000 m.
parts.answer: There is too little oxygen for them to survive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why distilled water, rather than tap water, is used for preparing solutions in a chemistry laboratory.
parts.answer: Tap water contains dissolved substances (salts, chlorine); these could react with or contaminate the chemicals / affect results.
parts.working: B1 tap water impure; B1 interferes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two substances in natural water that are beneficial, and say why.
parts.answer: Dissolved oxygen – needed by aquatic life; minerals/metal ions such as calcium – needed for health (bones/teeth).

parts.label: c
parts.text: In some areas, ground water from tube wells contains arsenic compounds. Suggest why this water is not safe to drink even though it looks clear.
parts.answer: Arsenic compounds are dissolved (invisible) and toxic.

practice.stem:
A student evaporates 250 cm³ of a tap-water sample to dryness in a weighed evaporating basin.
Mass of empty basin = 52.316 g
Mass of basin + residue = 52.401 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of dissolved solids in the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of dissolved solids in g/dm³.
parts.answer: 0.34 g/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: The sample boils at 100.1 °C. Explain what this, and the residue, show about the water.
parts.answer: It is not pure; dissolved substances raise the boiling point and leave a residue.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a balance reading to 0.001 g is needed.
parts.answer: The mass of residue is very small, so a less precise balance would give a large percentage error.

practice.stem:
A student compares the dissolved solids in three water samples. She evaporates 100 cm³ of each sample to dryness in a weighed basin.
Sample | mass of empty basin / g | mass of basin + residue / g
river water | 45.210 | 45.262
tube-well water | 44.875 | 44.931
bottled water | 46.020 | 46.035

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of residue from each sample.
parts.answer: river 0.052 g; tube-well 0.056 g; bottled 0.015 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of dissolved solids in the tube-well water in g/dm³.
parts.answer: 0.56 g/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which sample contained the most dissolved solids? State one other test she should do before deciding that this water is unsafe to drink.
parts.answer: Tube-well water; e.g. test for harmful microbes / test for toxic metal compounds or nitrates (dissolved solids are not all harmful).
parts.working: Tube-well B1; sensible further test B1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat each sample and take a mean / use a larger volume of water.

practice.stem:
A water works serving a small town treats 12 000 m³ of water each day. It adds chlorine at a dose of 0.50 mg per dm³ of water.
[1 m³ = 1000 dm³. Ar: Cl, 35.5. One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chlorine, in kg, needed each day.
parts.answer: 6.0 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of chlorine molecules, Cl₂, in this mass. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 84.5 mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of this chlorine at r.t.p., in dm³, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2030 dm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why chlorine is added to drinking water.
parts.answer: To kill bacteria/microbes that cause disease.

practice.stem:
Analysis of a lake shows a phosphate concentration of 0.15 mg/dm³. The lake contains 2.4 × 10⁶ m³ of water.
[1 m³ = 1000 dm³]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of phosphate in the lake, in kg.
parts.answer: 360 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fertiliser run-off adds 40 kg of phosphate each month. Assuming no phosphate is removed, calculate the concentration after three months, in mg/dm³.
parts.answer: 0.20 mg/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why phosphate run-off can lead to the death of fish in the lake.
parts.answer: Phosphate causes rapid growth of algae; algae die and bacteria decompose them; bacteria use up dissolved oxygen so fish die.
parts.working: B1 algal bloom; B1 decomposition by bacteria; B1 oxygen depleted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two greenhouse gases.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide and methane

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each gas, state one human activity that increases its amount in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide: burning fossil fuels (or deforestation). Methane: livestock farming (cattle) / rice paddies / landfill waste decomposition.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
A combustion of wood
B photosynthesis
C respiration
D decomposition of dead leaves
parts.answer: B photosynthesis
parts.working: Green plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis to make glucose. Combustion, respiration and decomposition all release carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process adds methane to the atmosphere?
A digestion of food in cattle
B photosynthesis in crops
C combustion of coal in excess air
D dissolving of carbon dioxide in the oceans
parts.answer: A digestion of food in cattle
parts.working: Waste gases from digestion in animals such as cattle contain methane. Photosynthesis removes CO₂; complete combustion of coal gives CO₂, not methane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration of glucose.
parts.answer: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare this equation with the equation for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Photosynthesis is the reverse: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of each process on the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Respiration adds carbon dioxide; photosynthesis removes it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Sort these activities into those that increase and those that decrease the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere:
burning coal in a power station, planting trees, making lime from limestone, cutting down forests, photosynthesis by phytoplankton in the ocean
parts.answer: Increase: burning coal, making lime from limestone, cutting down forests. Decrease: planting trees, photosynthesis by phytoplankton.
parts.working: B3 all five correct; B2 four; B1 three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation that shows why heating limestone releases carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how greenhouse gases cause the Earth's surface to warm up.
parts.answer: Thermal energy from the Sun warms the Earth's surface, which emits infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb this infrared radiation; they re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the Earth, so less escapes to space and the surface warms.
parts.working: Earth's surface emits infrared/thermal energy B1; greenhouse gases absorb it B1; re-emit it back towards Earth (less escapes to space) B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two possible effects of climate change.
parts.answer: Any two of: rising sea levels; melting glaciers/ice caps; more frequent floods, droughts or heatwaves; changes in crop yields; loss of habitats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation and the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
parts.answer:
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
parts.working: Word equation B1; balanced symbol equation B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two processes in the carbon cycle that return carbon dioxide to the air.
parts.answer: respiration and combustion (also decomposition)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how cutting down large areas of forest affects the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Fewer trees carry out photosynthesis, so less CO₂ is removed (and burning or decay of the trees releases CO₂), so the amount increases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three ways a country could reduce its emissions of carbon dioxide and methane.
parts.answer: Any three of: use renewable energy (solar, wind, hydroelectric) instead of fossil fuels; increase use of hydrogen as a fuel; plant trees; reduce livestock farming; reduce waste in landfill; improve public transport/energy efficiency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using electric cars charged from coal-fired power stations does little to reduce carbon dioxide emissions.
parts.answer: The coal burned in the power station still produces carbon dioxide.

practice.stem: Measurements of atmospheric carbon dioxide in the Northern Hemisphere show the concentration falls every summer and rises every winter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the concentration falls each summer.
parts.answer: Plants grow fast and photosynthesise more in summer (more light, leaves on trees); more CO₂ is removed than is released.
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis increases; B1 removal greater than release.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the concentration rises each winter.
parts.answer: Less photosynthesis, while respiration/decay and burning of fuels for heating continue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Despite these ups and downs, the yearly average keeps rising. Give the main reason.
parts.answer: Increasing combustion of fossil fuels (and deforestation).

practice.stem: In many villages in Punjab, cow dung is put into biogas digesters. The methane produced is burned for cooking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the complete combustion of methane.
parts.answer: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why burning the methane from the dung is better for the climate than letting it escape into the air.
parts.answer: Methane is a more powerful greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide; burning it changes it into CO₂ (and gives useful energy instead of wood or other fuels).
parts.working: B1 methane stronger greenhouse gas; B1 converted to CO₂ / replaces other fuels.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how greenhouse gases warm the Earth.
parts.answer: They absorb thermal (infrared) energy radiated from the Earth's surface and re-emit it, so heat is kept in the atmosphere.
parts.working: B1 absorb infrared/thermal energy from Earth; B1 re-emit/trap it, reducing heat loss to space.

practice.stem:
Two identical sealed plastic bottles are placed 30 cm from a lamp. Bottle 1 contains air. Bottle 2 contains air enriched with carbon dioxide. The temperature inside each is recorded.
Time / min | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10
Bottle 1 (air) / °C | 22.0 | 23.1 | 24.0 | 24.7 | 25.2 | 25.5
Bottle 2 (CO₂-enriched) / °C | 22.0 | 23.6 | 25.0 | 26.1 | 26.9 | 27.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise in each bottle after 10 minutes.
parts.answer: air: 3.5 °C; carbon dioxide-enriched: 5.4 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the results suggest about carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide traps more heat / is a greenhouse gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept the same for this to be a fair test.
parts.answer: Any two: size of bottles; distance from lamp; starting temperature; position of thermometer; same lamp.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why this model does not fully represent the atmosphere.
parts.answer: The concentration of CO₂ used is far higher than in the air / the atmosphere is not a sealed container / no Earth surface radiating.

practice.stem:
A household uses natural gas (methane) for cooking. In one month it burns 1.6 kg of methane.
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
[Ar: H, 1; C, 12; O, 16. One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced.
parts.answer: 4.4 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of this carbon dioxide at r.t.p., in dm³.
parts.answer: 2400 dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Methane that leaks without burning is also a problem. Explain why.
parts.answer: Methane is a greenhouse gas (stronger than carbon dioxide), so leaks add to global warming.

practice.stem:
The table shows the average concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, measured at a remote observatory.
Year | 1960 | 1980 | 2000 | 2020
CO₂ / parts per million (ppm) | 317 | 339 | 370 | 414

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average increase per year between 1960 and 1980, and between 2000 and 2020.
parts.answer: 1.1 ppm per year; 2.2 ppm per year

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average increase per year over the whole period 1960–2020, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.62 ppm per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the trend and suggest a reason for it.
parts.answer: The concentration increases, and the rate of increase is getting faster; more fossil fuels are burned (more energy use, vehicles, industry) and more deforestation.
parts.working: Increasing at an increasing rate B1; reason B1

practice.stem:
A small car uses 6.0 dm³ of petrol to travel 100 km. Treat petrol as pure octane, C₈H₁₈, with a density of 0.75 kg/dm³.
[Mr: C₈H₁₈ = 114; CO₂ = 44]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of octane burned per 100 km, in g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of octane, C₈H₁₈.
parts.answer: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced per kilometre. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 139 g per km

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing carbon dioxide emissions from road transport.
parts.answer: Use more efficient/smaller engines, public transport, or electric vehicles charged from renewable electricity.

practice.stem:
Data for two fuels:
Fuel | equation for complete combustion | energy released / kJ per mole of fuel
methane | CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O | 890
octane | C₈H₁₈ + 12½O₂ → 8CO₂ + 9H₂O | 5470
[Mr: CO₂ = 44]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide released per 1000 kJ (1 MJ) of energy for each fuel. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: methane 49.4 g; octane 64.4 g
parts.working: M1 methane: 1 mol CO₂ (44 g) per 890 kJ; A1 44 × 1000/890 = 49.4 g; M1 octane: 8 mol CO₂ (352 g) per 5470 kJ; A1 352 × 1000/5470 = 64.4 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to suggest why switching power stations from oil to natural gas reduces carbon dioxide emissions.
parts.answer: Natural gas (methane) releases less CO₂ for the same amount of energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why burning natural gas still contributes to climate change.
parts.answer: It still produces carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas (and leaks release methane).

parts.label: a
parts.text: NPK fertilisers provide three elements needed for plant growth. Name the three elements.
parts.answer: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one compound used in fertilisers to provide nitrogen.
parts.answer: ammonium nitrate (or ammonium sulfate / ammonium phosphate / potassium nitrate)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why farmers add fertilisers to their fields.
parts.answer: To replace elements removed by crops and improve plant growth / crop yield.

practice.stem: A wheat crop in a field near Faisalabad grows slowly and has pale yellow leaves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest which element the crop is probably short of.
parts.answer: nitrogen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two compounds that could supply this element.
parts.answer: Any two: ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulfate, urea, ammonium phosphate, potassium nitrate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name a compound that supplies potassium.
parts.answer: potassium chloride (or potassium sulfate / potassium nitrate)

practice.stem: Ammonium sulfate can be made in the laboratory by titration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the acid and alkali used to make ammonium sulfate.
parts.answer: sulfuric acid and ammonia (aqueous ammonia)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a titration is used to make this salt.
