parts.answer: Both reactants are soluble (in solution), so exact amounts must be mixed to avoid an excess of either.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the acid and the alkali that react to make each fertiliser:
(i) ammonium nitrate (ii) ammonium phosphate (iii) potassium sulfate
parts.answer: (i) nitric acid + ammonia (ii) phosphoric acid + ammonia (iii) sulfuric acid + potassium hydroxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which of these three fertilisers supplies two of the elements N, P and K?
parts.answer: ammonium phosphate

parts.label: a
parts.text:
From this list, choose the compounds that supply nitrogen to plants:
ammonium chloride, potassium chloride, urea, calcium carbonate, potassium nitrate
parts.answer: ammonium chloride, urea, potassium nitrate

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which compound in the list supplies both nitrogen and potassium?
parts.answer: potassium nitrate

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why crops grown in the same field year after year need fertilisers.
parts.answer: Each crop removes nitrogen/phosphorus/potassium from the soil; fertilisers replace these elements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which fertiliser a farmer should choose to supply the most nitrogen per kilogram.
parts.answer: ammonium nitrate

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative formula mass of diammonium phosphate, (NH₄)₂HPO₄.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of phosphorus to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a farmer might choose this fertiliser rather than ammonium nitrate.
parts.answer: It supplies two essential elements (N and P) instead of only N.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen and of potassium in potassium nitrate, KNO₃. Give each answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of potassium in a 25 kg bag of pure potassium nitrate, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the third main element in NPK fertilisers that potassium nitrate does not supply.
parts.answer: phosphorus

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why nitrate fertilisers are easily washed out of the soil by rain.
parts.answer: All nitrates are soluble in water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one environmental problem caused when these nitrates reach a lake.
parts.answer: Eutrophication: algae grow rapidly, then die and decompose; bacteria use up oxygen so fish die.
parts.working: B1 algal bloom; B1 oxygen loss / fish die.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways a farmer can reduce the amount of fertiliser washed into waterways.
parts.answer: Any two: apply only the amount needed; avoid spreading before heavy rain/irrigation; leave strips of plants beside ditches; use slow-release fertiliser.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ammonium sulfate contains 21.2 % nitrogen. Calculate the mass of ammonium sulfate that supplies the same mass of nitrogen as 100 kg of ammonium chloride, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 123 kg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a high percentage of nitrogen is an advantage when fertiliser is transported a long way.
parts.answer: Less mass needs to be transported for the same amount of nitrogen, so transport costs are lower.

practice.stem:
A farmer in Sahiwal compares two nitrogen fertilisers. (The prices are invented for this question.)
Fertiliser | formula | mass of bag | price of bag
urea | CO(NH₂)₂ | 50 kg | Rs 4800
ammonium nitrate | NH₄NO₃ | 50 kg | Rs 4200
[Ar: H, 1; C, 12; N, 14; O, 16]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of nitrogen in one bag of urea, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of 1 kg of nitrogen from each fertiliser, to the nearest rupee, and state which is better value.
parts.answer: urea Rs 206 per kg N; ammonium nitrate Rs 240 per kg N; urea is better value

parts.label: c
parts.text: The soil is also acidic. Explain why the farmer should not add lime at the same time as ammonium nitrate.
parts.answer: The base reacts with ammonium ions, releasing ammonia gas, so nitrogen is lost.

practice.stem: A farmer in Okara needs to add 120 kg of nitrogen per hectare to a cotton field of 2.5 hectares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total mass of nitrogen needed for the field.
parts.answer: 300 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ammonium nitrate contains 35 % nitrogen by mass. Calculate the mass of ammonium nitrate needed, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 857 kg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ammonium nitrate is sold in 50 kg bags. How many bags must the farmer buy?
parts.answer: 18 bags

parts.label: d
parts.text: Show that ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, contains 35 % nitrogen by mass. [Ar: H, 1; N, 14; O, 16]

practice.stem:
A fertiliser factory makes ammonium nitrate by reacting ammonia with nitric acid.
[Ar: H, 1; N, 14; O, 16. 1 tonne = 10⁶ g]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of ammonia with nitric acid.
parts.answer: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ammonium nitrate, in tonnes, made from 1.7 tonnes of ammonia.
parts.answer: 8.0 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the industrial process used to make the ammonia and give its raw materials.
parts.answer: Haber process; nitrogen (from air) and hydrogen (from methane/natural gas).

practice.stem:
A student tests a white fertiliser powder.
Test 1: warm with aqueous sodium hydroxide – a gas turns damp red litmus paper blue.
Test 2: dissolve in water, add dilute nitric acid, then aqueous barium nitrate – white precipitate.
Test 3: a fresh solution of the fertiliser is acidified with dilute nitric acid and tested with aqueous silver nitrate – no precipitate forms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the cation in the fertiliser. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Ammonium ion, NH₄⁺; ammonia gas is given off on warming with NaOH (turns damp red litmus blue).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the anion in the fertiliser.
parts.answer: sulfate, SO₄²⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the fertiliser.
parts.answer: ammonium sulfate

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the solution is acidified with nitric acid before barium nitrate is added in test 2.
parts.answer: To remove carbonate (or sulfite) ions, which would also give a white precipitate.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain what the result of test 3 shows about the anion.
parts.answer: No chloride ions are present: chloride ions would give a white precipitate of silver chloride.
parts.working: B1 no chloride ions (a white precipitate of silver chloride would form if chloride were present).

practice.stem:
2.00 g of an impure ammonium sulfate fertiliser is warmed with excess aqueous sodium hydroxide. All the ammonia is collected; its volume is 0.672 dm³ at r.t.p.
(NH₄)₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O
[Mr: (NH₄)₂SO₄ = 132. One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of ammonia given off.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of ammonium sulfate in the sample.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage purity of the fertiliser.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the approximate percentage by volume of nitrogen in clean, dry air?
A 21 %
B 50 %
C 78 %
D 99 %
parts.working: Clean dry air is about 78 % nitrogen and 21 % oxygen, with small amounts of argon and carbon dioxide. 21 % is the figure for oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the approximate percentage by volume of (i) argon and (ii) carbon dioxide in clean, dry air.
parts.answer: (i) about 0.9 % (ii) about 0.04 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the two gases that together make up about 99 % of clean, dry air.
parts.answer: nitrogen and oxygen

practice.stem: A classroom measures 8 m long, 6 m wide and 3 m high. It is filled with clean, dry air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the classroom in m³.
parts.answer: 144 m³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen in the room, in m³, to 3 significant figures. (Take oxygen as 21 % of air.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of nitrogen in the room, in m³, to 3 significant figures. (Take nitrogen as 78 % of air.)
parts.answer: 112 m³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test for oxygen, giving the result.
parts.answer: A glowing splint relights.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a test for carbon dioxide, giving the result.
parts.answer: Bubble through limewater; it turns milky (cloudy white).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student blows her breath through limewater and draws room air through a second tube of limewater for the same time. Predict which tube turns milky first and explain.
parts.answer: The breath tube; exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide (produced by respiration).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the gas in air that:
(i) is used in respiration
(ii) is used by plants in photosynthesis
(iii) is unreactive and used to fill packets of crisps
(iv) is a noble gas used in filament lamps and in welding
parts.answer: (i) oxygen (ii) carbon dioxide (iii) nitrogen (iv) argon

practice.stem:
100 cm³ of dry air is pushed backwards and forwards between two gas syringes over a tube of heated copper powder. The copper turns black. The apparatus is allowed to cool and the volume is measured. This is repeated until the volume stops changing.
Reading | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4
Volume of gas / cm³ | 85 | 80 | 79 | 79

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of copper with oxygen.
parts.answer: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the apparatus is cooled before each reading.
parts.answer: Gases expand when hot, so a hot gas would give a volume that is too large.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the main gas left in the syringe and one other gas present in small amounts.
parts.answer: nitrogen; argon (or carbon dioxide)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which list shows the gases in clean, dry air in order of decreasing percentage by volume?
A nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide
B nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, argon
C oxygen, nitrogen, argon, carbon dioxide
D nitrogen, argon, oxygen, carbon dioxide
parts.answer: A nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide
parts.working: Nitrogen about 78 %, oxygen about 21 %, argon about 0.9 %, carbon dioxide about 0.04 %. B is the common error of placing CO₂ above argon.

practice.stem: Damp iron wool is pushed to the top of a graduated tube. The tube is inverted in a trough of water, trapping 50.0 cm³ of air. After one week the volume of gas in the tube is 39.6 cm³ (measured at the same temperature and pressure).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen used.
parts.answer: 10.4 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the water level rises in the tube.
parts.answer: Iron rusts, using up oxygen from the trapped air; the gas volume decreases, so water is pushed up to take its place.
parts.working: B1 oxygen removed by rusting; B1 volume/pressure falls.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the iron wool is dampened.
parts.answer: Rusting needs water as well as oxygen.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest why the experiment is left for one week.
parts.answer: Rusting is slow; time is needed for all the oxygen to be used up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student burns a candle under an upturned jar standing in water. He says the rise of the water shows the percentage of oxygen in the air. Give two reasons why this method is inaccurate.
parts.answer: Any two: burning candle produces carbon dioxide (gas) which replaces some of the oxygen; the candle goes out before all the oxygen is used; heating expands the air so some escapes at the start.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a substance that can be heated in a measured volume of air to remove all the oxygen without producing another gas.
parts.answer: copper (or iron / phosphorus)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the main gas left when all the oxygen has been removed from air.
parts.answer: nitrogen

practice.stem: [Ar: O, 16. One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of oxygen molecules in 2.40 dm³ of dry air at r.t.p. (Take oxygen as 21 % of air.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of this oxygen, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the gas that makes up most of the rest of the sample.
parts.answer: nitrogen

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the composition of air is usually given for dry air.
parts.answer: The amount of water vapour varies a lot from place to place and day to day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the air in Karachi in August contains more water vapour than the air in Quetta in January.
parts.answer: Karachi is coastal and hot (more evaporation); Quetta in winter is cold and dry.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how you could show that ordinary air contains water vapour.
parts.answer: Cool a surface (e.g. a beaker of ice); collect the droplets that form and test them with anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (white → blue) or cobalt(II) chloride paper (blue → pink).
parts.working: B1 condense on cold surface; B1 chemical test with result.

practice.stem:
100.0 cm³ of air is passed repeatedly over excess heated copper until the volume stops changing. 21.0 cm³ of oxygen reacts.
2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO
[Ar: O, 16; Cu, 64. One mole of gas occupies 24 000 cm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of oxygen that react. Give your answer in standard form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of copper that reacts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the increase in mass of the solid in the tube.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the colour change seen in the tube.
parts.answer: pink-brown (orange) to black

practice.stem:
Air is separated into its main components by fractional distillation of liquid air.
Gas | boiling point / °C
nitrogen | −196
argon | −186
oxygen | −183

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why water vapour and carbon dioxide are removed before the air is cooled.
parts.answer: They would freeze/solidify at low temperature and block the pipes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The liquid air is then allowed to warm up slowly. Which gas boils off first? Explain.
parts.answer: Nitrogen; it has the lowest boiling point (−196 °C).
parts.working: B1 nitrogen; B1 lowest boiling point.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is difficult to obtain argon completely free of oxygen by this method.
parts.answer: Their boiling points are very close (−186 °C and −183 °C).

practice.stem: 100.0 cm³ of dried exhaled breath is passed through aqueous sodium hydroxide; its volume falls to 95.8 cm³. The gas is then passed over heated copper until all the oxygen has reacted; the volume falls to 79.8 cm³. All volumes are measured at r.t.p.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by volume of carbon dioxide and of oxygen in the dried exhaled air.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide 4.2 %; oxygen 16.0 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why aqueous sodium hydroxide removes carbon dioxide but not oxygen.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is an acidic oxide and reacts with the alkali; oxygen does not react.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the two main gases in the 79.8 cm³ that remain.
parts.answer: nitrogen and argon

parts.label: d
parts.text: Compare the percentages of carbon dioxide and oxygen with those in clean air and explain the differences.
parts.answer: Exhaled air has more CO₂ (4.2 % vs about 0.04 %) and less O₂ (16 % vs 21 %), because respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide.

practice.stem:
Magnesium ribbon burns in air to form magnesium oxide.
[Ar: Mg, 24. One mole of gas occupies 24 000 cm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen, in cm³ at r.t.p., needed to burn 0.36 g of magnesium completely.
parts.answer: 180 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the minimum volume of air needed, to 3 significant figures. (Take oxygen as 21 % of air.)
parts.answer: 857 cm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the magnesium might not burn completely in a sealed flask of 900 cm³ of air.
parts.answer: As oxygen is used up its concentration becomes too low for burning to continue / some magnesium reacts with nitrogen instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a reaction pathway diagram the products are at a lower energy than the reactants. What does this show?
A The reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.
B The reaction is endothermic and ΔH is positive.
C The reaction is exothermic and ΔH is positive.
D The reaction has no activation energy.
parts.answer: A The reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.
parts.working: Energy is released to the surroundings, so products are lower and ΔH is negative. C has the wrong sign: exothermic means ΔH < 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A catalyst is added to a reaction. What happens to the activation energy and to the enthalpy change, ΔH?
A activation energy decreases; ΔH stays the same
B activation energy decreases; ΔH decreases
C activation energy increases; ΔH stays the same
D activation energy stays the same; ΔH decreases
parts.answer: A activation energy decreases; ΔH stays the same
parts.working: A catalyst provides a pathway with lower activation energy; the energies of reactants and products do not change, so ΔH is unchanged. B wrongly suggests the catalyst changes ΔH.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by activation energy.
parts.answer: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The combustion of methane is exothermic. State whether ΔH is positive or negative and whether the products are above or below the reactants on its reaction pathway diagram.
parts.answer: ΔH is negative; the products are below the reactants.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a gas cooker needs a spark or flame to light it, even though the reaction is exothermic.
parts.answer: The spark supplies the activation energy needed to start the reaction (after that, energy released keeps it going).

practice.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram, the reactants are at 120 kJ/mol, the top of the energy 'hump' is at 310 kJ/mol and the products are at 40 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the forward reaction.
parts.answer: 190 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction and state whether it is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: ΔH = −80 kJ/mol; exothermic

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a reaction pathway diagram, what does the activation energy, Ea, represent?
A the energy difference between the reactants and the products
B the minimum energy that colliding particles need in order to react
C the energy given out when bonds form in the products
D the total energy of the products
parts.answer: B the minimum energy that colliding particles need in order to react
parts.working: Ea is measured from the reactants up to the top of the energy barrier: the minimum energy needed for a collision to be successful. A describes ΔH, not Ea.

practice.stem:
Magnesium ribbon reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid in a test-tube.
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: The temperature of the acid rises during the reaction. State whether ΔH is positive or negative.
parts.answer: negative

parts.label: b
parts.text: On the reaction pathway diagram, state whether the products are above or below the reactants.
parts.answer: below
parts.working: energy is released to the surroundings

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is shown by an arrow drawn from the reactants up to the highest point of the curve.
parts.answer: the activation energy

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what is shown by an arrow drawn from the reactants down to the products.
parts.answer: the enthalpy change, ΔH (energy released)

practice.stem: For reaction P, the reaction pathway diagram shows the reactants at 0 kJ/mol, the top of the energy barrier at +95 kJ/mol and the products at −285 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy.
parts.answer: 95 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔH and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: −285 kJ/mol; exothermic
parts.working: B1 value with sign; B1 exothermic

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the energy difference between the products and the top of the barrier.
parts.answer: 380 kJ/mol

practice.stem: For a thermal decomposition reaction, the reactants are at 0 kJ/mol, the top of the energy hump is at +250 kJ/mol and the products are at +90 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy and ΔH for the reaction without a catalyst.
parts.answer: activation energy 250 kJ/mol; ΔH = +90 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: With a catalyst the top of the hump is at +170 kJ/mol. Calculate the activation energy with the catalyst and state the value of ΔH with the catalyst.
parts.answer: 170 kJ/mol; ΔH = +90 kJ/mol (unchanged)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic? Give a reason.
parts.answer: Endothermic: the products have more energy than the reactants (ΔH positive).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen can be kept at room temperature without reacting, but it explodes when a spark is applied. Explain this using the idea of activation energy.
parts.answer: At room temperature too few colliding molecules have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so the rate is negligible. The spark gives molecules enough energy to exceed the activation energy; the energy released then supplies other molecules.
parts.working: B1 particles at room temperature do not have energy ≥ Ea; B1 spark supplies the activation energy (then the reaction sustains itself).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O and it is strongly exothermic. Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction. Say where reactants and products are and how ΔH and the activation energy are shown.
parts.answer: Reactants (2H₂ + O₂) on the left at a higher level; a curve rising to a peak then falling to products (2H₂O) at a lower level. Activation energy: arrow from reactants up to the peak. ΔH: arrow from reactants down to products (negative).
parts.working: B1 products below reactants; B1 Ea from reactant level to top of curve; B1 ΔH arrow from reactants down to products.

practice.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. ΔH = −98 kJ per mole of H₂O₂. The activation energy is 75 kJ/mol without a catalyst and 58 kJ/mol with manganese(IV) oxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the decrease in activation energy caused by the catalyst.
parts.answer: 17 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of ΔH for the catalysed reaction.
parts.answer: −98 kJ/mol
parts.working: B1 a catalyst does not change ΔH.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles and energy, why the catalysed reaction is faster.
parts.answer: With a lower activation energy, a larger fraction of colliding particles have energy equal to or above the activation energy, so there are more successful collisions per second.
parts.working: B1 more particles have energy ≥ Ea; B1 more successful collisions per unit time.

practice.stem: Lime kilns near Rohri in Sindh heat limestone to make quicklime.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calcium carbonate is decomposed in a lime kiln: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, ΔH = +178 kJ/mol. Describe the reaction pathway diagram you would draw for this reaction, including how each label is placed.
parts.answer: Energy axis upward; reactant level CaCO₃ lower, product level CaO + CO₂ higher; curve from reactants rising to a peak above the product level, then down to products; activation energy shown by an arrow from reactants to the peak; ΔH (+178 kJ/mol) shown by an upward arrow from reactants to products.
parts.working: B1 products higher than reactants; B1 curve with a peak above both levels; B1 Ea arrow reactants → peak; B1 ΔH arrow reactants → products, labelled positive / +178.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the kiln must be heated strongly all the time, not just to start the reaction.
parts.answer: The reaction is endothermic: it takes in energy continuously, so heat must be supplied throughout.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a reaction pathway diagram the reactants are at 80 kJ/mol, the top of the energy barrier is at 200 kJ/mol and the products are at 140 kJ/mol. Which row is correct?
A Ea = 200 kJ/mol; ΔH = +60 kJ/mol
B Ea = 120 kJ/mol; ΔH = +60 kJ/mol
C Ea = 120 kJ/mol; ΔH = −60 kJ/mol
D Ea = 60 kJ/mol; ΔH = +120 kJ/mol
parts.answer: B Ea = 120 kJ/mol; ΔH = +60 kJ/mol
parts.working: Ea = 200 − 80 = 120 kJ/mol; ΔH = 140 − 80 = +60 kJ/mol (products higher, endothermic). C has the wrong sign; A measures Ea from zero instead of from the reactants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a match does not catch fire on its own at room temperature, even though burning is exothermic.
parts.answer: the reactants need energy to overcome the activation energy; at room temperature few/no particles have enough energy

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why striking the match starts the reaction.
parts.answer: friction supplies (heat) energy to reach the activation energy

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the match continues to burn after it has been lit.
parts.answer: the reaction is exothermic; the energy released provides the activation energy for more of the reactants

practice.stem:
A catalytic converter in a car exhaust removes carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide.
2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂   ΔH = −746 kJ
Without a catalyst the activation energy is 250 kJ/mol; on the catalyst surface it is 120 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the decrease in activation energy caused by the catalyst.
parts.answer: 130 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of ΔH for the catalysed reaction. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: −746 kJ (per equation as written); a catalyst does not change the energies of the reactants or products

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the catalysed pathway differs from the uncatalysed pathway on the same diagram.
parts.answer: the curve has a lower peak; reactants and products at the same levels

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the catalyst makes the reaction faster.
parts.answer: provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy; a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to react

practice.stem: Compound D decomposes. ΔH = +40 kJ/mol. The activation energy is 210 kJ/mol without a catalyst. The activation energies with three catalysts are: X 140 kJ/mol; Y 95 kJ/mol; Z 160 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which catalyst is the most effective? Give a reason.
parts.answer: Y; it gives the lowest activation energy

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in activation energy when catalyst Y is used, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of ΔH when catalyst Z is used. Explain.
parts.answer: +40 kJ/mol; catalysts do not change ΔH

practice.stem: A reversible reaction has a forward activation energy of 160 kJ/mol and ΔH = −45 kJ/mol for the forward reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy for the reverse reaction.
parts.answer: 205 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 the peak is 160 kJ/mol above reactants and products are 45 kJ/mol below reactants; A1 160 + 45 = 205.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State ΔH for the reverse reaction.
parts.answer: +45 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: A catalyst lowers the forward activation energy to 110 kJ/mol. Calculate the new activation energy for the reverse reaction.
parts.answer: 155 kJ/mol
parts.working: B1 110 + 45 = 155 (a catalyst lowers both by the same amount).

practice.stem: The energy profile of a reaction shows: reactants at 50 kJ/mol, the peak at 300 kJ/mol and products at 230 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the forward reaction.
parts.answer: +180 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the forward reaction and of the reverse reaction.
parts.answer: forward 250 kJ/mol; reverse 70 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: In this reaction, is more energy taken in when bonds break or given out when bonds form? Explain.
parts.answer: More energy is taken in to break bonds than is released when new bonds form, because ΔH is positive (endothermic).
parts.working: B1 bond breaking > bond making; B1 linked to positive ΔH / endothermic.

practice.stem:
Data for two reactions:
Reaction A: activation energy 30 kJ/mol, ΔH = −20 kJ/mol
Reaction B: activation energy 180 kJ/mol, ΔH = −400 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which reaction would you expect to be faster at room temperature? Explain.
parts.answer: Reaction A: its activation energy (30 kJ/mol) is much lower, so many more colliding particles have enough energy to react.
parts.working: B1 A; B1 lower Ea → greater proportion of collisions successful.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which reaction releases more energy per mole? Calculate how many times more.
parts.answer: Reaction B; 20 times more

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says: 'Reaction B has a very negative ΔH, so it must be very fast.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: The statement is wrong. ΔH only tells how much energy is released overall; rate depends on the activation energy. B has a high activation energy, so it is slow at room temperature even though it is very exothermic.
parts.working: B1 ΔH does not determine rate; B1 rate depends on Ea, which is high for B.

practice.stem: An endothermic reaction has ΔH = +60 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student claims that the activation energy of this reaction is 40 kJ/mol. Explain why this cannot be correct.
parts.answer: the products are 60 kJ/mol above the reactants; the top of the barrier must be higher than the products, so Ea must be greater than 60 kJ/mol
parts.working: B1 products 60 above; B1 Ea > ΔH

parts.label: b
parts.text: The true activation energy is 135 kJ/mol. Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
parts.answer: 75 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction, including labels for Ea and ΔH.
parts.answer: products drawn higher than reactants; curve rises to a peak; Ea arrow from reactants to peak; ΔH arrow from reactants up to products (labelled +60)
parts.working: B1 relative levels; B1 both arrows correctly placed

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using the idea of activation energy, why raising the temperature increases the rate of reaction.
parts.answer: particles have more kinetic energy; more collide more often; a greater proportion of collisions have energy ≥ Ea

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate in a different way from raising the temperature.
parts.answer: a catalyst lowers the activation energy (alternative pathway) rather than giving the particles more energy; so more of the existing collisions are successful

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one economic advantage of using a catalyst in an industrial process.
parts.answer: lower temperature can be used, saving energy/fuel costs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process is endothermic?
A burning petrol in a car engine
B dissolving ammonium nitrate in water
C adding dilute hydrochloric acid to sodium hydroxide solution
D the rusting of iron
parts.answer: B dissolving ammonium nitrate in water
parts.working: Dissolving ammonium nitrate takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature falls (used in cold packs). Neutralisation (C) gives out heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an exothermic reaction and by an endothermic reaction.
parts.answer: Exothermic: transfers thermal energy to the surroundings (temperature of surroundings rises). Endothermic: takes in thermal energy from the surroundings (temperature falls).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Classify each process as exothermic or endothermic:
(i) burning natural gas in a stove
(ii) photosynthesis in leaves
(iii) thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
(iv) magnesium reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid
parts.answer: (i) exothermic (ii) endothermic (iii) endothermic (iv) exothermic

practice.stem:
A student mixes 25 cm³ of four different pairs of solutions, A–D, in a polystyrene cup and records the temperatures.
reaction: initial temperature / final temperature (°C)
A: 22.0 / 31.5
B: 22.5 / 16.0
C: 21.0 / 21.5
D: 23.0 / 35.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature change for each reaction. Use + for a rise and − for a fall.
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which reaction is endothermic? Give a reason.
parts.answer: B, because the temperature fell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which reaction is the most exothermic? Give a reason.
parts.answer: D, because it has the largest temperature rise.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student used the same volume of solution each time.
parts.answer: To make it a fair test: the same volume means temperature changes can be compared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cold pack for sports injuries contains solid ammonium nitrate and a separate bag of water. When the pack is squeezed the solid dissolves and the pack gets cold. Explain why it gets cold.
parts.answer: Dissolving ammonium nitrate is endothermic; it takes in thermal energy from the surroundings (the pack and the skin), so the temperature falls.
parts.working: B1 endothermic; B1 energy taken in from surroundings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A self-heating hand warmer works by the slow oxidation of iron powder. State whether this reaction is exothermic or endothermic and state the sign of ΔH.
parts.answer: Exothermic; ΔH is negative.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process is exothermic?
A melting ice
B electrolysis of molten sodium chloride
C respiration in cells
D thermal decomposition of copper(II) carbonate
parts.answer: C respiration in cells
parts.working: Respiration releases energy (ΔH negative). Melting, electrolysis and thermal decomposition all need a continuous energy input, so they are endothermic.

practice.stem: Citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate are mixed with water in a fizzy sweet. The temperature of the mixture falls from 23 °C to 17 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: endothermic

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sign of ΔH.
parts.answer: positive

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mixture feels cold to the hand.
parts.answer: energy (heat) is taken in from the surroundings, including the hand

practice.stem: Some self-heating food cans have a compartment containing calcium oxide. When water is added, the can gets hot.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and the sign of ΔH.
parts.answer: exothermic; negative

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain where the energy that warms the food comes from.
parts.answer: it is released by the chemical reaction to the surroundings (the food)

practice.stem: Changes of state involve energy changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each change as exothermic or endothermic: (i) boiling water; (ii) steam condensing on a cold window; (iii) water freezing; (iv) solid iodine turning to gas when warmed.
parts.answer: (i) endothermic (ii) exothermic (iii) exothermic (iv) endothermic

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why melting is endothermic.
parts.answer: energy is needed to overcome the forces of attraction between particles

practice.stem:
A student adds aqueous sodium hydroxide, 5 cm³ at a time, to 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup with a lid and records the highest temperature after each addition.
volume of NaOH added / cm³: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35
temperature / °C: 24.0, 27.1, 30.0, 32.8, 35.2, 35.0, 34.1, 33.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the maximum temperature rise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the results to estimate the volume of sodium hydroxide that exactly neutralises the acid.
parts.answer: about 20 cm³ (where the temperature is highest)
parts.working: B1 20 cm³ (accept 20–22 cm³ from the highest temperature).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the temperature falls after 20 cm³ of alkali has been added.
parts.answer: The acid has all reacted, so no more heat is released; adding more (cooler) alkali cools the mixture, and heat is lost to the surroundings.
parts.working: B1 reaction complete / no more energy released; B1 cooler solution added / heat loss.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a polystyrene cup with a lid is used rather than a glass beaker.
parts.answer: Polystyrene is a good insulator and the lid reduces heat loss, so the temperature rise measured is more accurate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether bond breaking and bond making are exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: Bond breaking is endothermic; bond making is exothermic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The burning of hydrogen is exothermic. Explain this in terms of the energy changes when bonds are broken and made.
parts.answer: The energy released when the new O–H bonds form is greater than the energy taken in to break the H–H and O=O bonds.
parts.working: B1 energy released forming bonds; B1 greater than energy absorbed breaking bonds.

practice.stem:
A student adds 1.0 g of a powdered metal to 25 cm³ of aqueous copper(II) sulfate in an insulated cup. The starting temperature is 20.0 °C each time.
metal: highest temperature / °C
magnesium: 58.5
zinc: 31.0
iron: 26.5
silver: 20.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise for each metal.
parts.answer: magnesium 38.5 °C; zinc 11.0 °C; iron 6.5 °C; silver 0.0 °C
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the results to put the four metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first.
parts.answer: magnesium > zinc > iron > silver

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why there was no temperature change with silver.
parts.answer: Silver is less reactive than copper, so it does not displace copper and no reaction occurs.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one variable, other than the volume of solution, that must be kept the same.
parts.answer: Mass of metal / particle size (powder) / concentration of copper(II) sulfate / starting temperature.

practice.stem:
Many homes in Pakistan use LPG cylinders containing propane.
C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O   ΔH = −2220 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when 11 kg of propane burns completely. [Mr: C₃H₈, 44]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of propane, in g, that must burn to release 44 400 kJ.

practice.stem: A reusable hand warmer contains a solution of sodium ethanoate and a small metal disc.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When the disc is clicked, sodium ethanoate crystallises and the pack becomes warm. State whether crystallisation is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: exothermic

parts.label: b
parts.text: The pack is reset by placing it in boiling water until all the crystals dissolve. State whether this process is exothermic or endothermic and explain.
parts.answer: endothermic; energy is taken in from the hot water

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of this hand warmer over a single-use one based on iron rusting.
parts.answer: it can be reused many times

practice.stem:
A student adds excess zinc powder to 25 cm³ of aqueous copper(II) sulfate of different concentrations in a polystyrene cup and records the temperature rise.
concentration / mol/dm³: temperature rise / °C
0.25: 6.4
0.50: 12.9
0.75: 19.1
1.00: 25.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the concentration of copper(II) sulfate and the temperature rise.
parts.answer: temperature rise is (directly) proportional to concentration (doubling concentration doubles the rise)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the temperature rise with 0.60 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate.
parts.answer: about 15.4 °C

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why zinc is used in excess.
parts.answer: so that all the copper(II) sulfate reacts / zinc is not the limiting reactant

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why powdered zinc is better than zinc granules.
parts.answer: reaction is faster, so less heat is lost before the maximum temperature is reached

practice.stem: A student dissolves 5.0 g of potassium nitrate in 50 cm³ of water in a polystyrene cup. The temperature falls from 21.5 °C to 15.3 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature change with 5.0 g of potassium nitrate.
parts.answer: −6.2 °C (a fall of 6.2 °C)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the temperature change is proportional to the mass dissolved in the same volume of water, predict the final temperature when 10.0 g is dissolved, starting at 21.5 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In practice the measured fall with 10.0 g was smaller than predicted. Suggest one reason.
parts.answer: Heat is absorbed from the surroundings during the experiment (more time to dissolve), or not all the solid dissolved.

practice.stem:
A student compares two liquid fuels by heating 200 cm³ of water in a copper can with a spirit burner.
fuel: mass burned / g, temperature rise / °C
X: 0.92, 18.4
Y: 1.25, 30.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise per gram of fuel burned for each fuel.
parts.answer: fuel X: 20.0 °C per g; fuel Y: 24.0 °C per g
parts.working: M1 rise ÷ mass; A1 both values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which fuel releases more energy per gram? Explain.
parts.answer: Fuel Y, because it gives the larger temperature rise per gram for the same mass of water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why the results are lower than the true values, and suggest one improvement.
parts.answer: Heat lost to the air and to the can; incomplete combustion (soot on the can); some heat warms the can not the water. Improvement: shield the flame from draughts / put a lid on the can / keep the flame close to the can.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sources of error; 1 mark for a matching improvement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complete combustion of methane has ΔH = −890 kJ/mol. Calculate the energy released when 4.0 g of methane is burned. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: 2NH₃ → N₂ + 3H₂, ΔH = +92 kJ (for 2 mol of ammonia). Calculate the energy needed to decompose 3.4 g of ammonia. (Ar: N = 14, H = 1)
parts.answer: 9.2 kJ
parts.working: M1 Mr NH₃ = 17, moles = 0.20; M1 energy per mol NH₃ = 46 kJ; A1 0.20 × 46 = 9.2 kJ.

practice.stem:
Enthalpy changes of combustion:
hydrogen, H₂ (Mr 2): ΔH = −286 kJ/mol
methane, CH₄ (Mr 16): ΔH = −890 kJ/mol
octane, C₈H₁₈ (Mr 114): ΔH = −5470 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per gram for each fuel. Give answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: hydrogen 143 kJ/g; methane 55.6 kJ/g; octane 48.0 kJ/g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrogen releases the most energy per gram. Give two disadvantages of hydrogen as a fuel for cars.
parts.answer: difficult to store (gas, needs high pressure/large tanks); explosive/flammable risk; few filling stations; often made using fossil fuels

practice.stem:
Quicklime is made in lime kilns.
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂   ΔH = +178 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to decompose 1.00 tonne (1.00 × 10⁶ g) of calcium carbonate. [Mr: CaCO₃, 100]

parts.label: b
parts.text: The kiln is heated by burning methane, ΔH = −890 kJ/mol. Only 60% of the energy released reaches the limestone. Calculate the mass of methane, in kg, needed per tonne of calcium carbonate. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. [Mr: CH₄, 16]

practice.stem: Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂   ΔH = +2800 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy absorbed when a plant makes 9.0 g of glucose. [Mr: C₆H₁₂O₆, 180]
parts.answer: 140 kJ

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy absorbed to make 1.0 kg of glucose. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the source of this energy and explain why respiration is exothermic.
parts.answer: sunlight (light energy); respiration is the reverse of photosynthesis, so the energy stored is released (ΔH = −2800 kJ/mol)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431.
What is the enthalpy change for this reaction?
A −184 kJ/mol
B +184 kJ/mol
C +247 kJ/mol
D −862 kJ/mol
parts.answer: A −184 kJ/mol
parts.working: Bonds broken 436 + 242 = 678; bonds made 2 × 431 = 862; ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol. B has the wrong sign (made − broken); C uses only one H–Cl bond.

practice.stem:
H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr
Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Br–Br 193, H–Br 366

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants.
parts.answer: 629 kJ

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when the bonds in the products form.
parts.answer: 732 kJ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction and state whether it is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: −103 kJ/mol; exothermic

practice.stem:
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy released when the bonds in the products form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the combustion of methane.
parts.answer: −818 kJ/mol

practice.stem:
Methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight.
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–H 413; Cl–Cl 242; C–Cl 346; H–Cl 431

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants.
parts.answer: 655 kJ

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when the new bonds form.
parts.answer: 777 kJ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate ΔH and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: −122 kJ/mol; exothermic

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to break all the bonds in 1 mol of ammonia, NH₃. [N–H 391 kJ/mol]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to break all the bonds in 1 mol of water, H₂O. [O–H 464 kJ/mol]
parts.answer: 928 kJ

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether bond breaking is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: endothermic

practice.stem:
In car engines nitrogen and oxygen react to form nitrogen monoxide.
N₂ + O₂ → 2NO
Bond energies in kJ/mol: N≡N 945; O=O 498; N=O 630

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction.
parts.answer: +183 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: endothermic

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this reaction happens inside a hot car engine but not in the air around us.
parts.answer: the high temperature supplies the energy needed (to break the strong N≡N bond / overcome activation energy)

practice.stem:
Ammonia is made by the Haber process, for example at the fertiliser plants in Pakistan.
Bond energies in kJ/mol: N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–H 391

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.
parts.answer: −93 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy change when 1 mole of ammonia is formed.
parts.answer: −46.5 kJ/mol

practice.stem: Bond energies in kJ/mol: C=C 612, C–C 347, C–H 413, H–H 436

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the reaction C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆, which bonds are broken and which bonds are made? (You may ignore bonds that are present on both sides.)
parts.answer: Broken: C=C and H–H. Made: C–C and two C–H bonds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction.
parts.answer: −125 kJ/mol

practice.stem: Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, O=O 498, O–H 464

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
parts.answer: −486 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per mole of hydrogen burned.
parts.answer: 243 kJ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hydrogen is used as a fuel in some buses. Give one advantage of hydrogen as a fuel.
parts.answer: The only product is water (no carbon dioxide).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
F₂ + H₂ → 2HF
Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436; F–F 158; H–F 565.
What is the enthalpy change for this reaction?
A −536 kJ/mol
B +536 kJ/mol
C −594 kJ/mol
D −1130 kJ/mol
parts.answer: A −536 kJ/mol
parts.working: Bonds broken: 436 + 158 = 594; bonds made: 2 × 565 = 1130; ΔH = 594 − 1130 = −536 kJ/mol. B reverses the sign; C ignores the bonds made; D ignores the bonds broken.

practice.stem:
Ethene reacts with hydrogen to form ethane.
C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C=C 612; C–H 413; C–C 347; H–H 436

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants.
parts.working: C=C 612 + 4 × C–H 413 + H–H 436 = 2700 (B1 for the correct bonds counted; B1 total)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy released when the bonds in the product form.
parts.working: C–C 347 + 6 × C–H 413 = 2825 (B1 for six C–H and one C–C; B1 total)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction and state whether it is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: −125 kJ/mol; exothermic

practice.stem:
Ethene reacts with bromine.
C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C=C 612; C–C 347; Br–Br 193; C–Br 290

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which bonds are broken and which bonds are made in this reaction (ignore C–H bonds, which are unchanged).
parts.answer: broken: C=C and Br–Br; made: C–C and two C–Br

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction.
parts.answer: −122 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is seen when ethene is bubbled into bromine water.
parts.answer: orange/brown colour disappears (decolourised)

practice.stem:
C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–C 347; C–H 413; O=O 498; C=O 805; O–H 464

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the complete combustion of propane.
parts.answer: −2054 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when 1.00 kg of propane burns, to 3 significant figures. [Mr: C₃H₈, 44]

practice.stem:
H₂ + F₂ → 2HF   ΔH = −542 kJ/mol
Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, H–F 568

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the bond energy of the F–F bond.
parts.answer: 158 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to explain why fluorine is very reactive.
parts.answer: The F–F bond is weak (needs little energy to break), and strong bonds form in the products.

practice.stem: Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–H 413, C–C 347, C–O 358, O–H 464, O=O 498, C=O 805

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the bonds broken in one molecule of ethanol, C₂H₅OH.
parts.answer: 5 C–H, 1 C–C, 1 C–O, 1 O–H
parts.working: B1 all four types with correct numbers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the complete combustion of ethanol: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
parts.answer: −1276 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: The data-book value is −1367 kJ/mol. Suggest why the value calculated from bond energies is different.
parts.answer: Bond energies are average values from many compounds (and the data assume all substances are gases).

practice.stem: Bond energies in kJ/mol: O–H 464, O–O 146, O=O 498

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. Each H₂O₂ molecule has the structure H–O–O–H. Calculate ΔH for the equation as written.
parts.answer: −206 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that, in this reaction, the only bonds that really change are two O–O single bonds broken and one O=O double bond made, and that this gives the same answer.
parts.answer: The four O–H bonds are present on both sides and cancel. ΔH = 2 × 146 − 498 = −206 kJ/mol.

practice.stem:
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃   ΔH = −93 kJ/mol
Bond energies in kJ/mol: N≡N 945; H–H 436

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy of the bonds broken in the reactants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use ΔH to calculate the total energy released when the bonds in 2 mol of ammonia form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the bond energy of the N–H bond.
parts.answer: 391 kJ/mol

practice.stem:
Hydrazine, H₂N–NH₂, is used as a rocket fuel.
N₂H₄ + O₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O
Bond energies in kJ/mol: N–H 391; O=O 498; N≡N 945; O–H 464

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an expression for ΔH in terms of x, the N–N bond energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ΔH is −580 kJ/mol. Calculate the N–N bond energy.
parts.answer: 159 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this reaction is useful for powering spacecraft thrusters.
parts.answer: it is very exothermic and produces gases (that push the craft)

practice.stem:
Methanol is tested as a fuel for small generators.
2CH₃OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 4H₂O
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–H 413; C–O 358; O–H 464; O=O 498; C=O 805

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the equation as written.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per mole and per gram of methanol, to 3 significant figures. [Mr: CH₃OH, 32]
parts.answer: 658 kJ/mol; 20.6 kJ/g

practice.stem:
Ammonia is being tested as a carbon-free fuel for ships.
4NH₃ + 3O₂ → 2N₂ + 6H₂O
Bond energies in kJ/mol: N–H 391; O=O 498; N≡N 945; O–H 464

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the equation as written.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per mole of ammonia.
parts.answer: 318 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one environmental advantage of ammonia over fuel oil for ships.
parts.answer: no carbon dioxide is produced (contains no carbon)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property is typical of transition elements?
A low density
B they form coloured compounds
C low melting points
D they react vigorously with cold water
parts.answer: B they form coloured compounds
parts.working: Transition elements form coloured compounds (and have high densities and melting points). D describes Group I metals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the melting points and densities of iron and sodium.
parts.answer: Iron has a much higher melting point and a much higher density than sodium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which iron or its compounds are used as a catalyst.
parts.answer: Iron is the catalyst in the Haber process for making ammonia.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour of a solution of a typical copper(II) compound, such as copper(II) sulfate.
parts.answer: blue

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two properties of copper that make it suitable for electrical wiring in homes.
parts.answer: good electrical conductor; ductile (can be drawn into wires)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Copper is a transition element. State one physical property, other than conductivity, that copper has in common with other transition elements.
parts.answer: high density (or high melting point)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Copper roofs on old buildings turn green. Suggest what this shows about copper compounds.
parts.answer: Copper forms coloured compounds.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property is shown by transition elements but NOT by Group I metals?
A They conduct electricity.
B They have a shiny surface when freshly cut.
C They have high densities.
D They form positive ions.
parts.answer: C They have high densities.
parts.working: Transition elements are dense (e.g. iron about 7.9 g/cm³) while Group I metals have low densities (lithium, sodium and potassium float on water). A, B and D are true of all metals, so they do not distinguish the two groups.

practice.stem: A student is given three solutions labelled P, Q and R: aqueous copper(II) sulfate, aqueous iron(II) sulfate and aqueous sodium sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which two solutions are coloured.
parts.answer: copper(II) sulfate and iron(II) sulfate

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these two solutions are coloured but the third is not.
parts.answer: copper and iron are transition elements, which form coloured compounds; sodium is a Group I metal and its compounds are white/colourless

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour of aqueous copper(II) sulfate.
parts.answer: blue

practice.stem:
Data for two metals:
nickel: melting point 1455 °C, density 8.9 g/cm³
potassium: melting point 63 °C, density 0.86 g/cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to give two differences in physical properties between nickel and potassium.
parts.answer: nickel has a much higher melting point; nickel has a much higher density

parts.label: b
parts.text: Nickel is used as a catalyst when vegetable oils are hardened with hydrogen to make vanaspati ghee. State what is meant by a catalyst.
parts.answer: a substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged (chemically) at the end

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one other transition element, or its compound, used as an industrial catalyst and name the process.
parts.answer: iron in the Haber process (or vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Iron forms two chlorides, FeCl₂ and FeCl₃. Give the oxidation number of iron in each.
parts.answer: +2 in FeCl₂; +3 in FeCl₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name FeCl₃ using an oxidation number.
parts.answer: iron(III) chloride

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test with aqueous sodium hydroxide that distinguishes solutions of the two chlorides. Give both results.
parts.answer: FeCl₂ gives a green precipitate; FeCl₃ gives a red-brown precipitate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the property of transition elements shown by iron forming both chlorides.
parts.answer: They have variable oxidation numbers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the catalyst used in the Contact process and give the oxidation number of vanadium in it.
parts.answer: vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅; +5

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why transition elements and their compounds are useful in industry as catalysts.
parts.answer: They speed up reactions (by providing a lower activation energy route) without being used up, so less energy/lower temperatures are needed and costs are reduced.
parts.working: B1 increase rate / lower activation energy; B1 not used up / saves energy or cost

practice.stem:
The table gives some properties of four metals, J, K, L and M.
J: melting point 98 °C; density 0.97 g/cm³; compounds white
K: melting point 1538 °C; density 7.87 g/cm³; compounds green or red-brown
L: melting point 650 °C; density 1.74 g/cm³; compounds white
M: melting point 1085 °C; density 8.96 g/cm³; compounds blue or green

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which two elements are most likely to be transition elements? Give two pieces of evidence from the table.
parts.answer: K and M; they have high melting points, high densities and coloured compounds.
parts.working: B1 K and M; B2 any two pieces of evidence

parts.label: b
parts.text: Element J reacts rapidly with cold water. Suggest which group J is in.
parts.answer: Group I

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of the transition element in: (i) TiCl₄ (ii) CoCl₂ (iii) MnSO₄ (iv) Cu₂O.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name TiCl₄ and Cu₂O using oxidation numbers.
parts.answer: titanium(IV) chloride; copper(I) oxide

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Roman numerals are used in the names of many transition element compounds but not in the name sodium chloride.
parts.answer: transition elements have variable oxidation numbers; sodium only forms +1

practice.stem:
A student adds 0.5 g of different powdered solids to 20 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide solution and measures the volume of oxygen given off in 60 s.
solid: volume of oxygen in 60 s / cm³
none: 1
magnesium oxide: 1
iron(III) oxide: 18
copper(II) oxide: 30
manganese(IV) oxide: 72

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which solid was the most effective catalyst?
parts.answer: manganese(IV) oxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: What do the three most effective solids have in common?
parts.answer: they are oxides of transition elements

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the student could show that manganese(IV) oxide is not used up in the reaction.
parts.answer: weigh the solid before; filter, wash and dry it after the reaction and reweigh; mass is unchanged
parts.working: B1 weigh before and after; B1 filter/dry

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the same mass of each powder was used.
parts.answer: to make it a fair test (surface area/amount affects the rate)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of manganese in MnO₂ and in KMnO₄.
parts.answer: +4 and +7

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₃ and in K₂Cr₂O₇.
parts.answer: +3 and +6

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to state a property that manganese and chromium share with other transition elements.
parts.answer: variable oxidation numbers (form ions/compounds with different oxidation numbers)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name manganese(IV) oxide's role when it is added to hydrogen peroxide.
parts.answer: catalyst

practice.stem:
Chromium is extracted by heating chromium(III) oxide with aluminium powder.
Cr₂O₃ + 2Al → Al₂O₃ + 2Cr   [Ar: O, 16; Cr, 52]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₃ and in Cr.
parts.answer: +3 and 0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether chromium(III) oxide is oxidised or reduced in this reaction.
parts.answer: Reduced: it loses oxygen / chromium's oxidation number decreases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chromium formed from 76 g of chromium(III) oxide.
parts.working: Mr Cr₂O₃ = 152; moles = 0.50 M1; Cr = 1.0 mol × 52 = 52 g A1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Chromium is used to plate steel taps. Suggest two reasons.
parts.answer: It resists corrosion; it is hard / shiny and attractive.

practice.stem: Chlorine is bubbled into pale green aqueous iron(II) chloride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: 2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour change of the solution.
parts.answer: pale green to yellow/orange-brown

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of electrons, which species is oxidised.
parts.answer: iron(II) ions are oxidised; each Fe²⁺ loses one electron to become Fe³⁺
parts.working: B1 Fe²⁺ oxidised; B1 loses electrons

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how aqueous sodium hydroxide could show that the reaction has happened. Give the results before and after.
parts.answer: before: green precipitate; after: red-brown precipitate

practice.stem: 1.12 g of iron is heated in chlorine and combines with 2.13 g of chlorine. [Ar: Cl, 35.5; Fe, 56]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of iron atoms and of chlorine atoms in the sample.
parts.answer: Fe 0.0200 mol; Cl 0.0600 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the formula of the chloride and the oxidation number of iron in it.
parts.answer: FeCl₃; +3

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second chloride of iron has the formula FeCl₂. Calculate the mass of chlorine that combines with 1.12 g of iron in FeCl₂.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the property of transition elements that is shown by iron forming two chlorides.
parts.answer: variable oxidation number

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which halogen is a red-brown liquid at room temperature?
A fluorine
B chlorine
C bromine
D iodine
parts.answer: C bromine
parts.working: Bromine is a red-brown liquid. Chlorine (B) is a pale yellow-green gas; iodine is a grey-black solid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the colour and state of the halogens change from chlorine to iodine.
parts.answer: Colour gets darker (pale yellow-green → red-brown → grey-black); state changes from gas to liquid to solid.
parts.working: B1 colour darker; B1 gas → liquid → solid

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chlorine is added to the water supply in cities such as Lahore. State why.
parts.answer: To kill bacteria (sterilise the water).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the reactivity of the halogens changes down the group.
parts.answer: It decreases.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which trend is seen going down Group VII from chlorine to iodine?
A The colour becomes lighter.
B The melting point increases.
C The reactivity increases.
D The state changes from solid to gas.
parts.answer: B The melting point increases.
parts.working: Melting and boiling points increase down the group (chlorine gas, bromine liquid, iodine solid). C is wrong because reactivity decreases down Group VII; A and D are the reverse of the true trends.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of electrons in the outer shell of a halogen atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why chlorine, bromine and iodine have similar chemical properties.
parts.answer: they have the same number of outer-shell electrons (7)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Halogens exist as diatomic molecules. Write the formula of a bromine molecule.
parts.answer: Br₂

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write the formula of (i) the compound of iodine with hydrogen and (ii) the compound of chlorine with calcium.
parts.answer: (i) HI (ii) CaCl₂

practice.stem:
melting point and boiling point of the halogens (°C):
fluorine: −220, −188
chlorine: −101, −34
bromine: ?, 59
iodine: 114, 184

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict a melting point for bromine.
parts.answer: any value between −101 °C and 59 °C, e.g. about −10 °C (actual −7 °C)
parts.working: B1 below 25 °C and above −101 °C, and below its boiling point

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the physical state of each halogen at 25 °C.
parts.answer: fluorine gas; chlorine gas; bromine liquid; iodine solid
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark for three

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the trend in boiling point down the group.
parts.answer: increases

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the colour of chlorine gas.
parts.answer: pale green / yellow-green

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mixture of aqueous solutions reacts to form a new halogen?
A iodine + potassium chloride
B bromine + potassium chloride
C chlorine + potassium bromide
D iodine + potassium bromide
parts.answer: C chlorine + potassium bromide
parts.working: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its halide: chlorine displaces bromine. In A, B and D the halogen is less reactive than the halide's halogen, so no reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen when chlorine water is added to colourless aqueous potassium bromide.
parts.answer: The solution turns orange (yellow-orange).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why there is no reaction when bromine water is added to aqueous potassium chloride.
parts.answer: Bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot displace chlorine from chloride ions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State which species is oxidised in (b).
parts.answer: bromide ions, Br⁻

practice.stem: Astatine, At, is below iodine in Group VII.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the state and colour of astatine at room temperature.
parts.answer: solid; black

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether astatine will react with aqueous potassium iodide. Explain.
parts.answer: No; astatine is less reactive than iodine because reactivity decreases down Group VII.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the formula of the compound formed between sodium and astatine.
parts.answer: NaAt

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Aqueous bromine is added to aqueous sodium iodide. Which row is correct?
A colour change: orange to brown; equation: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂
B colour change: none; equation: no reaction
C colour change: orange to colourless; equation: I₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2I⁻ + Br₂
D colour change: brown to orange; equation: Br₂ + 2Na⁺ → 2NaBr
parts.answer: A colour change: orange to brown; equation: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂
parts.working: Bromine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces iodine; the solution turns brown as iodine forms. B would be true for bromine + chloride; C has the reverse reaction.

practice.stem:
Two bottles contain solutions of halogens in water, X and Y. Each is added to aqueous potassium chloride, potassium bromide and potassium iodide.
X: no change with KCl; turns orange with KBr; turns brown with KI
Y: no change with KCl; no change with KBr; turns brown with KI

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the halogen in X and in Y.
parts.answer: X chlorine; Y bromine

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Y reacts with potassium iodide but not with potassium chloride.
parts.answer: bromine is more reactive than iodine so displaces it; bromine is less reactive than chlorine so cannot displace it

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of X with potassium bromide.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the oxidising agent in the reaction Cl₂ + 2NaI → 2NaCl + I₂.
parts.answer: chlorine

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of electron transfer, why this is a redox reaction.
parts.answer: iodide ions lose electrons (oxidised); chlorine gains electrons (reduced)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the change that happens to the iodide ions, showing electrons.
parts.answer: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻

practice.stem:
A student adds aqueous solutions of halogens to aqueous solutions of potassium halides and records whether the colour changes.
chlorine + potassium bromide: ?
bromine + potassium iodide: ?
iodine + potassium bromide: ?
chlorine + potassium iodide: brown colour

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the result for each blank: (i) chlorine with potassium bromide; (ii) bromine with potassium iodide; (iii) iodine with potassium bromide.
parts.answer: (i) orange/yellow-brown colour – bromine formed; (ii) brown colour – iodine formed; (iii) no reaction

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the results to put chlorine, bromine and iodine in order of reactivity, most reactive first.
parts.answer: chlorine > bromine > iodine

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for reaction (ii).
parts.answer: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂

practice.stem: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂   [Ar: Cl, 35.5; I, 127]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iodine formed when 0.710 g of chlorine reacts with excess aqueous potassium iodide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fluorine is at the top of Group VII. Predict how its reactivity compares with chlorine and suggest why it is not used in school experiments.
parts.answer: More reactive than chlorine; it is extremely reactive / toxic and dangerous.

practice.stem: A water treatment plant serving a city adds chlorine at a dose of 2.0 mg per dm³ of water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chlorine, in kg, needed for 5.0 × 10⁶ dm³ of water.
parts.answer: 10 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of Cl₂ in this mass, to 3 significant figures. [Ar: Cl, 35.5]
parts.answer: 141 mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why chlorine is added to drinking water.
parts.answer: to kill bacteria/microbes (sterilise)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the dose is kept small.
parts.answer: chlorine is toxic / gives a taste or smell

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why fluorine is more reactive than chlorine.
parts.answer: a fluorine atom is smaller / has fewer shells; the outer shell is closer to the nucleus (less shielding); so an incoming electron is attracted more strongly / more easily gained

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether iodine will react with aqueous potassium bromide. Give a reason and, if there is a reaction, write the ionic equation.
parts.answer: no reaction; iodine is less reactive than bromine, so it cannot displace bromide ions
parts.working: B1 no reaction, with the reason (iodine is less reactive than bromine, so it cannot displace Br⁻); B1 no equation is written because there is no reaction

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An element is in Group III and Period 3 of the Periodic Table. What is its electronic configuration?
A 2,3
B 2,8,3
C 2,3,8
D 2,8,8,3
parts.working: Period 3 = three occupied shells; Group III = three outer electrons: 2,8,3 (aluminium). A has only two shells (Period 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An element has the electronic configuration 2,8,6. State its group and period, and name it.
parts.answer: Group VI; Period 3; sulfur

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the group number of an element is related to its electronic configuration.
parts.answer: Group number = number of electrons in the outer shell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the period number is related to its electronic configuration.
parts.answer: Period number = number of occupied electron shells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Elements in the same group of the Periodic Table have the same
A number of electron shells.
B number of outer-shell electrons.
C number of neutrons.
D mass number.
parts.answer: B number of outer-shell electrons.
parts.working: The group number equals the number of outer-shell electrons. A describes elements in the same period.

practice.stem: The elements of Period 2 are lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine and neon (proton numbers 3 to 10).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which element forms an ion with a 1+ charge?
parts.answer: lithium
parts.working: Li forms Li⁺ (Group I atom loses one electron). Be forms Be²⁺, B forms B³⁺, O forms O²⁻ and F forms F⁻, so only lithium gives 1+.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which element is a noble gas?
parts.answer: neon

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which element forms an ion with a 2− charge?
parts.answer: oxygen

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which element is in Group IV? Give its electronic configuration.
parts.answer: carbon; 2,4

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How does the nature of the oxides of the elements change across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine?
A acidic to basic
B basic to acidic
C basic to neutral
D they are all basic
parts.answer: B basic to acidic
parts.working: Metal oxides on the left (Na₂O, MgO) are basic; non-metal oxides on the right (SO₂, P₄O₁₀) are acidic. A reverses the trend.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify sodium, silicon and chlorine as metal, metalloid-like (semi-metal) or non-metal, and describe the trend in metallic character across a period.
parts.answer: sodium metal; silicon non-metal with some metallic properties (semi-metal); chlorine non-metal; metallic character decreases from left to right.
parts.working: B1 classification; B1 silicon; B1 decreases across

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how metallic character changes down Group IV, from carbon to lead.
parts.answer: It increases (carbon non-metal, tin and lead metals).

practice.stem: Melting points of the Period 3 elements (°C): Na 98, Mg 650, Al 660, Si 1410, P 44, S 115, Cl −101, Ar −189.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the element with the highest melting point and explain it in terms of structure.
parts.answer: Silicon; it has a giant covalent structure; many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.
parts.working: B1 silicon; B1 giant covalent; B1 many strong bonds broken

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why chlorine has a low melting point.
parts.answer: It is made of simple molecules (Cl₂); only weak forces between molecules need to be overcome.
parts.working: B1 simple molecular; B1 weak intermolecular forces

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which elements in the table are solids at 100 °C?
parts.answer: magnesium, aluminium, silicon and sulfur

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An element has proton number 20. Where is it in the Periodic Table?
A Group II, Period 4
B Group IV, Period 2
C Group II, Period 3
D Group VIII, Period 2
parts.answer: A Group II, Period 4
parts.working: Electronic configuration 2,8,8,2: 2 outer electrons (Group II) and 4 shells (Period 4). C counts only three shells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the property used to put the elements in order in the modern Periodic Table.
parts.answer: proton (atomic) number

parts.label: b
parts.text: Argon (relative atomic mass 39.9) comes before potassium (relative atomic mass 39.1). Explain why.
parts.answer: argon has proton number 18 and potassium 19; argon has the properties of a noble gas and potassium of a Group I metal

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the properties of elements change across a period.
parts.answer: from metallic to non-metallic

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each oxide as basic, amphoteric or acidic: sodium oxide, aluminium oxide, sulfur dioxide.
parts.answer: sodium oxide basic; aluminium oxide amphoteric; sulfur dioxide acidic

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one reaction that shows aluminium oxide is amphoteric.
parts.answer: it reacts with both acids (e.g. HCl) and with alkalis (e.g. NaOH)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Link the type of oxide to the position of the element in Period 3.
parts.answer: metals on the left form basic oxides; non-metals on the right form acidic oxides

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formulae of the chlorides of sodium, magnesium and aluminium.
parts.answer: NaCl, MgCl₂, AlCl₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the pattern in the number of chlorine atoms per atom of the element from sodium to silicon (SiCl₄).
parts.answer: it increases by one for each group (equal to the group number / valency 1, 2, 3, 4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Germanium is below silicon in Group IV. Predict the formula of germanium chloride.
parts.answer: GeCl₄

parts.label: a
parts.text: Strontium is in Group II, Period 5. Predict (i) the formula of strontium chloride, (ii) whether strontium oxide is acidic or basic, (iii) how its reactivity compares with that of magnesium.
parts.answer: (i) SrCl₂; (ii) basic; (iii) more reactive than magnesium

parts.label: b
parts.text: Selenium is in Group VI, below sulfur. Predict the formula of its hydride and the type of oxide it forms.
parts.answer: H₂Se; acidic oxide

parts.label: a
parts.text: Element Q forms an ion Q²⁻ that has 18 electrons. Identify Q and give its group.
parts.answer: sulfur; Group VI
parts.working: atom has 16 electrons → S B1; Group VI B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Element R forms an ion R³⁺ that has 10 electrons. Identify R.
parts.answer: aluminium

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the formula of the compound formed between R and Q.
parts.answer: Al₂S₃

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain, in terms of their positions, why R and Q form an ionic compound.
parts.answer: R is a metal on the left of the period and loses electrons; Q is a non-metal on the right and gains electrons.
parts.working: B1 R metal loses e⁻; B1 Q non-metal gains e⁻

practice.stem: Element E is in Group III and Period 4 of the Periodic Table.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of outer-shell electrons and the number of occupied electron shells in an atom of E.
parts.answer: 3 outer electrons; 4 shells

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether E is a metal or a non-metal. Give a reason.
